q: P'ang Te killed Kuo Yüan with his own hand in the battle at P'ing-yang. According to P'ei Sung-chih's commentary, how was Kuo Yüan related to Chung Yao? And how did Chung Yao react when he saw the head — what did he say?
reply:
**Conclusion:** According to Pei Songzhi's commentary (quoting the *Weilüe*), Guo Yuan was Zhong Yao's **nephew — his sister's son** (外甥). When Zhong Yao saw the head, he **wept**; Pang De apologized to him, and Zhong Yao replied that although Guo Yuan was his nephew, he was a traitor to the state, so there was no need to apologize.

**Evidence (from the commentary):**

Pei Songzhi's note to the *Pang De* biography, citing the *Weilüe*:

「德手斬一級，不知是援。戰罷之後，眾人皆言援死而不得其首。援，鍾繇之甥。德晚後於鞬中出一頭，繇見之而哭。德謝繇，繇曰：『援雖我甥，乃國賊也。卿何謝之？』」[2]

In English: Pang De cut off a head with his own hand, not knowing it was Guo Yuan's. After the battle, everyone said Guo Yuan was dead but his head could not be found. Guo Yuan was Zhong Yao's nephew (外甥, sister's son). Later Pang De took a head out of his quiver; when Zhong Yao saw it, he wept. Pang De apologized to Zhong Yao, and Zhong Yao said: "Although Guo Yuan was my nephew, he was a traitor to the state. Why should you apologize?"

**Supporting context from the main text:** The *Pang De* biography records that Pang De served as the vanguard against Guo Yuan and Gao Gan at Pingyang and broke them, 「親斬援首」[1] ("personally cut off Guo Yuan's head"). The *Zhong Yao* biography likewise records the same battle, ending 「大破之，斬援，降單于」[3].

Note the nuance: the main text says Pang De personally beheaded Guo Yuan, while the *Weilüe* note says he cut off a head without knowing it was Guo Yuan's and only produced it later from his quiver. These are complementary rather than contradictory — the note supplies the detail that Pang De did not recognize the head at the time.

q: At Sun Hao's banquets, what was the minimum amount of wine every guest had to drink? Wei Yao could barely hold his liquor — how did Sun Hao accommodate him in the early days?
reply:
**Answer**

At Sun Hao's banquets the minimum was **seven *sheng* (升) of wine per guest**, regardless of whether the person could actually drink. Wei Yao (韦曜, originally named Wei Zhao 韦昭, changed to avoid the Jin taboo) could normally drink no more than two *sheng*. In the early period, while he was still treated with special favor, Sun Hao would **reduce the quota for him, and sometimes secretly give him tea (茶荈) to drink in place of wine**. Once Wei Yao fell out of favor, however, he was pressed harder and punished for not complying.

**Evidence**

On the seven-*sheng* minimum and Wei Yao's two-*sheng* capacity, with Sun Hao's early accommodation:

「皓每饗宴，無不竟日，坐席無能否率以七升為限，雖不悉入口，皆澆灌取盡。曜素飲酒不過二升，初見禮異時，常為裁減，或密賜茶荈以當酒，至於寵衰，更見逼強，輒以為罪。」[1]

(In Chen Shou's text: every banquet of Sun Hao's lasted all day; at the seats, able or not, all were limited to seven *sheng* — and even if they could not get it all down, it was poured down their throats. Wei Yao normally drank no more than two *sheng*; when he was first treated with special courtesy, [Sun Hao] often had it reduced for him, or secretly gave him tea to serve as wine; but when his favor waned, he was forced harder, and it was treated as a crime.)

That this was Sun Hao's general practice — getting the whole company drunk, with attendants posted to report faults — is stated in the *Annals of the Three Last Rulers*:

「初，皓每宴會羣臣，無不咸令沈醉。」[2]

(Initially, whenever Sun Hao feasted his assembled ministers, he had them all made dead drunk.)

For context on the danger of these drinking bouts, Wang Fan was executed at one such banquet: at a great assembly in the second year of Ganlu, 「蕃沈醉頓伏……皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之」[8] (Wang Fan, dead drunk, collapsed; Sun Hao flew into a rage and shouted to his attendants to behead him below the hall).

Wei Yao's name itself: 裴松之按 records 「曜本名昭，史爲晉諱，改之」[13] — his original name was Zhao; the histories changed it to avoid the Jin taboo.

**Inference**

Putting the two passages together, the seven-*sheng* limit applied to every guest without exception, so Wei Yao's own tolerance of about two *sheng* was far below it. The text itself distinguishes two phases: while he enjoyed favor, Sun Hao lowered the amount for him or substituted tea; after his favor declined, the accommodation stopped and his inability to drink became a charge against him. This fits the broader pattern in which these banquets functioned as occasions to catch and punish ministers' faults [2].

q: When Gao Rou submitted a memorial opposing the ban on commoners hunting deer, how many deer did he estimate the tigers in the imperial preserves were eating each year? How many tigers did he reckon the preserves held?
reply:
## 结论

据裴注引《魏名臣奏》所载高柔的奏疏:

- 他估算皇家禁苑(禁地)里共有大小老虎 **六百头**（「有虎大小六百頭」）[4]；
- 这些老虎每年吃掉的鹿,他估算为 **七万二千头**（「一虎一歲百二十鹿，是為六百頭虎一歲食七萬二千頭鹿也」）[4]。

## 依据

《三国志·魏书·韩崔高孙王传》正文记,当时「殺禁地鹿者身死，財產沒官，有能覺告者厚加賞賜」,高柔因此上疏,主张放宽禁令、让百姓捕鹿[5]。裴松之注引《魏名臣奏》保存了他另一篇（或同一篇的详算部分）奏疏,原文如下:

「今禁地廣輪且千餘里，臣下計無慮其中有虎大小六百頭，狼有五百頭，狐萬頭。使大虎一頭三日食一鹿，一虎一歲百二十鹿，是為六百頭虎一歲食七萬二千頭鹿也。使十狼日共食一鹿，是為五百頭狼一歲共食萬八千頭鹿。鹿子始生，未能善走，使十狐一日共食一子，比至健走一月之間，是為萬狐一月共食鹿子三萬頭也。大凡一歲所食十二萬頭。其鵰鶚所害，臣置不計。」[4]

据此,他逐项算出的年损耗是:虎食鹿 7.2 万头,狼食鹿 1.8 万头,狐食幼鹿 3 万头,合计 **12 万头**;雕鹗所害还未计入[4]。

（另可注意:老虎的数量六百头出自裴注引《魏名臣奏》[4],陈寿正文只记其反对猎禁、请开民捕鹿的主张[5],未载这些数字。）

q: When I Chi went as an envoy to Wu, Sun Ch'üan deliberately asked him whether serving an unprincipled lord was tiring. How did I Chi reply?
reply:
## 结论

伊籍的回答是「一拜一起，未足為勞」[1]——只行一拜一起之礼，算不上辛苦。

## 依据

《三国志·蜀书·伊籍传》记载：

> 先主之在荊州，籍常往來自托。表卒，遂隨先主南渡江，從入益州。益州既定，以籍為左將軍從事中郎……遣東使于吳，孫權聞其才辨，欲逆折以辭。籍適入拜，權曰︰「勞事無道之君乎？」籍即對曰︰「一拜一起，未足為勞。」籍之機捷，類皆如此，權甚異之。[1]

白话大意：先主在荆州时，伊籍常来投托；刘表死后，伊籍随先主南渡长江、入益州。益州平定后，任伊籍为左将军从事中郎，派他出使吴国。孙权听说他有辩才，想用言辞迎头折挫他。伊籍刚进来行拜礼，孙权就说：「辛苦侍奉无道的君主吗？」伊籍立即回答：「一拜一起，不足以称辛苦。」伊籍的机敏便捷大多如此，孙权觉得他很不一般。[1]

## 推断

孙权这句话是把伊籍对刘备的君臣之礼曲解为「事无道之君」，伊籍不正面辩解、也不承认，只把「劳」字落在当下这一拜一起的礼节动作上，据此推断：他既回避了为刘备辩护而可能激怒孙权的风险，又在字面上「答其所问」，所以说这是「機捷」之对，无怪乎「權甚異之」[1]。

（以上是唯一一处记载伊籍此行的原文，别处未搜到相关异文。）

q: When Han Ji was in charge of iron smelting, what did he replace the horse-driven bellows with? By how much did output improve?
reply:
**Answer:** Han Ji (韓暨, courtesy name Gongzhi 公至) replaced the horse-driven bellows with a **water-driven bellows (水排)**, powered by a long-flowing stream, and the output was **three times what it had been before** ("三倍於前").

**Evidence (from the record):**

The original text says that in the old smelting works they used horse bellows ("馬排"), and every time one "stone" of iron was smelted, a hundred horses were needed; then they switched to human bellows ("人排"), which was also labor-intensive. Han Ji then built a water bellows using a long stream:

「舊時冶，作馬排，每一熟石用馬百匹；更作人排，又費功力；曁乃因長流為水排，計其利益，三倍於前。」[1]

English paraphrase: "Formerly in smelting they made horse bellows, and for each smelted stone of iron they used a hundred horses; then they made human bellows, which also cost much effort; Han Ji thereupon used the long-flowing stream to make water bellows, and reckoned its benefit to be three times the former." [1]

So: **horse bellows → water bellows (water-powered bellows, shuipai 水排), and output rose threefold.**

**Context:** The same passage notes he held the post for seven years, that tools and supplies became ample, and that an imperial edict commended him, promoting him on the spot to Colonel of Metals (司金都尉), ranked just below the Nine Ministers:

「在職七年，器用充實。制書襃歎，就加司金都尉，班亞九卿。」[1]

Before this, he had been made Inspector of Smelting (監冶謁者) after serving as Administrator of Leling, following Cao Cao's pacification of Jingzhou [1].

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载: 水排 is a water-powered bellows used in iron smelting, driven by a waterwheel to blow air into the furnace; the passage above is the record of its use by Han Ji.

q: What was the original surname of He Qi's family? Why did they change it to He?
reply:
**Short answer:** He Qi's (賀齊) family was originally surnamed **Qing (慶)**. They changed it to **He (賀)** to avoid the naming taboo on the personal name of Emperor An of Han's father, the "Xiaode Emperor" (孝德皇), whose name was 慶 (Qing).

**Evidence**

This is not in Chen Shou's main text; it comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary, quoting Yu Yu's *Jin Shu*:

> 「虞預《晉書》曰：賀氏本姓慶氏。齊伯父純，儒學有重名，漢安帝時為侍中、江夏太守，去官，與江夏黃瓊、廣漢楊厚俱公車徵。避安帝父孝德皇諱，改為賀氏。齊父輔，永寧長。」[1]

Pei's commentary citing Yu Yu's *Jin Shu* says: the He clan was originally the Qing clan. He Qi's uncle Qing Chun (慶純), famed for Confucian learning, served as Palace Attendant and Administrator of Jiangxia under Emperor An of Han; after leaving office he was summoned by public carriage together with Huang Qiong of Jiangxia and Yang Hou of Guanghan. To avoid the taboo on the name of Emperor An's father, the Xiaode Emperor, [the family] changed [its surname] to He. He Qi's father He Fu (賀輔) was Chief of Yongning.

**So the mechanism was a naming taboo (避諱):** Qing Chun's surname 慶 was the same character as the given name of Emperor An's father, so the family substituted the near-homophonous 賀 ("He").

**Following points of inference (my inference, not stated in the text):** Since the text ties the change to "Emperor An's time" (漢安帝時) and places Qing Chun's career in that reign, we can infer the change occurred during Emperor An's reign (roughly the late 100s CE), several generations before He Qi, who was active under Sun Ce and Sun Quan in the Jian'an era.

**Note on the source:** This account appears only in Pei Songzhi's commentary (裴注引虞預《晉書》), not in Chen Shou's main biography of He Qi, whose main text opens simply: 「賀齊字公苗，會稽山陰人也」[2].

q: Li Tien voluntarily moved his clan and retainers to Yeh. How many people did he move in total, and which Han-dynasty figure did Ts'ao Ts'ao tease him about?
reply:
**Answer**

Li Dian (Li Tien) moved **more than 13,000 people** — his retainers (*buqu*) and clan members — to Ye (Yeh). And Cao Cao (Ts'ao Ts'ao) teased him by asking whether he was trying to emulate **Geng Chun (耿純)**, a figure of the Han dynasty.

**Evidence**

The relevant passage records both the numbers and the joke. First, Li Dian's own request:

「典宗族部曲三千餘家，居乘氏，自請原徙詣魏郡。太祖笑曰：『卿欲慕耿純邪？』」[2]

*(Li Dian's clan and retainers numbered more than 3,000 households, living at Chengshi; he himself requested to move them to Wei commandery. Taizu [Cao Cao] laughed and said: "Do you wish to emulate Geng Chun?")* [2]

The outcome — how many actually moved:

「遂徙部曲宗族萬三千餘口居鄴。太祖嘉之，遷破虜將軍。」[1]

*(Thereupon he moved his retainers and clan, more than 13,000 persons, to live at Ye. Taizu commended him and promoted him to General Who Smashes the Caitiffs.)* [1]

So the source distinguishes the two figures: he petitioned on behalf of "more than 3,000 households" (三千餘家) [2], and the total actually relocated was "more than 13,000 persons" (萬三千餘口) [1].

As for the teasing, Cao Cao's remark is given as 「卿欲慕耿純邪？」[2] — a rhetorical question asking if Li Dian wanted to imitate Geng Chun. Li Dian's reply declines the comparison, saying he was merely doing his duty: 「典駑怯功微，而爵寵過厚，誠宜舉宗陳力……非慕純也。」[2]

**Note on Geng Chun**

The text only names him as 耿純; the Sanguozhi passage itself does not explain who he was or what he did. He appears here purely as the person Cao Cao invokes in his joke.

q: How old was Lü Tai when he died, and in which year did he die?
reply:
**Answer:** In the *Sanguozhi*, the Wu general who died at a great age is **Lü Dai (吕岱)**, not a "Lü Tai" — I could not find anyone named 吕泰 in the text. Lü Dai died in **Taiping 1 (太平元年)**, which the era tool converts to **256 CE**, at the age of **96**.

**Evidence**

The biography of Lü Dai states:

- 「太平元年，年九十六卒，子凱嗣。」[7] — "In Taiping 1 he died at the age of ninety-six; his son Lü Kai succeeded him."

The annals of Sun Liang corroborate the date and give a day within that year:

- 「己丑，大司馬呂岱卒。」[26] — Lü Dai was Grand Marshal (大司馬) at his death, in the ninth month of Taiping 1.

For the conversion, the era tool gives 太平1年 = 公元 256 年 (Sun Wu).

**Inference:** Since the biography says he was 96 at death in 256 CE, and it elsewhere notes 「時年已八十」 ("he was already eighty years old") when he was still serving actively [13], we can work out roughly that he was born around 160 CE — this is an inference from the recorded age, not a date given in the text.

If you meant someone else (for example the Shu official **Lü Kai 吕凯**, who was killed by rebelling Yi tribesmen and whose age at death is not recorded [25]), let me know and I'll look further.

q: When Liu Pei marched south from Chia-meng against Liu Chang, he left Huo Chün to hold the city. How long did Liu Chang's forces besiege it? How many soldiers did Huo Chün have, and how was the siege finally broken?
reply:
**Conclusion.** According to the *Huojun* biography in the *Shu Shu* of the *Sanguozhi*, Liu Zhang's commanders Fu Jin (扶禁) and Xiang Cun (向存) besieged Huo Jun (霍峻) at Jiameng for **nearly a year** without being able to take it. Huo Jun had **only a few hundred men** in the city. The siege was broken when he waited for the besiegers to slacken, picked out his best troops, sallied out, routed them, and cut off Xiang Cun's head on the spot.

**Evidence.**

- Liu Bei turned back south from Jiameng to attack Liu Zhang and left Huo Jun to hold the city:
  「先主自葭萌南還襲劉璋，留峻守葭萌城」[1]
- Zhang Lu first sent a general to lure him into handing over the city, and was refused:
  「張魯遣將楊帛誘峻，求共守城，峻曰：『小人頭可得，城不可得。』帛乃退去。」[1]
- The siege itself, its length, and the size of the garrison:
  「後璋將扶禁、向存等帥萬餘人由閬水上，攻圍攻峻，且一年，不能下。峻城中兵才數百人」[1]
- How it was broken:
  「伺其怠隙，選精銳出擊，大破之，即斬存首。」[1]

**Inference.** From these facts: the attacking force is given as over ten thousand (「萬餘人」) while the defenders were only a few hundred (「才數百人」), so Huo Jun was outnumbered by roughly twenty to one. Since the text says the besiegers could not reduce the city for nearly a year and that Huo Jun broke them only by a sortie at a moment of laxity, it follows that he did not win by superior numbers but by holding out and striking at a lapse — the point the biography's closing appraisal makes in calling it 「霍峻孤城不傾」 ("Huo Jun's lone city did not fall") [2]. This is inference from the quoted passages, not an additional recorded fact.

Note on dates: the *Sanguozhi* text here gives no year for the siege itself (it is narrated after Liu Bei's move south from Jiameng), so no calendar year is assigned.

q: After Shu-Han fell, Luo Xian held the city of Yong'an against the Wu army. How long was he besieged? Whom did Wu finally send, with how many troops, to reinforce the siege? And who came to relieve the city?
reply:
Here is what the《三国志》records say about Luo Xian's defense of Yong'an.

## Conclusion

- **How long besieged:** The《襄阳记》(in Pei Songzhi's commentary) says he was attacked for **six months** before relief arrived:「被攻凡六月日而救援不到」[41]. The Wu annals, however, date the siege from the 2nd month to the 7th month of Yong'an 7 (= 264 CE), which is about five months—the two records do not agree.
- **Whom Wu finally sent, with how many troops:** After Bu Xie's first attack was beaten off, Sun Xiu in anger「復遣陸抗等帥衆三萬人增憲之圍」—i.e., **Lu Kang and others with 30,000 troops** to reinforce the siege [41]. The Wu annals name them: 「鎮軍陸抗、撫軍步恊、征西將軍留平、建平太守盛曼，率衆圍蜀巴東守將羅憲」[48].
- **Who came to relieve the city:** Chen Qian reported to the Prince of Jin, who「遣荊州剌史胡烈救憲，抗等引退」—**Hu Lie, Inspector of Jingzhou** [41]. The Wu annals give his force: 「魏使將軍胡烈步騎二萬侵西陵，以救羅憲」—**20,000 foot and horse** [48].

## Evidence

**The initial situation.** After Wei invaded Shu, Yan Yu was recalled west, leaving 2,000 men, and Luo Xian was ordered to hold Yong'an:「留宇二千人，令憲守永安城」[41]. When word of Chengdu's fall came, the river-side officials fled; Luo Xian beheaded one man who spread word of chaos, and the people settled.

**Wu's pretext and first attack.** Wu raised troops westward, ostensibly to rescue but really to attack Luo Xian:「吳聞蜀敗，起兵西上，外讬救援，內欲襲憲」[41]. Luo Xian refused to surrender, saying Shu and Wu were "lip and teeth" to each other and Wu was breaking the alliance. Wu first「使步協率眾而西」[41]; Luo Xian fought him outside the walls and「大破其軍」[41].

**The reinforced siege and its length.**「孫休怒，復遣陸抗等帥衆三萬人增憲之圍。被攻凡六月日而救援不到，城中疾病大半」[41]. Someone urged Luo Xian to flee, but he refused, saying he would die there. The Wu annals date this siege to Yong'an 7, 2nd month [48] (Yong'an 7 = 264 CE).

**The relief.**「陳騫言於晉王，遣荊州剌史胡烈救憲，抗等引退」[41]. The Wu annals record it as: 「魏使將軍胡烈步騎二萬侵西陵，以救羅憲，陸抗等引軍退」[48]. The Wei annals also note that after Shu was pacified, Wu troops pressed on Yong'an and「遣荊、豫諸軍掎角赴救」，and「七月，賊皆遁退」[04].

## A point on the sources

The two accounts of the siege's length differ: 《襄阳记》(Pei Songzhi's commentary) says six months, while the Wu annals' month-by-month dating (2nd to 7th month of Yong'an 7) implies roughly five. Pei Songzhi notes only that the name is written "獻" in one place and "憲" in the biography, and does not resolve the question of length. Per the instructions, both versions are given rather than choosing one.

(Note: this all appears in Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting the《襄阳记》, attached to the biography of Huo Jun/Huo Yi, and in the Wu annals of Sun Xiu.)

q: Ts'ao Ts'ao asked P'ei Ch'ien about Liu Pei's abilities. How did P'ei Ch'ien assess him?
reply:
**Conclusion:** When Cao Cao (Ts'ao Ts'ao) asked Pei Qian (P'ei Ch'ien, 裴潛, courtesy name Wenxing) how he rated Liu Bei's (Liu Pei's) ability and judgment, Pei Qian answered that if Liu Bei were placed in the Central Plains he could throw things into chaos but could not govern well; but if he took advantage of an opening and held a strategic strongpoint, he could be enough to become the lord of one region.

**The source (Chen Shou, *Sanguozhi*, "Weishu," biography of Pei Qian):**

Pei Qian had earlier fled the disorder to Jing Province, where Liu Biao treated him as a guest. The record says: 「太祖定荊州，以潛參丞相軍事，出歷三縣令，入爲倉曹屬。太祖問潛曰：『卿前與劉備俱在荊州，卿以備才略何如？』潛曰：『使居中國，能亂人而不能爲治也。若乘閒守險，足以爲一方主。』」[1]

In English: After Cao Cao (then 太祖 / "the Grand Progenitor") pacified Jing Province, he made Pei Qian a military adviser on the staff of the Chancellor, then had him serve outside as magistrate of three counties and brought him in as an officer of the Cangcao (Granary Section). Cao Cao asked Pei Qian: "You were formerly together with Liu Bei in Jing Province — how do you rate Liu Bei's ability and judgment?" Pei Qian replied: "If he were placed in the Central Plains, he could throw men into disorder but could not govern. If he exploits an opening and holds a strategic strongpoint, he is sufficient to be the lord of one region." [1]

**Context note:** The account shows that Pei Qian's low opinion of Liu Bei was formed from having observed him in Jing Province, the same period when he privately told Wang Can and Sima Zhi that Liu Biao "lacked the talent of a hegemon" and was doomed. His assessment of Liu Bei is thus a judgment about Liu Bei as a disruptive force who could hold a region but not run an ordered state — in contrast to the "Grand Progenitor" Cao Cao, who is shown questioning him.

q: Zhongli Mu, as Grand Administrator of Wuling, put down a rebellion of the Five Streams tribes stirred up by Guo Chun, an agent sent by Wei. In which year was this, and how many troops did he have?
reply:
## 结论

- **年份**:永安六年,即公元 263 年(孙吴永安六年 = 公元 263 年)。
- **兵力**:钟离牧所率约 **三千兵**。

## 依据

《三国志·吴书·钟离牧传》记载:

「永安六年,蜀併於魏,武陵五谿夷與蜀接界。時論懼叛亂,乃以牧為平魏將軍,領武陵太守,往之郡。魏遣漢葭縣長郭純試守武陵太守,率涪陵民入蜀遷陵界,屯於赤沙,誘致諸夷邑君,或起應純,又進攻酉陽縣,郡中震懼。」[1]

钟离牧主张趁郭纯根基未深时迅速扑灭,抚夷将军高尚劝阻他时,明确点出他的兵力:

「撫夷將軍高尚說牧曰:『昔潘太常督兵五萬,然後以討五谿夷耳。……今既無往日之援,而郭純已據遷陵,而明府以三千兵深入,尚未見其利也。』牧曰:『非常之事,何得循舊?』即率所領,晨夜進道,緣山險行,垂二千里,從塞上,斬惡民懷異心者魁帥百餘人及其支黨凡於余級,純等散,五谿平。」[1]

所以:**永安六年(公元 263 年)**,魏派汉葭县长郭纯试守武陵太守,煽动五溪诸夷;吴以钟离牧为平魏将军、领武陵太守,他以 **三千兵** 深入,行军近二千里,斩杀魁帅及党羽千余人,郭纯等逃散,五溪平定。

## 说明

- 裴注引《会稽典录》也提到"三千"这个数目,不过是钟离牧在濡须时追述往事之语:「潘太常討武陵,吾又有三千人」[15]。这与正文高尚所说的"三千兵"可互相印证。
- 据以上事实推断:高尚以"昔潘太常督兵五萬"对比"明府以三千兵深入",可见钟离牧此次所领确为三千人左右,兵力远少于从前潘濬讨五溪时的五万之众。

q: When Du Xi was Chief of Xi'e county, a Jing Province army of more than ten thousand came to attack the town. How many people did he muster to defend it? How did the defense turn out? And in which year did this battle take place?
reply:
**结论**

杜袭守西鄂时，把县里能担任抵抗守城的吏民**五十多人**全部召来，立誓死守。战果是：临阵斩杀敌人数百，自己一方战死三十多人，其余十八人全部受伤，城被攻破；杜袭又率伤兵突围而出，部下死伤殆尽，但没有一人背叛，随后收集散民迁往摩陂军营。

至于年份，陈寿正文只说"建安初"；裴注引《九州春秋》则明确记为**建安六年**，即公元 201 年。

**依据**

- 守城人数与战况：「會荊州出步騎萬人來攻城，襲乃悉召縣吏民任拒守者五十餘人，與之要誓。」「於是身執矢石，率與戮力。吏民感恩，咸爲用命。臨陳斬數百級，而襲衆死者三十餘人，其餘十八人盡被創，賊得入城。襲帥傷痍吏民決圍得出，死喪略盡，而無反背者。遂收散民，徙至摩陂營，吏民慕而從之如歸。」[1]
- 年份：正文记此事在「建安初，太祖迎天子都許」之后，未写具体年号年份 [1]。裴注引《九州春秋》曰：「建安六年，劉表攻西鄂，西鄂長杜子緒帥縣男女嬰城而守。」[2] 按年号换算，建安六年为公元 201 年。

**说明（推断部分）**

据此推断：这次攻西鄂的"荆州"军就是刘表的军队；《九州春秋》把年份定在**建安六年（201 年）**，而陈寿正文只笼统说"建安初"，两处说法在时间精度上不一致，我按各自原文分别列出，不替读者裁定哪一个为准 [1][2]。

**以下不是《三国志》的记载：**

问题说进攻的是"荆州军队一万多人"，正文作「會荊州出步騎萬人來攻城」，即步骑一万人 [1]；裴注引《九州春秋》则说攻西鄂的是刘表本人所部 [2]。两处记载相合，并非演义独有的说法。

另外，西鄂县（当时的地名）大致在今河南南阳市一带。

q: Which painter, while painting a screen for Sun Quan, let a drop of ink fall on the silk by mistake and turned it into a fly — so lifelike that Sun Quan took it for a real fly and raised his hand to flick it away?
reply:
**Cao Buxing (曹不興).**

The story is recorded in Pei Songzhi's commentary to the *Sanguozhi*, in the biography of Zhao Da (Zhao Da is grouped with Wu Fan and Liu Dun in the *Wushu*). Pei Songzhi quotes the *Wulu*:

「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1]

— "Cao Buxing was skilled at painting. Sun Quan had him paint a screen; he accidentally let his brush touch the white silk, and thereupon made it into a fly. When it was presented to the emperor, Sun Quan took it for a living fly and raised his hand to flick it away."

Two points of accuracy:

- The phrase in the original is 「誤落筆點素」 — his brush fell on the silk by mistake, and he then worked the mark into a fly (「因就以作蠅」). So it was a stray brushstroke rather than, strictly speaking, "a drop of ink," but the sense of an accidental mark turned into a fly is exactly as the question has it.
- This passage is not Chen Shou's main text but Pei Songzhi's annotation citing the *Wulu* (裴注引《吳錄》); it appears in the list of the eight marvels of Wu, where Cao Buxing is named alongside the calligrapher Huang Xiang, the go-player Yan Wu, the dream-interpreter Song Shou, the physiognomist Zheng Yu of Gu City, and Wu Fan, Liu Dun and Zhao Da [1].

q: When Liu Bei was gravely ill, Huang Yuan, the Grand Administrator of Hanjia, rebelled and burned Linqiong. How did Yang Hong work out where Huang Yuan would go, and how was he captured?
reply:
## 结论

杨洪判断黄元不会去围攻成都、也不会去越巂占据南中，而是会**顺江东下**——如果先主平安，就自缚请罪；如果先主已死，就逃奔吴国求生。于是他命陈曶、郑绰在南安峡口拦截，果然生擒黄元。

## 依据

**事情的背景**：《三国志·蜀书·杨洪传》载：

- 「先主既稱尊號，征吳不克，還住永安。漢嘉太守黃元素為諸葛亮所不善，聞先主疾病，懼有後患，舉郡反，燒臨邛城。時亮東行省疾，成都單虛，是以元益無所憚。」[1] ——黄元因怕诸葛亮不容，趁先主病重、诸葛亮东下探病、成都空虚而举郡反，烧临邛城。
- 「洪即啟太子，遣其親兵，使將軍陳曶、鄭綽討元。」[1] ——杨洪禀告太子（刘禅），派太子亲兵，由陈曶、郑绰讨伐。

**杨洪的推断与部署**：

- 众人之议：「眾議以為元若不能圍成都，當由越囗據南中。」[1] ——别人认为黄元若不能围成都，就会经越巂去据南中。
- 杨洪的判断：「元素信凶暴，無他恩信，何能辦此？不過乘水東下，冀主上平安，面縛歸死；如其有異，奔吳求活耳。敕曶、綽但於南安峽口遮即便得矣。」[1] ——黄元凶暴而无恩信，办不成据南中的大事；他只可能顺水东下，看先主是否平安而决定自缚请罪或奔吴求生，所以在南安峡口拦截即可。
- 结果：「曶、綽承洪言，果生獲元。」[1]

**先主传的对应记载**：「三年春二月，丞相亮自成都到永安。三月，黃元進兵攻臨邛縣。遣將軍陳曶討元，元軍敗，順流下江，為其親兵所縛，生致成都，斬之。」[17] 据年号换算，这里的「三年」即章武三年，为公元 223 年[era]。可见黄元军败后确如杨洪所料顺流东下，被自己的亲兵捆绑，活着送到成都处斩。

## 推断

据以上事实推断：杨洪之所以能料定黄元的去向，是先从黄元「素信凶暴，無他恩信」这一性格与人望入手，判断他没有据南中、围成都的实力和号召力[1]；再顺着形势看——成都虽虚，但朝廷已发兵，黄元只有沿水路东下这一条退路，而东下正夹在先主所驻的永安（上游朝廷势力）与吴国之间，所以他的出路只有「面縛歸死」或「奔吳求活」两种[1]。南安峡口是这条水路东下的必经关口，故在此拦截必能擒获。这与先主传所记「元軍敗，順流下江」的结果相合[17]。

q: A woman from Jiuquan avenged her father by stabbing his killer to death in broad daylight in front of the city post-house, then went to the county office and gave herself up. Who was she, and in which year did this happen?
reply:
**Short answer:** She was **Pang E'qin (龐娥親)** — better known in the record as **Zhao E (趙娥)**, daughter of Zhao Jun'an (趙君安) of Lufu (祿福) in Jiuquan commandery, and wife of Pang Zixia (龐子夏) of Biaoshi; she was the mother of Pang Yu (龐淯), who has a biography in the *Wei Shu*. She killed her father's murderer Li Shou (李壽) in broad daylight in front of the *duting* (都亭, the city post-house/wayside pavilion), then walked to the county office and gave herself up. The year given in the source is **the second year of Guanghe (光和二年) = 179 CE**.

**What the sources say**

Chen Shou's main text (in the biography of her son Pang Yu) records the deed but no year:

「初，淯外祖父趙安為同縣李壽所殺，淯舅兄弟三人同時病死，壽家喜。淯母娥自傷父讎不報，乃幃車袖劍，白日刺壽於都亭前，訖，徐詣縣，顏色不變，曰：『父讎己報，請受戮。』祿福長尹嘉解印綬縱娥，娥不肯去，遂強載還家。會赦得免，州郡嘆貴，刊石表閭。」[13]

("Earlier, Pang Yu's maternal grandfather Zhao An was killed by Li Shou of the same county; Pang Yu's three maternal uncles all died of illness at the same time, and Li Shou's household rejoiced. Pang Yu's mother E, grieving that her father's enemy was unavenged, screened her carriage and hid a sword in her sleeve, and in broad daylight stabbed Li Shou in front of the *duting*; that done, she walked slowly to the county office, her expression unchanged, saying: 'My father's vengeance is avenged; I ask to receive execution.' The Chief of Lufu, Yin Jia, unsealed his seal-cord and set E free; E refused to leave, so she was forcibly carried home. She escaped punishment when an amnesty came; the commandery and province marveled and honored her, and had a stone inscribed to honor her village gate.")

The date comes from Pei Songzhi's note, quoting Huangfu Mi's *Lienü zhuan* (皇甫謐《列女傳》), which also gives her full identity:

「皇甫謐《列女傳》曰：酒泉烈女龐娥親者，表氏龐子夏之妻，祿福趙君安之女也。君安為同縣李壽所殺……」[1]

The note then describes the killing itself:

「至光和二年二月上旬，以白日清時，於都亭之前，與壽相遇，便下車扣壽馬，叱之……遂拔其刀以截壽頭，持詣都亭，歸罪有司，徐步詣獄，辭顏不變。」[3]

("In the first ten days of the second month of the second year of Guanghe, at a clear time of day, she met Shou in front of the *duting*; she got down, seized Shou's horse, and shouted at him… then drew his own sword and cut off Shou's head, carried it to the *duting*, submitted to the officials, and walked slowly to prison, her words and face unchanged.")

The same note adds that the Chief of Lufu, Yin Jia of Hanyang (祿福長漢陽尹嘉), refused to try her and resigned his office to let her go, that she insisted on submitting to the law, and that later the Inspector of Liangzhou, Zhou Hong, and the Administrator of Jiuquan, Liu Ban, petitioned in her praise and had a stone erected; the Grand Master of Ceremonies Zhang Huan honored her, and Liang Kuan wrote a biography of her [2][3].

**Points worth noting**

- The killing is recorded by Chen Shou only as a *retrospective* ("初", "earlier") inside her son Pang Yu's biography; Chen Shou gives no year. The precise date (Guanghe 2, early second month = 179 CE) comes only from Pei Songzhi's quotation of Huangfu Mi's *Lienü zhuan*.
- Pei's note and the main text agree on the essentials (Li Shou, the *duting*, the walk to the county office, Yin Jia, the eventual amnesty), so the two accounts corroborate rather than conflict.
- Her being "from Jiuquan" fits both: her father's household was in Lufu (祿福), Jiuquan commandery, and the *Lienü zhuan* note calls her "the stalwart woman of Jiuquan" (酒泉烈女) [1].

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The tale of Zhao E is also told in later collections of exemplary women and in later drama; the *Sanguozhi* record above (main text plus Pei's quotation of Huangfu Mi) is the version given here.

q: A wealthy man gave a ride to a woman on the road. She told him she was a messenger from Heaven sent to burn down his house, but because he had been kind to her she let him go home first and move his valuables out. Who was this wealthy man?
reply:
**The wealthy man was Mi Zhu (麋竺), courtesy name Zizhong, of Qu county in Donghai commandery — a man whose family had been merchants for generations and whose fortune was enormous.**

The story comes not from Chen Shou's main text but from Pei Songzhi's commentary, which quotes the *Soushenji* (《搜神記》):

「竺嘗從洛歸，未達家數十里，路傍見一婦人，從竺求寄載。行可數里，婦謝去，謂竺曰：『我天使也，當往燒東海麋竺家，感君見載，故以相語。』竺因私請之，婦曰：『不可得不燒。如此，君可馳去，我當緩行，日中火當發。』竺乃還家，遽出財物，日中而火大發。」[1]

In English: Mi Zhu was once returning home from Luo (Luoyang) and, still several tens of *li* short of home, saw by the roadside a woman who asked him for a ride. After a few *li* she thanked him and took her leave, saying to him: "I am a messenger of Heaven. I am to go burn down the house of Mi Zhu of Donghai. Because I was moved by your giving me a ride, I am telling you." Mi Zhu then privately begged her [to spare him]. She said: "It cannot be that it is not burned. If so, you may gallop home; I will go slowly, and the fire will break out at midday." Mi Zhu then hurried home and hastily brought out his property, and at midday the fire blazed up greatly.

**The man's background** (from Chen Shou's main text): 「麋竺字子仲，東海朐人也。祖世貨殖，僮客萬人，貲產鉅億。」[2] — Mi Zhu, courtesy name Zizhong, a man of Qu in Donghai; his family had been merchants for generations, with tens of thousands of servants and retainers and property worth hundreds of millions. He later served as a subordinate of Tao Qian, and after Tao Qian's death he welcomed the First Sovereign (Liu Bei) at Xiaopei, giving him his sister as a wife along with slaves, retainers, gold and silver to fund his army [2].

Note: this tale is a supernatural anecdote, and it is recorded only in Pei Songzhi's commentary citing the *Soushenji* [1]; it is not part of Chen Shou's own narrative. No year is given for the incident in the source.

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** The burning-house story is a marvel tale from the *Soushenji* (a collection of supernatural accounts), preserved only as Pei Songzhi's annotation, not as Chen Shou's own record.

q: A soldier who went out and never came back was treated as a deserter, and his wife and children were made government slaves. His wife protested everywhere without success. Which Commandant of Justice eventually discovered that the soldier had been murdered for money by a man from his own camp, and who was the murderer?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The Commandant of Justice (廷尉) was **Gao Rou (高柔, courtesy name Wenhui)**, and the murderer was **Jiao Ziwen (焦子文)**, a soldier of the same camp, who had killed Dou Li (窦礼) over a debt.

**The case, as recorded in the *Sanguozhi*:**

The soldier was **Dou Li (窦礼)** of the Protector's camp. He went out and did not return; his camp assumed he had deserted, reported him for pursuit and arrest, and confiscated his wife **Ying (盈)** and their children as government slaves:

「頃之，護軍營士竇禮近出不還。營以為亡，表言逐捕，沒其妻盈及男女為官奴婢。」[1]

His wife protested repeatedly at the provincial and commandery offices, but no one paid attention, so she appealed to the Commandant of Justice (廷尉), i.e. Gao Rou:

「盈連至州府，稱冤自訟，莫有省者。乃辭詣廷尉。」[1]

Gao Rou questioned her about why she was sure her husband had not fled, and whether he had any enemy or money dealings. She said he had lent money to a fellow soldier, **Jiao Ziwen**, and had been unable to get it back:

「又曰：『汝夫不與人交錢財乎？』對曰：『嘗出錢與同營士焦子文，求不得。』」[1]

Jiao Ziwen happened to be in prison at the time on a minor matter. Gao Rou went to see him, and when asked whether he had ever borrowed anyone's money, Jiao denied it. Gao Rou caught his expression change and pressed him:

「柔察子文色動，遂曰：『汝昔舉竇禮錢，何言不邪？』子文恠知事露，應對不次。柔曰：『汝已殺禮，便宜早服。』」[1]

Jiao Ziwen then kowtowed and confessed the whole story of how he had killed Dou Li, and where he had buried the body. Gao Rou sent officers to dig, and the corpse was found at once. An edict restored Ying and her children to commoner status, and the case was circulated throughout the realm as a warning:

「子文於是叩頭，具首殺禮本末，埋藏處所。柔便遣吏卒，承子文辭往掘禮，即得其屍。詔書復盈母子為平民。班下天下，以禮為戒。」[1]

**Background on Gao Rou:** He was Gao Rou, courtesy name Wenhui, of Yu County in Chenliu Commandery, son of Gao Jing, who served as Commandant of Shu Commandery (「高柔字文惠，陳留圉人也。父靖，為蜀郡都尉。」[3]). He served as Commandant of Justice for twenty-three years (「在官二十三年」[6]).

**Inference (clearly marked as such):** From the fact that Dou Li had lent money to Jiao Ziwen and could not recover it [1], and that Jiao killed him and buried the body, it may be inferred that the murder was committed for money — the debt was the motive — though the text does not spell out the motive in so many words; it only records that Gao Rou inferred the killing from the money link and that Jiao confessed.

q: P'ei Sung-chih's commentary records a Wei Grand Administrator of a frontier commandery: Sun Ch'üan suddenly arrived with tens of thousands of men, rain had washed out the city palisade and there was no time to repair it, so he ordered everyone in the city to hide while he himself lay in his quarters and did not get up, and Sun Ch'üan withdrew, suspecting an ambush. Who was this man? What difference does P'ei Sung-chih note between this account and the man's main biography?
reply:
## Answer

The man is **Wen Ping (文聘, Wen Ping), courtesy name Zhongye (仲業)**, Grand Administrator (太守) of **Jiangxia (江夏)** — a Wei frontier commandery bordering Wu.

### The Pei Songzhi note (quoting the *Wei Lüe*)

Pei's commentary to Wen Ping's biography quotes the *Wei Lüe*:

> 「孫權嘗自將數萬眾卒至。時大雨，城柵崩壞，人民散在田野，未及補治。聘聞權到，不知所施，乃思惟莫若潛默可以疑之。乃敕城中人使不得見，又自臥捨中不起。權果疑之，語其部黨曰：『北方以此人忠臣也，故委之以此郡，今我至而不動，此不有密圖，必當有外救。』遂不敢攻而去。」[1]

("Sun Quan once came suddenly in person with tens of thousands of men. It was raining hard, the city palisade had collapsed, the people were scattered in the fields, and there was no time to repair it. Wen Ping, on hearing Quan had arrived and not knowing what to do, thought that nothing was better than to keep silent and so make the enemy suspicious. He therefore ordered the people in the city not to let themselves be seen, and he himself lay down in his quarters and did not get up. Quan indeed grew suspicious and said to his followers: 'The north regards this man as a loyal subject, and so entrusted this commandery to him. Now that I have come he does not stir — either he has some secret plan, or he must have outside relief.' So he did not dare attack, and withdrew." [1])

### The difference Pei Songzhi notes

Immediately after quoting the *Wei Lüe*, **Pei Songzhi himself observes: 「魏略此語，與本傳反。」** [1] — "This statement of the *Wei Lüe* is contrary to the main biography."

The main biography (Chen Shou's text) gives a different account:

> 「孫權以五萬眾自圍聘於石陽，甚急，聘堅守不動，權住二十餘日乃解去。聘追擊破之。」[4]

("Sun Quan with fifty thousand men besieged Wen Ping in person at **Shiyang**, very urgently. Wen Ping held firm and did not stir; Quan stayed more than twenty days before lifting the siege and leaving. Wen Ping pursued and defeated him." [4])

So the points of divergence that Pei flags are:

| | *Wei Lüe* (Pei's quoted source) [1] | Main biography [4] |
|---|---|---|
| Place | (not named) | **Shiyang (石陽)** |
| Circumstances | Sun Quan arrived **suddenly**; heavy rain had wrecked the palisade, no time to repair | Sun Quan besieged him **urgently** with 50,000 |
| Wen Ping's conduct | Ordered the city to hide; **lay in his quarters and did not get up**, using silence to feign an ambush | 「堅守不動」 — **held firm and did not stir** |
| Sun Quan's withdrawal | Withdrew because he **suspected an ambush / secret plan or outside relief** | Withdrew only **after 20-plus days** |
| Aftermath | (no pursuit mentioned) | Wen Ping **pursued and broke him** [4] |

The Mingdi ji also records this campaign in brief: 「孫權攻江夏郡，太守文聘堅守」 — "Sun Quan attacked Jiangxia commandery; the Grand Administrator Wen Ping held firm" [2] — with the court debating sending relief and Emperor Ming remarking that Sun Quan, used to river warfare, dared come ashore only hoping to catch the defense unprepared, and would not stay long [2]. This agrees with the main biography's picture of a firm defense rather than the *Wei Lüe*'s ruse.

### What this means

This is a case where Pei Songzhi explicitly **juxtaposes two conflicting versions and declines to decide between them**: the main biography (Chen Shou) has Wen Ping holding firm under a prolonged siege at Shiyang and then counterattacking; the *Wei Lüe* has a sudden raid, a rain-wrecked palisade, and Wen Ping using calculated silence to bluff Sun Quan into retreating. Pei's own note — 「與本傳反」 — is a flag that the two accounts are irreconcilable, and he leaves both standing rather than ruling for one.

Jiangxia (江夏) was a commandery on the middle Yangzi; in Wei hands its seat lay in what is now eastern Hubei / the Wuhan–Anlu area, facing Wu across the river. Grand Administrator (太守) was the chief civil-and-military official of a commandery.

q: In the first year of Huangwu, the Wu fleet ran into a great storm at Dongkou and many ships capsized. Men in the water clung to the big ships and cried for help, but the other ships pushed them off with halberds and spears. Who ordered that those in the water be hauled aboard, and how many were saved?
reply:
**Answer: Wu Can (吾粲) and Huang Yuan (黄渊) ordered the men hauled aboard; they saved over a hundred people (百餘人).**

**Evidence from the record**

The event is recorded in Wu Can's biography in the *Wu Shu* (Book of Wu):

「黃武元年，與呂范、賀齊等俱以舟師拒魏將曹休於洞口。值天大風，諸船綆紲斷絕，漂沒著岸，為魏軍所獲，或覆沒沉溺，其大船尚存者，水中生人皆攀緣號呼，他吏士恐船傾沒，皆以戈矛撞擊不受。粲與黃淵獨令船人以承取之，左右以為船重必敗。粲曰：『船敗，當俱死耳！人窮，奈何棄之。』粲、淵所活者百餘人。」[1]

Translation of the key parts: In the first year of Huangwu, Wu Can, together with Lü Fan and He Qi and others, commanded the naval force resisting the Wei general Cao Xiu at Dongkou. A great wind arose; the cables and hawsers of the ships snapped, ships drifted and sank or were driven ashore and captured by Wei troops, and some capsized and drowned. On the large ships that survived, the living men in the water clung to the hulls and cried out. The other officers and men, fearing their ships would capsize, pushed them off with halberds and spears and would not take them in. Only Wu Can and Huang Yuan ordered the ship's crew to pick them up. Their attendants thought the ships, now heavy, would surely be lost. Wu Can said: "If the ship is lost, we all die together — but a man in extremity, how can we abandon him?" Those saved by Wu Can and Huang Yuan numbered over a hundred.

**Supporting context**

The disaster is also recorded in the *Wu Zhu* (Sun Quan's annals), which gives the scale of the losses:

「冬十一月，大風。呂範等兵溺死者數千，餘軍還江南。」[7]

In winter, the eleventh month, there was a great wind; several thousand of Lü Fan's and the others' troops drowned, and the rest of the army returned south of the river. Lü Fan's own biography likewise records that "時遭大風，船人覆溺，死者數千" — thousands died in the storm [11].

**Inference**

From these facts: the storm struck the Wu fleet at Dongkou, drowning thousands and leaving many men struggling in the water [7][11]; the surviving large ships' crews generally pushed the swimmers away for fear of overloading [1]. It follows that Wu Can and Huang Yuan, by ordering their crews to take the men aboard, went against the prevailing practice, and that the "over a hundred" they saved were a fraction of those lost in the storm — the sources give no total for the saved, only this figure for the two men's own ships.

q: An official of Shu-Han dreamed that a mulberry tree grew out of a well. The dream interpreter told him he would not live past forty-eight, and sure enough he died at forty-eight. Who was this official, and who interpreted the dream?
reply:
**The official was He Zhi (何祗), and the dream interpreter was Zhao Zhi (赵直).**

The story comes from a Pei Songzhi annotation to the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (Shu book, biography of Yang Hong, where He Zhi is appended). Pei cites the *Yibu Qijiu Zhuan Zaji* (《益部耆舊傳雜記》):

- The dream: 「嘗夢井中生桑，以問占夢趙直」 — "He once dreamed that a mulberry tree grew in a well, and asked the dream interpreter Zhao Zhi about it" [3].
- The interpretation: 「直曰：『桑非井中之物，會當移植；然桑字四十下八，君壽恐不過此。』祗笑言『得此足矣』」 — Zhao Zhi said, "The mulberry is not a thing of the well; it will surely be transplanted. Moreover, the character *sang* (桑) is 'forty' above and 'eight' below, so I fear your lifespan will not exceed this." He Zhi laughed and said, "That is enough for me" [3]. (Zhao Zhi read the graph 桑 as 十 + 八 stacked under 四, giving forty-eight.)
- The outcome: 「轉祗為犍為。年四十八卒，如直所言」 — He Zhi was transferred to be Administrator of Qianwei, and died at forty-eight, exactly as Zhao Zhi had said [18].

**Background on He Zhi:** He was a Shu-Han official, styled Junsu (君肅), of poor and humble origins when young. He served under Yang Hong, then as military supervisor (督軍從事), magistrate of Chengdu (and concurrently of Pi county), Administrator of Wenshan, and finally of Qianwei. He was known for his extraordinary memory and mental arithmetic — Zhuge Liang, coming to inspect the prisons without warning, found He Zhi had already memorized all the case records overnight [3].

This same Zhao Zhi also interpreted a dream for Jiang Wan (蔣琬), who dreamed of a bleeding ox-head before his gate; Zhao Zhi read the ox-horn-and-nose as forming the character 公, foretelling that Jiang Wan would rise to the rank of one of the Three Excellencies [8].

Note: no year in the source text is given as a Western (AD) year, so I have not supplied one.

The tale is recorded in Pei Songzhi's annotation, not in Chen Shou's main text, and it is a dream-omen story of the sort that later became popular in *Records of the Three Kingdoms* lore and the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*.

q: A man opened up wasteland at Yongxing and planted twenty-odd mu of rice. Just as it was ripening, a local claimed it as his own; the man simply let him have the rice, and when the county Chief wanted to punish the local, he even pleaded on his behalf. Who was this man?
reply:
The man was **Zhongli Mu (鍾離牧)**, courtesy name **Zigan (子幹)**, of Shanyin in Kuaiji commandery — a Wu official, and a seventh-generation descendant of Zhongli Yi, Chancellor of Lu in the Han.

**The account**

The story appears in his biography in the *Wu Shu* (Book of Wu):

「少爰居永興，躬自墾田，種稻二十餘畝。臨熟，縣民有識認之。牧曰：『本以田荒，故墾之耳。』遂以稻與縣人。縣長聞之，召民繋獄，欲繩以法，牧為之請。」[1]

*(In his youth he moved to Yongxing, personally opened up wasteland, and planted more than twenty mu of rice. When it was about to ripen, a commoner of the county came to claim it as his. Mu said: "I opened it only because the land was waste." So he gave the rice to the man of the county. When the county Chief heard of it, he summoned the man and put him in prison, intending to punish him by law, and Mu pleaded on his behalf.)*

The exchange with the Chief, and the outcome, continue:

「長曰：『君慕承宮，自行義事，僕為民主，當以法率下，何得寢公憲而從君邪？』牧曰：『此是郡界，緣君意顧，故來蹔住。今以少稻而殺此民，何心復留？』遂出裝，還山陰，長自往止之，為釋繋民。民慚懼，率妻子舂所取稻得六十斛米，送還牧，牧閉門不受。民輸置道旁，莫有取者。牧由此發名。」[1]

*(The Chief said: "You admire Cheng Gong and do righteous deeds on your own; but I am the people's magistrate and must lead my subordinates by law — how can I set aside public law and follow you?" Mu said: "This is the boundary of the commandery; it was out of regard for you that I came to stay here temporarily. Now for a little rice to kill this man — with what heart could I remain?" So he packed up to return to Shanyin, and the Chief himself went to stop him, and released the imprisoned man for his sake. The man, ashamed and afraid, led his wife and children to husk the rice he had taken, getting sixty hu of rice, and brought it back to Mu; Mu shut his door and would not accept it. The man deposited it by the roadside, and no one took it. From this Mu became famous.)*

**The background to the Chief's remark**

The Chief's reference to Cheng Gong (承宮) is explained in Pei Songzhi's commentary, which cites the *Xu Han Shu*:

「《續漢書》曰：宮字少子，琅邪人，嘗在蒙陰山中耕種禾黍，臨熟，人就認之，宮便推與而去，由是發名，位至左中郎將、侍中。」[3]

*(The Xu Han Shu says: Gong, courtesy name Shaozi, a man of Langye, once farmed grain in the Mengyin mountains; when it was about to ripen someone came and claimed it, and Gong simply yielded it and left. From this he became famous, rising to Left Palace Attendant [左中郎將] and Palace Attendant [侍中].)*

So the Chief was saying that Zhongli Mu was consciously imitating Cheng Gong's famous act of yielding — while he himself, as magistrate, was bound to enforce the law.

**Pei Songzhi's supplementary material**

Pei Songzhi also quotes the *Kuaiji Dianlu* on Zhongli Mu's family and youth: his father Zhongli Xu was a Tower-Ship Commandant, his elder brother Zhongli Yin an accounts messenger; Mu as a small child was called dull and slow-spoken, and his brother used to say, "Mu will surely surpass me — do not slight him," though people of the time thought otherwise [20].

A contrasting evaluation is preserved from Xu Zhong (裴注引徐眾評), who argued that Mu "may be called hard to match, but cannot be called benevolent and yielding," since the commoner who falsely claimed the rice was himself acting unethically, and the sage repays virtue with virtue but repays resentment with straightforwardness [21]. Pei Songzhi quotes this as a dissenting opinion, not as a verdict.

**Note on the place name**

Yongxing (永興) here is a county of Kuaiji commandery in Wu territory, where Zhongli Mu was living at the time. Pei Songzhi notes in another passage that "the present Yongxing county has Gaoqian Bridge" [10] — evidence the name was still in use in his day.

q: One of Cao Cao's military-planning officers (junmou yuan) ran into Cao Zhi on a muddy road inside the palace gate at Ye after a rain. He neither made way nor saluted, and even argued with Cao Zhi that 'the king's envoy, however lowly, ranks above the feudal lords.' Who was he, and what did he later gain from this?
reply:
**The officer was Han Xuan 韓宣 (courtesy name Jingran 景然), a man of Bohai 勃海.** He was a 丞相軍謀掾 — a military-planning officer (junmou yuan) on the Chancellor's staff, that is, on Cao Cao's staff. Later he gained an imperial pardon, and after that provincial and central offices.

**Who he was and what happened**

The story is preserved in Pei Songzhi's commentary to the *Wei shu* biography of Pei Qian, drawn from Yu Huan's *Weilüe*:

- 韓宣字景然，勃海人也。爲人短小。建安中，丞相召署軍謀掾，宂散在鄴。[20] ("Han Xuan, courtesy name Jingran, a man of Bohai. He was short in stature. In the Jian'an period the Chancellor summoned him to serve as a military-planning officer, and he was at leisure in Ye.")
- 嘗於鄴出入宮，於東掖門內與臨菑侯植相遇。時天新雨，地有泥潦。宣欲避之，閡潦不得去。乃以扇自障，住於道邊。[20] (Once, going in and out of the palace at Ye, inside the Eastern Side Gate he met the Marquis of Linzi, Cao Zhi. It had just rained and the ground was muddy and flooded. Xuan wanted to get out of the way, but was blocked by the water and could not leave, so he shielded himself with his fan and stood by the roadside.)

Cao Zhi, annoyed that Han Xuan neither withdrew nor saluted, stopped his carriage and had an attendant ask what office Han Xuan held. Han Xuan replied he was a 丞相軍謀掾, and then defended himself:

- 「春秋之義，王人雖微，列于諸侯之上，未聞宰士而爲下士諸侯禮也。」[13] ("By the meaning of the *Chunqiu*, the king's man, though of low rank, is placed above the feudal lords; I have never heard that a minister's officer must perform the humble-subject's courtesy toward a feudal lord.")

Cao Zhi pressed him again ("as you say, if you are a father's officer, should you show courtesy on meeting his son?"), and Han Xuan answered that in ritual, a subject and a son are treated alike — and he was also the elder. Cao Zhi, seeing his arguments were hard to refute, let him go, and afterwards told the heir (the Crown Prince, i.e. Cao Pi) about it in detail, praising his eloquence: 具爲太子言，以爲辯。[13]

**What he later gained from this**

The very fact that Cao Zhi reported the exchange to the heir became the source of Han Xuan's later fortune:

- 黃初中，爲尚書郎，嘗以職事當受罰於殿前，已縛，束杖未行。文帝輦過，問：「此爲誰？」左右對曰：「尚書郎勃海韓宣也。」帝追念前臨菑侯所說，乃寤曰：「是子建所道韓宣邪！」特原之，遂解其縛。[13] ("In the Huangchu period he was a Secretariat Gentleman, and once, for a matter of duty, he was to be punished in front of the hall; he was already bound and the rods made ready but not yet applied. Emperor Wen, passing by in his carriage, asked who he was... The Emperor recalled what the former Marquis of Linzi had said, and woke to it: 'So this is the Han Xuan that Zijian spoke of!' He specially pardoned him and had him untied.")

The anecdote continues that Han Xuan had already taken off his trousers for the beating and, when pardoned, could not undo his loincloth cord, so he hurried off as he was; Cao Pi watched him go and laughed: 「此家有瞻諦之士也。」[13] ("This family has a man who looks carefully about.")

Afterwards:

- 後出爲清河、東郡太守。明帝時，爲尚書大鴻臚，數歲卒。[13] ("Later he went out as Administrator of Qinghe and Dongjun. In Emperor Ming's time he was a 尚書 and 大鴻臚, and died several years later.")

Pei Songzhi's own note adds that Han Xuan appears nowhere in the main text and survives only through the *Weilüe*, and that the *Shiyu* ranked him among famous ministers: 案本志，宣名都不見，惟《魏略》有此傳，而《世語》列於名臣之流。[21]

**Inference (drawn from the above facts, not stated outright in the source)**

Putting these passages together: the *Weilüe* account records that Cao Zhi reported Han Xuan's retort to the Crown Prince and called it eloquent [13]; the same account records that years later, in the Huangchu period, Emperor Wen recalled precisely this remark when Han Xuan was bound for punishment and pardoned him [13]. So, by inference, what Han Xuan "gained" was that his clever defense of his rank before Cao Zhi was remembered by the man who became Emperor Wen, and that memory directly won him a pardon — and the passage then has him going on to the posts of Administrator of Qinghe and Dongjun, and under Emperor Ming to the offices of 尚書 and 大鴻臚 [13].

**Note on dating**

The *Weilüe* places the encounter only as 建安中 (mid-Jian'an), when Cao Zhi was 臨菑侯 (a title he held from Jian'an 19), so no exact year can be given for it. The pardon is dated only to 黃初中 (the Huangchu period, beginning 220). [13][20]

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** The designation "軍謀掾" as used here is the office of a staff officer on the Chancellor's headquarters; the source itself renders it as 丞相軍謀掾, "the Chancellor's military-planning officer."

q: During the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs, when Sima Yi removed Cao Shuang, which two ministers did he send to take over the camps of Cao Shuang and Cao Xi respectively, and what did Sima Yi say to one of them?
reply:
## Answer

During the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs (嘉平元年 / the first year of Jiaping), when Sima Yi (司馬宣王) moved against Cao Shuang, he sent **Gao Rou (高柔)** to occupy Cao Shuang's camp and **Wang Guan (王觀)** to occupy the camp of Cao Shuang's younger brother **Cao Xi (曹羲)**.

To one of them — **Gao Rou** — Sima Yi made a remark: 「君為周勃矣」 ("You have become Zhou Bo").

## Evidence

**Gao Rou takes Cao Shuang's camp, and Sima Yi's words:**
- 「太傅司馬宣王奏免曹爽，皇太后詔召柔假節行大將軍事，據爽營。太傅謂柔曰：『君為周勃矣。』」[19] — The Grand Tutor Sima Xuanwang memorialized to strip Cao Shuang of office; the Empress Dowager issued an edict summoning Gao Rou, granting him a tally and authorizing him to act as Grand General, to occupy Cao Shuang's camp. The Grand Tutor said to Gao Rou: "You have become Zhou Bo."

**Wang Guan takes Cao Xi's camp:**
- 「司馬宣王誅爽，使觀行中領軍，據爽弟羲營，賜爵關內侯，復為尚書，加駙馬都尉。」[25] — When Sima Xuanwang executed Cao Shuang, he had Wang Guan act as Central Army Commander (中領軍) to occupy the camp of Cao Shuang's younger brother Cao Xi, granted him the title of Marquis within the Passes, and restored him to the post of Minister (尚書), adding the title of Commandant of the Imperial Cavalry.

## Notes on the sources

- The main account of the coup is in the *Wei Shu*, "Biography of Cao Shuang" (諸夏侯曹傳·曹真·子爽), where Sima Yi's memorial against Cao Shuang is preserved: 「臣輒勑主者及黃門令罷爽、羲、訓吏兵，以侯就第……」[16], and the *San Shao Di Ji* (三少帝紀·齊王) records the date: 「嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵。太傅司馬宣王奏免大將軍曹爽……」[1].
- Gao Rou's biography explains the phrase "Zhou Bo": Zhou Bo was the Han minister who moved to seize the armies and preserve the Liu house — hence Sima Yi's comparison of Gao Rou's role to Zhou Bo's.

(以下不是《三国志》的記載:) The comparison "君為周勃矣" alludes to the Han founding minister Zhou Bo (周勃), who as Grand Commandant took control of the Northern Army and thereby secured the Han imperial house — Sima Yi is casting Gao Rou's seizing of Cao Shuang's camp in that same light.

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
## Answer

The man was **Wang Fan (王蕃, courtesy name Yongyuan 永元)** of Lujiang, who at the time held the office of **Regular Palace Attendant of the Cavaliers (散騎中常侍)**. The year was **266 CE** — the second year of Sun Wu's *Ganlu* 甘露 era (the same calendar year in which Sun Hao later changed the era name to *Baoding* 寶鼎).

### The record

Chen Shou's biography of Wang Fan states:

「甘露二年，丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣，蕃沉醉頓伏。皓疑而不悅，舉蕃出外。頃之請還，酒亦不解。蕃性有威嚴，行止自若，皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之。衛將軍滕牧、征西將軍留平請，不能得。」[1]

(In the second year of Ganlu, when Ding Zhong returned from his embassy to Jin, Sun Hao held a great assembly of the assembled ministers; Wang Fan, dead drunk, collapsed. Sun Hao grew suspicious and displeased, and had Wang Fan carried outside. After a while Wang Fan asked to return to his seat, his drunkenness still not gone. Wang Fan by nature had a dignified bearing and behaved as usual, so Sun Hao flew into a rage and shouted to his attendants to behead him below the hall. General of the Guard Teng Mu and General of the Western Conquest Liu Ping begged for mercy, but could not obtain it.)

His earlier office is given in the same biography: under Sun Xiu he and He Shao, Xue Ying and Yu Si all served as 散騎中常侍, each additionally given the title of Commandant of the Household Cavalry (駙馬都尉), and after Sun Hao came to the throne he re-entered court as 常侍 [11][12].

**The year:** the era *Ganlu*, year 2 = **266 CE**; *Baoding*, year 1, the era Sun Hao adopted in the eighth month of that same year, also = **266 CE**. This matches Sun Hao's own annals, which date Ding Zhong's mission to Jin to the first month of Baoding 1 and record the era change in the eighth month [5].

### Note on conflicting accounts (Pei Songzhi's commentary)

The killing of Wang Fan is told differently by other sources, and Pei Songzhi flags the discrepancy:

- Pei's annotation quotes the *Jiangbiao zhuan*: Sun Hao, misled by shamans, thought the Jianye palace inauspicious and, fearing the ministers would not accept a move of the capital to Wuchang, held a great banquet, asked Wang Fan the meaning of the saying "in archery the piercing of the target is not what matters, for men's strength is not of the same grade," and when Wang Fan could not answer, beheaded him on the spot, then had his head mauled. Pei notes: 「此與本傳不同」 ("this differs from the main biography") [4].
- The same annotation quotes the *Wu lu*: at Sun Hao's drinking parties the attendants were made to mock the ministers; Wang Fan mocked Wan Yu (then Left Chancellor), who retorted, and the two traded insults [4].
- Pei Songzhi's own note (臣松之按) reconciles the chronology: the main biography says Wang Fan was killed at the banquet for Ding Zhong's return; since Ding Zhong came back from the north in the spring of that year, while Wan Yu did not become Chancellor until the autumn, the *Wu lu* account does not fit [4].

So the main biography (Chen Shou) gives the banquet-and-drunkenness version; the *Jiangbiao zhuan* gives a different version, and Pei Songzhi leaves the discrepancy on record rather than adjudicating it.

**Sources:** Chen Shou, *Sanguo zhi*, Wu shu, biography of Wang Fan [1][11][12]; Sun Hao's annals [5]; Pei Songzhi's annotations quoting the *Jiangbiao zhuan* and *Wu lu* [4].

q: In the Records of the Three Kingdoms, which men were given the posthumous title 'Marquis Gang' (Gang hou, the 'Resolute Marquis')?
reply:
**Answer: In the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, four men are recorded as receiving the posthumous title "Marquis Gang" (剛侯, "the Resolute Marquis"): Zhang Liao, Huang Zhong, Li Tong, and Su Ze.**

The evidence:

**1. Zhang Liao (張遼), Wei**
「遼病篤，遂薨於江都。帝爲流涕，諡曰剛侯。」[6]
(Zhang Liao fell gravely ill and died at Jiangdu. The Emperor wept for him and conferred the posthumous title Marquis Gang.)

**2. Huang Zhong (黃忠), Shu**
「明年卒，追諡剛侯。」[8]
(He died the following year and was posthumously titled Marquis Gang.)

**3. Li Tong (李通), Wei**
「文帝踐阼，謚曰剛侯。」[13]
(When Emperor Wen ascended the throne, he was posthumously titled Marquis Gang. The same passage records the edict praising Li Tong's loyalty in the troubles of Yuan Shao's era.)

**4. Su Ze (蘇則), Wei**
「黃初四年，左迁东平相。未至，道病薨，谥曰刚侯。」[30]
(In the fourth year of Huangchu he was demoted to Chancellor of Dongping; before reaching the post he fell ill on the road and died, and was posthumously titled Marquis Gang.)

**On the search:** I looked for this title under several phrasings (谥号 刚侯, 追谥 刚侯, 谥曰刚侯, 谥为刚侯, and a targeted search of the Wu chapters). The four men above are the only ones the text explicitly records as receiving the posthumous title 剛侯. I found no instance in the Wu records (《吳書》).

**A related but distinct case to avoid confusion:** Cao Qin, son of Emperor Wu, appears as 「剛殤公子勤」[2] — this is the title "Gang-shang Gong" (剛殤公), a ducal (公) rather than marquis (侯) title, and it is the title under which he was enfeoffed, not a Marquis Gang.

**Inference (my reasoning):** Based on the fact that all four citations explicitly use the phrase 剛侯 (Marquis Gang) as the conferred posthumous title, and that no other such conferral appears in the material I searched, the group consists of these four — three from Wei (Zhang Liao, Li Tong, Su Ze) and one from Shu (Huang Zhong). I note that absence of a record for others is not proof that none existed, only that no such conferral is recorded in the passages I was able to retrieve.

**Background note (not from the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*):**
As a posthumous designation, 剛 ("resolute, firm") was in the traditional 諡法 used to honor men noted for strength of will or stern firmness.

q: In the course of pacifying the Shanyue, which new counties did He Qi successively petition to have established?
reply:
## Answer

According to He Qi's biography in the *Sanguozhi*, the new counties he had established (several by petitioning the throne, 表) as he pacified the Shanyue were:

**In 建安十年 (Jian'an 10)** — after the campaigns against the rebels at 建安/汉兴/南平 and then at 上饶:
- **建平县 (Jianping)** — 「十年，轉討上饒，分以為建平縣」[3]. (Earlier, after the 建安八年 campaign, the text only says 「復立縣邑」[3] "counties and towns were re-established," without naming them.)

**In 建安十三年 (Jian'an 13)**, while campaigning against the 黟 and 歙 of 丹陽:
- **始新县 (Shixin)** — 「時武強、葉鄉、東陽、豐浦四鄉先降，齊表言以葉鄉為始新縣」[4] ("He Qi petitioned, saying that 葉鄉 be made into 始新县").
- **新定县 (Xinding), 黎阳县 (Liyang), 休阳县 (Xiuyang)** — 「齊復表分歙為新定；黎陽、休陽」[4] ("He Qi again petitioned to divide 歙 into 新定, 黎阳, 休阳").

These, together with the existing 黟 and 歙, made six counties: 「並黟、歙凡六縣。權遂割為新都郡，齊為太守，立府於始新，加偏將軍」[4] — Sun Quan then carved these out to form **新都郡 (Xindu Commandery)**, with He Qi as Administrator, his headquarters at 始新.

## Basis

- 「十年，轉討上饒，分以為建平縣」[3]
- 「齊表言以葉鄉為始新縣」[4]
- 「齊復表分歙為新定；黎陽、休陽。並黟、歙凡六縣。權遂割為新都郡」[4]

So the counties he is recorded as petitioning/establishing, in sequence, are: **建平 (Jian'an 10), then 始新, 新定, 黎阳, 休阳 (Jian'an 13)**.

The 裴注 attached to these passages (e.g. the 《抱朴子》 story of the Shanyue "禁咒" master, 60-0002n0) adds anecdotes about the fighting but names no additional counties.

q: Who were the 'Eight Masters of Wu', and what was each of them famous for?
reply:
## The "Eight Marvels of Wu" (八絕)

First, a note on the name: the *Sanguozhi* does not call them the "Eight Masters of Wu." The term used in the text is **八絕 ("the Eight Marvels / Eight Excellences")**. This list is not in Chen Shou's main text; it comes from **Pei Songzhi's commentary**, which quotes the *Wulu* (《吳錄》), attached to the biography of Zhao Da (Zhao Da, Wu Fan, Liu Dun, in *Wu Shu* ch. 63).

The passage reads: 「《吳錄》曰：皇象字休明，廣陵江都人。幼工書……嚴武字子卿，衞尉畯再從子也，圍棊莫與爲輩。宋壽占夢，十不失一。曹不興善畫……孤城鄭嫗能相人，及範、惇、達八人，世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云。」[1] (Pei's note quoting the *Wulu*: Huang Xiang of Guangling Jiangdu was skilled in calligraphy from youth… Yan Wu, courtesy Ziqing, was a second cousin of the Commandant of the Guards Yan Jun; no one could match him at *weiqi*. Song Shou interpreted dreams and was never wrong once in ten. Cao Buxing excelled at painting… the old woman Zheng of Gucheng could read faces; together with [Wu] Fan, [Liu] Dun, and [Zhao] Da — eight men in all — the age called them all marvelous and termed them the "Eight Marvels.")

### The eight, and what each was famed for

**1. Huang Xiang 皇象 (courtesy Xiuming 休明), of Guangling Jiangdu — calligraphy.**
「幼工書。時有張子並、陳梁甫能書。甫恨逋，並恨峻，象斟酌其間，甚得其妙，中國善書者不能及也。」[1] He was skilled at calligraphy from youth; Chen Liangfu's fault was slowness, Zhang Zibing's was severity, and Huang Xiang balanced between them, attaining the subtlety — no calligrapher of the Central Plain could match him.

**2. Yan Wu 嚴武 (courtesy Ziqing 子卿), second cousin of the Commandant of the Guards Yan Jun 嚴畯 — *weiqi* (go).**
「圍棊莫與爲輩。」[1] No one was his peer at *weiqi*.

**3. Song Shou 宋壽 — dream interpretation.**
「宋壽占夢，十不失一。」[1] He interpreted dreams and was not wrong once in ten.

**4. Cao Buxing 曹不興 — painting.**
「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1] Sun Quan had him paint a screen; he accidentally dropped a brush-dot on the silk, turned it into a fly, and when it was presented, Sun Quan took it for a live fly and reached out to flick it away.

**5. The old woman Zheng of Gucheng 孤城鄭嫗 — physiognomy (reading faces).**
「孤城鄭嫗能相人。」[1] She could judge people by their features.

**6–8. Wu Fan 吳範, Liu Dun 劉惇, Zhao Da 趙達 — divination and the esoteric arts (術數).** These three are the ones with their own joint biography (*Wu Shu* ch. 63):

- **Wu Fan 吳範 (courtesy Wenze 文則), of Kuaiji Shangyu.** 「以治曆數知風氣聞於郡中」[44] — famed in his commandery for calendrical calculation and for knowing things through "wind and qi." He predicted Liu Bei's acquisition of Yi Province, and he foretold Guan Yu's capture: when Guan Yu fled, Wu Fan said 「雖去不免」, and named the time as the next midday; when noon passed he said the hour was not yet exactly centered, and shortly after Guan Yu was taken [50]. He died in the 5th year of Huangwu [45].

- **Liu Dun 劉惇 (courtesy Ziren 子仁), of Pingyuan.** 「以明天官達占數顯於南土」[31] — famed in the south for understanding the celestial offices and mastering divination. He predicted floods, droughts, and banditry in advance without fail, and Sun Fu made him military adviser, the army calling him "the God-like" (神明) [31]. 「惇於諸術皆善，尤明太乙」— he excelled at all the arts, especially *Taiyi*, and wrote over a hundred chapters [32].

- **Zhao Da 趙達, of Henan.** He studied the "Nine Palaces" calculation method and could answer instantly and as if divinely; he computed the number of a swarm of locusts, found hidden objects, and located a jar of wine and venison behind a wall [18]. 「孫權行師征伐，每令達有所推步，皆如其言」— whenever Sun Quan went on campaign he had Zhao Da calculate, and it always came out as he said [20]. He also foretold his own death to the day [20].

### A point of caution on the term

The group is a *Wulu*-based tradition reported by Pei Songzhi, not a formal institution or office in Chen Shou's text. Note also that the list as quoted gives us the fame of only some members explicitly (calligraphy, *weiqi*, dreams, painting, physiognomy); for Wu Fan, Liu Dun, and Zhao Da their specialty is documented in their own biography as divination and the esoteric arts (術數/占候), which is why the *Wulu* attaches their names to close the list of eight.

---

q: Who had the courtesy name Wenze?
reply:
**两个人在《三国志》里都字「文則」：魏国的于禁和吴国的吴范。**

**一、于禁（字文則）**

「于禁字文則，泰山鉅平人也。」[1] 他是泰山郡钜平县人，早年跟随鲍信，后来归附曹操，历任军司马、陷阵都尉、平虏校尉、裨将军、偏将军、虎威将军、左将军，封益寿亭侯 [1][3][5][6]。建安二十四年，他率七军救援樊城，遇汉水暴涨，七军皆没，于禁投降关羽；后来孙权送他回魏，魏文帝曹丕让他拜谒高陵，预先在陵屋画上关羽战胜、庞德愤怒、于禁降服之状，「禁見，慚恚發病薨」，谥号厉侯 [2]。

**二、吴范（字文則）**

「吳範字文則，會稽上虞人也。」[9] 他是会稽郡上虞县人，以研究历法、能凭风气预知吉凶闻名郡中，被举为有道；孙权在东南兴起后，吴范委身事奉他，每遇灾异祥瑞便推算陈说，「其術多效，遂以顯名」[9]。后来官至太史令 [13]。

**三、区分**

两人同名同字，但一在魏（于禁）、一在吴（吴范），《三国志》分属不同列传：于禁在《魏书·张乐于张徐传》[1]，吴范在《吴书·吴范刘惇赵达传》[9]。单说「字文则」，正史里这两人都符合，须看是魏人还是吴人才能定指。

（另：苏则字「文师」[12]，与「文则」不同，容易混淆，附此一提。）

q: Who was the man that Kuan Yü's troops called the 'White Horse General' (Baima jiangjun)?
reply:
**The man was Pang De (龐德, courtesy name Lingming 令明).**

According to the *Sanguozhi*, during the campaign around Fancheng, Pang De rode a white horse, and Guan Yu's troops nicknamed him the "White Horse General," fearing him:

「時德常乘白馬，羽軍謂之白馬將軍，皆憚之。」[12]

(Translation: "At that time De constantly rode a white horse; Yu's army called him the White Horse General, and all feared him.")

The context [12]: Pang De had surrendered to Cao Cao and was stationed at Fancheng under Cao Ren. When Guan Yu attacked, some of the generals below Fancheng suspected Pang De because his elder brother was in Hanzhong (on Liu Bei's side). Pang De declared he would personally fight Guan Yu, and he did — shooting Guan Yu in the forehead. Cao Ren then had Pang De camp ten *li* north of Fancheng. After over ten days of heavy rain the Han River flooded; Guan Yu attacked by boat, Pang De fought on until his arrows ran out, and he was finally captured and killed for refusing to surrender [12][16]. He was posthumously given the title "Marquis Zhuang" (壯侯) [16].

q: How many sons did Quan Cong have? What were their names, and what became of each of them?
reply:
## 全琮的儿子

《三国志》里明确记为全琮之子的，有**全绪、全寄、全怿、全吴**四人。另有全端，一处记载像儿子，一处记载是侄子，两说不一（见下）。全静、全祎、全仪则是孙辈（全怿之兄的儿子），不是全琮的儿子。

### 四位有明确记载的儿子

**1. 全绪（长子）**
裴注引《吴书》：「琮長子緒，幼知名，奉朝請，出授兵，稍遷揚武將軍、牛渚督。孫亮即位，遷鎮北將軍。東關之役，緒與丁奉建議引兵先出，以破魏軍，封一子亭侯，年四十四卒。」[2]
——自幼知名，历官扬武将军、牛渚督，孙亮即位后升镇北将军；东关之役与丁奉建议先出兵、击破魏军，朝廷封了他一个儿子为亭侯，四十四岁去世。

**2. 全寄（次子）**
裴注引《吴书》：「次子寄，坐阿黨魯王霸賜死。」[2]
——因依附鲁王孙霸获罪被赐死。此事正文多处可证：《顾雍传》记「時長公主婿衞將軍全琮子寄爲霸賓客，寄素傾邪」[10]；《孙霸传》记「時全寄、吳安、孫奇、楊笁等陰共附霸，圖危太子……霸賜死後，又誅寄、安、奇等」[17]；《陆逊传》记陆逊曾警告全琮「卿不師日磾，而宿留阿寄，終為足下門戶致禍矣」，全琮不听[16]。

**3. 全怿**
正文：「十二年卒，子懌嗣。後襲業領兵，救諸葛誕於壽春，出城先降，魏以為平東將軍，封臨湘侯。」[3]
——继承全琮爵位，承袭领兵；诸葛诞据寿春时率兵往救，出城先降魏，魏任为平东将军、封临湘侯。《钟会传》详记他是被钟会伪造书信、施反间所诱而出降的：「會建策，密為輝、儀作書……懌等恐懼，遂將所領開東城門出降，皆蒙封寵」[13]。《魏书·高贵乡公纪》亦载「吳大將全端、全懌等率衆降」[26]。

**4. 全吴（小子）**
裴注引《吴书》：「小子吳，孫權外孫，封都鄉侯。」[2]
——是孙权的外孙，封都乡侯。

### 全端：儿子还是侄子，记载不一

《顾雍传》正文把全端与全绪并列为全琮之子：「時琮群子緒、端亦並爲將」[10]（"群子"即几个儿子）。
但《钟会传》却说他是侄子：「琮子懌、孫靜、從子端、翩、緝等」[13]（"從子"即侄子）。

全端确为吴将，事迹有：东兴之役奉命守西城[20]；与文钦、唐咨等率步骑三万救诸葛诞[15]；甘露二年十二月随全怿等降魏[26]。至于他究竟是全琮之子还是侄，两处记载不同，我不替读者裁定。

### 容易误认成儿子的孙辈

《钟会传》里的全静，记为「孫靜」（孙子）[13]；《全琮传》里的全祎、全仪、全静则记为「懌兄子」（全怿之兄的儿子）[3]，即全琮的孙子。《孙亮传》说得更明确：「全緒子禕、儀以其母奔魏」[15]——全祎、全仪是全绪的儿子，所以是全琮的孙子，不是儿子。他们随全怿降魏，后「皆歷郡守列侯」[3]。

### 小结

据《全琮传》正文及裴注引《吴书》，全琮可确指的儿子是**全绪、全寄、全怿、全吴**四人：长子全绪官至镇北将军、四十四岁卒；次子全寄因党附鲁王孙霸被赐死；全怿继嗣、后降魏封临湘侯；幼子全吴是孙权外孙、封都乡侯。全端之子/侄身份两说并存，未可定论。

以下不是《三国志》的记载：全端究竟是全琮之子还是侄子，《三国志》本身两处记载互相矛盾（《顾雍传》作"群子"，《钟会传》作"从子"），并非另有正史定论可循。

q: The Weilüe mentions a man called 'Nukou' ('Slave Bandit'). Who was he, and which other generals' alternative names are given in the same passage?
reply:
## Answer

"Nukou" (奴寇) was one of the alternate names of **Zang Ba** (臧霸), styled Xuangao (宣高), a general who first followed Lü Bu and after Lü Bu's defeat was taken in and generously treated by Cao Cao, being entrusted with the coastal districts of Qing and Xu provinces [27].

The passage is a Pei Songzhi annotation quoting the *Weilüe* (裴注引《魏略》), attached to Zang Ba's biography in the *Wei Shu* (魏書·二李臧文吕许典二庞阎传). It reads:

「《魏略》曰：霸一名奴寇。孫觀名嬰子。吳敦名黯奴。尹禮名盧兒。」[1]

So the other generals whose alternate names are given in the same passage are:

- **Sun Guan** (孙观) — alternate name **Yingzi** (嬰子). He was styled Zhongtai (仲台), a Taishan man who rose together with Zang Ba against the Yellow Turbans, often led the van, and died of wounds received while attacking Sun Quan at Ruxu [25].
- **Wu Dun** (吴敦) — alternate name **Annu** (黯奴). He has no separate biography; he appears in the list of Taishan leaders (Zang Ba, Sun Guan, Wu Dun, Yin Li, Chang Xi) who gathered followers and followed Lü Bu, and were taken in by Cao Cao after Lü Bu's fall [27].
- **Yin Li** (尹礼) — alternate name **Lu'er** (盧兒). Likewise without a separate biography, listed among the same Taishan leaders [27].

In short, the *Weilüe* passage gives the *other names* (a kind of byname or childhood name) of four men of this Taishan group: Zang Ba = Nukou, Sun Guan = Yingzi, Wu Dun = Annu, Yin Li = Lu'er.

Note: the same *Weilüe* annotation continues on with events of the 24th year of Jian'an and afterwards (Zang Ba's troops dispersing when Cao Cao died; Emperor Wen stripping Zang Ba of his command) [1], but those are separate from the naming list you asked about.

---

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:**

The name "奴寇" is given by the *Weilüe* (a non-official history) as one of Zang Ba's names, and Pei Songzhi quotes it in his annotation rather than in Chen Shou's main text; such alternate names are not treated as formal *zi* (字).

q: Who was the Marquis of Panyu, and for what achievement was he given that title?
reply:
The Marquis of Panyu (番禺侯) was **Lü Dai (呂岱), courtesy name Dinggong (定公)**, of Guangling Hailing — a Wu general and official whose biography is in the *Wu Shu* (*Records of Wu*).

**The achievement:** He received the title for crushing the revolt of the Shi family in Jiaozhi. After the Jiaozhi Administrator Shi Xie (士燮) died, his son Shi Hui (士徽) refused to accept the replacement appointees, raised troops, and blocked the coast. Lü Dai asked to punish him, led 3,000 men by sea day and night, and took Shi Hui by surprise; Shi Hui and his brothers came out to surrender in submission, and Lü Dai had them all beheaded and their heads sent off. When Shi Hui's chief generals Gan Li (甘醴) and Huan Zhi (桓治) then attacked him with officials and people, Lü Dai struck hard and routed them — and it was for this that he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Panyu:

「徽聞岱至，果大震怖，不知所出，即率兄弟六人肉袒迎岱。岱皆斬送其首，徽大將甘醴，桓治等率吏民攻岱，岱奮擊大破之，進封番禺侯。」[1]

**Context:** This was a promotion in rank. Earlier, on succeeding Bu Zhi as Inspector of Jiaozhi in the first year of Yankang (延康元年), he had already been enfeoffed as Marquis of Duxiang (都鄉侯) [4]. After the Panyu enfeoffment, the text says he went on to subdue Jiuzhen and to send envoys who brought the kings of Funan, Linyi, and Tangming to send tribute, and Sun Quan, commending his merit, promoted him to General Who Guards the South (鎮南將軍) [1]. Later he served as Grand Marshal (大司馬) under Sun Liang and died at 96 in the first year of Taiping [9].

Note that the *Sanguozhi* text does not state the specific year in which the Panyu enfeoffment was made; it only says it followed these events.

q: Why was Wei Zhao put to death by Sun Hao?
reply:
**结论：韦昭（韦曜）被杀，直接原因是孙皓积怨——他不肯迎合孙皓、坚持史官立场，又因饮酒一事被强加罪名，最终在凤皇二年（273年）被下狱处死。**

孙皓杀他的具体经过和理由，裴松之注与正文中都有交代，分几点说明。

**一、因不迎合孙皓而积怨**

韦曜在孙皓即位后封高陵亭侯，任中书仆射，后改任侍中，常领左国史。他与孙皓结怨主要有两件事：

1. 各地争报祥瑞，孙皓拿这事问韦曜，韦曜说「此人家筐篋中物耳」[3]（意思是这不过是人家箱筐里的寻常东西罢了）。
2. 孙皓想为父亲孙和作"纪"，韦曜坚持孙和没有登帝位，应当称"传"：「皓欲為父和作紀，曜執以和不登帝位，宜名為傳」[3]。

正文说「如是者非一，漸見責怒」[3]，即这类事不止一次，孙皓渐渐对他责备恼怒。韦曜因此忧惧，自陈衰老，请求辞去侍中、史官二职，孙皓始终不听[3]。

**二、宴饮之事被强加罪名**

孙皓每次宴饮，一律以七升为限，即使喝不下也要灌尽。韦曜平素饮酒不过二升，「初見禮異時，常為裁減，或密賜茶荈以當酒，至於寵衰，更見逼強，輒以為罪」[3]——起初受礼遇时还为他减量，甚至暗中赐茶代替酒；到宠信衰减后，就被强逼，并被当作罪过。孙皓又让侍臣在酒后诘难折辱公卿，韦曜只问经义言论，孙皓便「以為不承用詔命，意不忠盡」[3]。

**三、下狱处死**

正文总结：「遂積前後嫌忿，收曜付獄，是歲鳳凰二年也」[3]。即孙皓累积前后嫌怨愤恨，把韦曜收捕下狱，这一年是凤皇二年（据年号换算为公元273年）。

下狱后韦曜上书自陈，请求完成所著《洞纪》《官职训》《辩释名》等书，孙皓更责怪他呈上的书稿「垢故」（污垢陈旧），又拿这个责问他[12]。华覈接连上疏相救，把韦曜比作汉代的司马迁，说「今曜在吳，亦漢之史遷也」，请求赦免一等之罪让他完成《吴书》[12]。孙皓不答应，「遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也」[11]——于是诛杀韦曜，把他的家属一百户迁到零陵，其子韦隆也有文学才能。

**以下不是《三国志》的记载：**
您问的"韦昭"，就是《三国志》里的韦曜，同一个人的不同写法。今人讲这段历史时常称他"韦昭"。

q: When Mi Chu married his sister to Liu Pei, how many retainers and how much property did he contribute along with her?
reply:
**结论 (先给答案):** 据《三国志·蜀书·麋竺传》记载，麋竺送妹妹给刘备作夫人的同时，献上的是 **奴客 (僮仆宾客) 二千人**，以及金银货币，用来资助军费；原文并没有给出金银货币的具体数额，只说「金銀貨幣以助軍資」。

**依据 (原文):**

- 传文先说他家底：「祖世貨殖，僮客萬人，貲產鉅億」[1] —— 世代经商，家中有僮仆宾客上万人，资产数以亿计。这是麋竺的家产总量，不是随妹妹陪送的数量，两者不要混为一谈。
- 建安元年 (公元 196 年，据年号换算)，吕布趁刘备出兵抵御袁术时袭取下邳，掳走刘备的妻子儿女；刘备转军到广陵海西，麋竺就在此时把妹妹献上：

「先主轉軍廣陵海西，竺于是進妹于先主為夫人，奴客二千，金銀貨幣以助軍資，于時困匱，賴此複振。」[1]

也就是说：随妹妹一同献上的是 **奴客二千人**，外加金银货币；当时刘备困窘匮乏，靠这批人和财物才重新振作起来 [1]。

**推断:** 据此推断，麋竺这次是「人 + 财」两样并送：人可确定是二千名奴客 (僮仆宾客，即依附于他的私属人口)，财则只有「金银货币」这样的笼统说法，陈寿没有记下具体数目，所以无法从《三国志》推知确切金额。至于「僮客萬人，貲產鉅億」，说的是麋家原有的总家业，可推知他拿得出这笔资助，但那上万僮客、上亿资产并非陪送妹妹的数目。

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** 问题里说「嫁给刘备」(marry his sister to Liu Pei)，严格说《三国志》用的词是「進妹于先主為夫人」[1]，即把妹妹献上作夫人；后世 (如《三国演义》) 常把这段写成正式婚嫁的情节，但《三国志》只记这一句，未载婚礼经过。

q: How did Xu Zhu realize that Xu Ta and the others were plotting to assassinate Cao Cao? And how did he deal with them?
reply:
## How Xu Chu discovered the plot and dealt with the assassins

**Short answer:** Xu Chu did not learn of the plot through any informant or investigation. The record says Xu Ta (徐他) and his confederates were afraid to act while Xu Chu was always at Cao Cao's side, so they waited for a day when Xu Chu was off duty. But when Xu Chu reached his resting quarters, his heart suddenly stirred (心動) — a premonition — and he went straight back to his guard post. The conspirators, not knowing he had returned, came into the tent carrying concealed knives, saw him, and were badly startled; Xu Chu caught the change in Xu Ta's expression and struck them down on the spot.

**The record (Wei Shu, biography of Xu Chu):**

「時常從士徐他等謀為逆，以褚常侍左右，憚之不敢發。伺褚休下日，他等懷刀入。褚至下捨心動，即還侍。他等不知，入帳見褚，大驚愕。他色變，褚覺之，即擊殺他等。太祖益親信之，出入同行，不離左右。」[1]

*Translation: At that time the regular attendant soldier Xu Ta and others plotted treason. Because Xu Chu was always in attendance at Cao Cao's side, they feared him and did not dare to act. They waited for a day when Xu Chu was off duty, and Xu Ta and the others came in carrying knives. Xu Chu, having reached his resting quarters, felt his heart stir, and at once returned to his post. Xu Ta and the others did not know this; entering the tent they saw Xu Chu and were greatly astonished. Xu Ta's expression changed, Xu Chu noticed it, and immediately struck and killed Xu Ta and the others. Taizu [Cao Cao] trusted and favored him all the more, going in and out together with him, never leaving his side.* [1]

So the sequence is: (1) the plotters deliberately chose a day Xu Chu was off duty; (2) Xu Chu's unexplained unease made him return early; (3) the plotters walked in unprepared and were visibly startled; (4) Xu Chu read Xu Ta's changed expression and killed them before they could act.

**On the name:** the main text writes 徐他; Pei Songzhi's commentary writes the same man as 徐佗. Pei Songzhi cites this very incident when arguing that Xu Chu deserved a place in the ancestral temple offerings:

「徐佗謀逆而許褚心動，忠誠之至遠同於日磾」 — Pei Songzhi's own comment [3]

*Translation (Pei Songzhi): "Xu Tuo plotted treason and Xu Chu's heart stirred; the extremity of his loyalty is comparable to Jin Midi's."*

This confirms it is the same event, and shows Pei Songzhi himself treats Xu Chu's premonition as an expression of his devotion to Cao Cao.

**Inference (my own reasoning, from the facts above):** Since the text says the conspirators were "afraid and did not dare to act" precisely because Xu Chu was always at Cao Cao's side, and that they only moved on a day he was off duty, it follows that Xu Chu's constant presence was itself the main obstacle to the plot — and his unplanned early return, whatever its cause, removed the only window of opportunity the assassins had. I am inferring this connection; the text does not itself explain their motive beyond the fear of Xu Chu.

---

*Background note (not from the Sanguozhi):* Pei Songzhi, quoted above, is the commentator whose notes are appended to Chen Shou's text; his remarks are marked as his own and are not part of Chen Shou's original narrative.

q: What happened when Zhuge Liang used the Empty Fort Strategy at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi?
reply:
## Conclusion

The "Empty Fort" episode at Yangping is **not in Chen Shou's main text of the *Sanguozhi*** at all. It survives only in a quotation that Pei Songzhi includes in his commentary, from a work called **Guo Chong's *Sanshi*** (郭沖《三事》) — and Pei Songzhi immediately appends a rebuttal ("難") arguing that the episode could not have happened as told. So the famous scene of Zhuge Liang opening the gates and bluffing Sima Yi away is a *commentary anecdote that the commentator himself rejects*, not accepted history.

## What Guo Chong's *Sanshi* says

As quoted by Pei Songzhi, Guo Chong relates:

- Zhuge Liang was camped at Yangping and had sent Wei Yan and the other armies east, leaving only 10,000 men to hold the city. 「亮屯于陽平，遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城」[3]
- Sima Yi ("Jin Xuandi") came with 200,000 troops and, having missed Wei Yan's column, arrived within about 60 *li* of Zhuge Liang; scouts reported that Zhuge Liang's force in the city was small and weak. 「晉宣帝率二十萬眾拒亮……當亮六十里所，偵候白宣帝說亮在城中兵少力弱」[3]
- Zhuge Liang knew Sima Yi was nearly upon him and could not reach Wei Yan in time; his officers turned pale. He then 「敕軍中皆臥旗息鼓，不得妄出菴幔，又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒」— ordered the banners lowered and drums silenced, forbade anyone to leave the tents, and had the four city gates thrown open and the ground swept and sprinkled. [3]
- Sima Yi, who always regarded Zhuge Liang as cautious, suspected an ambush and 「引軍北趣山」— withdrew his army north toward the hills. The next day at mealtime Zhuge Liang clapped his hands and laughed, saying Sima Yi must have thought him timid and imagined a strong ambush, and that he would have gone off along the mountains. Scouts confirmed it, and Sima Yi later "deeply regretted" it. 「司馬懿必謂吾怯，將有彊伏，循山走矣」[3]

## Pei Songzhi's rebuttal

Pei Songzhi (through the "難" he preserves) argues the story is impossible:

- Yangping is in Hanzhong; when Zhuge Liang first camped at Yangping, Sima Yi was still Inspector of Jingzhou, stationed at Wan, and only after Cao Zhen's death did he face Zhuge Liang in the Guanzhong region. 「案陽平在漢中。亮初屯陽平，宣帝尚為荊州都督，鎮宛城，至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳」[3]
- Wei once sent Sima Yi from Wan via Xicheng to attack Shu, but he was stopped by continuous rain — and there was no other engagement at Yangping before or after. 「此之前後，無復有於陽平交兵事」[3]
- Even granting Guo Chong's account, if Sima Yi had 200,000 men and already knew Zhuge Liang's force was small, he could simply have fortified and been cautious — why flee? 「就如沖言……何至便走乎？」[3]

## Inference

From these facts we can infer (this is my inference, not stated in the text): the *Sanguozhi* as compiled by Chen Shou does not record an "empty fort" ruse by Zhuge Liang; the only place it appears is a later anecdote (Guo Chong) that Pei Songzhi quotes precisely in order to refute it on chronological and geographical grounds. So the story cannot be treated as *Sanguozhi* history. Note also that elsewhere the *Sanguozhi*'s accounts of the Sima–Zhuge confrontations show Zhuge Liang repeatedly challenging and Sima Yi refusing battle and holding his ramparts (e.g., 「亮數挑戰，宣王堅壘不應」[12]), which is a different picture from the anecdote.

---
