q: How many different people named Zhao Da appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and what did each of them do?
reply:
## Conclusion

The name index for the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* returns **three entries** under the name **Zhao Da (趙達)**, but after checking the underlying texts, two of those entries describe the **same man** — the Wei 校事 Zhao Da, who is cited in two different biographies. So there are **two distinct individuals** named Zhao Da: one Wu astrologer/diviner, and one Wei 校事 (a secret-police-style "intelligence officer").

---

### 1. Zhao Da of Wu — the diviner (吳書·吳範劉惇趙達傳)

From Henan; studied under the Han 侍中 Shan Fu (單甫), and mastered the "Nine Palaces single-reckoning" art:

> 「趙達，河南人也。少從漢侍中單甫受學，用思精密。」「治九宮一算之術，究其微旨，是以能應機立成。」[1]

He could instantly reckon numbers, count a swarm of locusts, guess hidden things, count beans scattered on a mat, and "see" wine and venison hidden behind a wall [1].

Sun Quan used him for divination in campaigns, but Zhao Da refused to reveal his method, so he was slighted and his rank never rose; he also foretold the date of his own death:

> 「初，孫權行師征伐，每令達有所推步，皆如其言。權問其法，達終不語，由此見薄，祿位不至。」「後如期死。」[2]

He jealously guarded his art even from famous scholars like Kan Ze (闞澤) and Yin Li (殷禮), and tricked his disciple Gongsun Teng (公孫滕) out of receiving it [3]. Pei's commentary adds:

- Pei note quoting the *Wu Shu* (《吳書》): when Sun Quan took the imperial title, Zhao Da predicted his reign would be twice the Han founder's twelve years — 「高祖建元十二年，陛下倍之。」[7]
- Pei note quoting the *Wu Lu* (《吳錄》): he is counted among the eight "excellences" of Wu — 「及範、惇、達八人，世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云。」[11]

### 2. Zhao Da of Wei — the 校事

He was a **校事** (an officer set up to spy on and impeach officials) under Cao Cao (太祖), appointed together with Lu Hong (盧洪):

> 「時置校事盧洪、趙達等，使察羣下」[5]

Gao Rou (高柔) criticized the office; Cao Cao defended it, but Zhao Da and the others were later executed for corruption:

> 「達等後姧利發，太祖殺之以謝於柔。」[5]

He also appears in Xu Miao's (徐邈) biography, when Xu Miao was drinking in violation of the ban and Zhao Da questioned him on official business:

> 「校事趙達問以曹事，邈曰：『中聖人。』達白之太祖，太祖甚怒。」[12]

---

### Note on the count

The index lists three entries — the Wu Zhao Da (his own biography, 63-0012) and two Wei 校事 entries (cited in 24-0014 and 27-0000). **Inference:** the two Wei 校事 entries are the same person, since both describe a Wei 校事 named Zhao Da serving under Cao Cao (太祖), in the same office and era — one paired with Lu Hong and later executed [5], the other questioning Xu Miao and reporting him [12]. No third, distinct Zhao Da appears in the texts. Hence two distinct persons in all.

q: What is the story of Kuan Yü killing Ts'ai Yang at Ku-ch'eng?
reply:
## Conclusion

The《三国志》does **not** contain any story of Guan Yu killing Cai Yang at Gucheng (古城). In the histories, the man who defeated/killed Cai Yang is **Liu Bei** (or, in a parallel account, the local rebel Gong Du) — not Guan Yu, and no place called Gucheng figures in the episode at all. "Guan Yu kills Cai Yang at Gucheng" belongs to the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, not to the histories.

## What the histories actually say

**1. Cai Yang is sent by Cao Cao and killed by Liu Bei.**

In the *Record of the First Sovereign* (先主傳), the sequence is: after Cao Cao seized Guan Yu and Liu Bei fled to Yuan Shao, Guan Yu escaped and returned to Liu Bei —

> 「曹公與袁紹相拒於官渡，汝南黃巾劉辟等叛曹公應紹。紹遣先主將兵與辟等略許下。關羽亡歸先主。曹公遣曹仁將兵擊先主，先主還紹軍，陰欲離紹，乃說紹南連荊州牧劉表。紹遣先主將本兵復至汝南，與賊龔都等合，眾數千人。曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺。」[1]

So the text explicitly says: Cao Cao sent Cai Yang against him, and **「為先主所殺」** — "he was killed by the First Sovereign (Liu Bei)." Guan Yu's only role here is 「關羽亡歸先主」 — Guan Yu escaped and returned to Liu Bei.

**2. A second account: Cai Yang is defeated by Gong Du.**

The *Annals of Emperor Wu* (武帝紀) gives a slightly different version, in a passage dated to the sixth year of Jian'an:

> 「紹之未破也，使劉備略汝南，汝南賊共都等應之。遣蔡揚擊都，不利，為都所破。」[38]

Here Cao Cao sends "Cai Yang" (蔡揚) against Gong Du (共都), and he is defeated by Gong Du — not killed by Guan Yu. The two accounts of the histories thus differ on the details (killed by Liu Bei vs. defeated by Gong Du); neither involves Guan Yu.

**3. Guan Yu's actual departure from Cao Cao.**

Guan Yu's real "return to Liu Bei" is recorded in his own biography, but with no Cai Yang and no Gucheng:

> 「羽盡封其所賜，拜書告辭，而奔先主於袁軍。左右欲追之，曹公曰：『彼各為其主，勿追也。』」[2]

So Guan Yu left Cao Cao's service openly, after the victory at Baima (where he killed Yan Liang), and went back to Liu Bei in Yuan Shao's camp. The histories record no pursuit by Cai Yang, and Cao Cao expressly forbade pursuit.

## Inference

Putting these facts together: the histories place Cai Yang's defeat/killing in the Jian'an 5–6 period (200–201 CE) [3][4], during Liu Bei's operations in Runan (汝南) against Cao Cao, after Guan Yu had already returned to Liu Bei. Since the histories attribute the killing to Liu Bei (先主傳) or the defeat to Gong Du (武帝紀), and since Guan Yu is described only as having 「亡歸先主」, it is **inferred** that the deed was not Guan Yu's in the historical record. The name "Gucheng" appears nowhere in connection with this event.

## Background (not from the《三国志》)

The story of Guan Yu, after leaving Cao Cao, escorting Liu Bei's two wives through "five passes and slaying six generals," then meeting at Gucheng (古城) where he kills Cai Yang — this episode is not found in the《三国志》; it comes from the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国演义》) and related popular tradition. The historical《三国志》records only that Guan Yu left Cao Cao, sealed up his gifts, took his leave by letter, and returned to Liu Bei in Yuan Shao's camp [2], while Cai Yang was defeated and killed in the Runan campaign — by Liu Bei according to the 先主傳 [1], or by Gong Du according to the 武帝紀 [38].

q: A strategic proposal called for first occupying Jing and Yi Provinces, allying with Sun Quan, waiting for a change in the situation in the north, and then advancing along two routes. If Jing Province were lost, which key precondition of this strategy would no longer hold?
reply:
## Conclusion

The key precondition that would no longer hold is **「跨有荊、益」— holding Jing Province and Yi Province together** (and with it, the two-pronged advance, the "two routes," which depended on Jing as the base of the eastern army).

## The proposal and its conditions

In the Longzhong conversation (recorded in Zhuge Liang's biography), Zhuge Liang laid out the plan to Liu Bei:

「若跨有荊、益，保其巖阻，西和諸戎，南撫夷越，外結好孫權，內修政理；天下有變，則命一上將將荊州之軍以向宛、洛，將軍身率益州之眾出於秦川」[1]

("If you hold both Jing and Yi across, hold their crags and defiles, befriend the Rong in the west, pacify the Yi and Yue in the south, externally bind yourself in friendship to Sun Quan, and internally order your government; then when there is a change in the world, order one senior general to lead the army of Jing Province toward Wan and Luo, while you yourself lead the host of Yi Province out through Qin River.")

So the elements are: (1) 跨有荊、益 — holding both provinces; (2) 保其巖阻 — holding their natural defenses; (3) 西和諸戎、南撫夷越 — a settled rear; (4) 外結好孫權 — the alliance with Sun Quan; (5) 內修政理 — internal government. Only after these does the plan produce 「天下有變，則命一上將將荊州之軍以向宛、洛，將軍身率益州之眾出於秦川」[1] — the two-route attack, with the Jing army striking toward Wan and Luo and the Yi army toward Qin River.

## Why the loss of Jing kills it

The two routes are named by their provinces: 「一上將將荊州之軍」 and 「將軍身率益州之眾」[1]. Zhuge Liang had earlier described Jing as a key strategic hinge: 「荊州北據漢、沔，利盡南海，東連吳會，西通巴、蜀，此用武之國」[3] ("Jing Province holds the Han and Mian rivers on the north, its advantages run to the South Sea, it joins Wu and Kuaiji on the east, and connects to Ba and Shu on the west — this is a land for the use of arms").

Jing was in fact lost. In the twenty-fourth year of Jian'an, Sun Quan attacked Guan Yu; 「十二月，璋司馬馬忠獲羽及其子平、都督趙累等於章鄉，遂定荊州」[29] ("In the twelfth month, Ma Zhong, the Sima of Pan Zhang, captured Guan Yu, his son Guan Ping, and the Commander Zhao Lei and others at Zhangxiang, and Jing Province was settled [i.e., taken]"). Elsewhere: 「孫權殺關羽，并荊土」[12] ("Sun Quan killed Guan Yu and annexed the land of Jing").

**Inference (following from the facts above):** the plan required two armies, one based in Jing and one in Yi. Once Sun Quan had annexed Jing and Guan Yu — the general in charge of Jing — was dead, there was no longer a "荆州之軍" to send toward Wan and Luo, so the "cross-holding of Jing and Yi" was gone and the eastern arm of the two-route advance could not be mounted at all; only the Yi-province route toward Qin River remained. Note also that this precondition is bound up with the alliance clause 「外結好孫權」[1]: Jing was precisely the territory over which Liu Bei and Sun Quan had already come to blows — in Jian'an 20 Sun Quan had sent Lü Meng to seize Changsha, Lingling, and Guiyang, and the two sides redivided Jing, with 「長沙、江夏、桂陽以東屬權，南郡、零陵、武陵以西屬備」[27]. So the loss of Jing not only removed the eastern army's base but also meant the alliance was no longer the alliance of the original plan. (This last point is my inference, drawn from those two facts; the texts do not themselves say the plan thereby failed.)

q: This man originally served under Liu Zhang but later became one of Liu Bei's key advisers. He helped plan the seizure of Yi Province and accompanied Liu Bei in the contest for Hanzhong. He died of illness before Liu Bei did, and so had no part in the deathbed entrustment. Who was he?
reply:
The man is **Fa Zheng (法正), courtesy name Xiaozhi (孝直)** of Fufeng Mei.

**Why it fits**

- He first served Liu Zhang: 「建安初，天下饑荒，正與同郡孟達俱入蜀依劉璋，久之為新都令，後召署軍議校尉」[1] — early in Jian'an, during famine, Fa Zheng entered Shu with Meng Da to rely on Liu Zhang, served as magistrate of Xindu, then as military advisory commandant, but was not employed to his satisfaction.
- He became one of Liu Bei's key planners: through Zhang Song's recommendation he was sent as envoy to Liu Bei and secretly offered the plan to take Yi Province — 「正既宣旨，陰獻策於先主曰：『以明將軍之英才，乘劉牧之懦弱；張松，州之股肱，以響應於內；然後資益州之殷富，馮天府之險阻，以此成業，猶反掌也。』」[1]. After Chengdu fell, 「先主复領益州牧……法正為謀主」[2].
- He accompanied Liu Bei in the Hanzhong campaign: 「先主善其策，乃率諸將進兵漢中，正亦從行」[11]; at Dingjun Mountain 「正曰：『可擊矣。』先主命黃忠乘高鼓譟攻之，大破淵軍，淵等授首」[11].
- He died of illness before Liu Bei: 「先主立為漢中王，以正為尚書令、護軍將軍。明年卒，時年四十五。先主為之流涕者累日」[3]. Liu Bei became King of Hanzhong in the 24th year of Jian'an (= AD 219) [era: 建安24 = 219], so Fa Zheng died the following year.
- He therefore took no part in the deathbed entrustment, which came later: 「先主病篤，託孤於丞相亮，尚書令李嚴為副」[30], in the third year of Zhangwu (= AD 223) [era: 章武3 = 223].

**Inference (based on the above):** Since Fa Zheng's death is dated to the year after Liu Bei became King of Hanzhong (219), i.e. c. 220, and Liu Bei's deathbed entrustment to Zhuge Liang and Li Yan is placed in Zhangwu 3 (223), Fa Zheng had already been dead about three years and could not have been present. The text itself underscores the gap: Zhuge Liang later sighed, 「法孝直若在，則能制主上，令不東行；就復東行，必不傾危矣」[3] — "if Fa Xiaozhi were alive, he could have restrained the ruler…"

**Note:** The phrase "key adviser" is a description, not a title; the text calls him 「謀主」[2] (chief strategist) after the conquest of Yi Province.

q: In the Battle of Bowang, how did Zhuge Liang set the fire ambush against Xiahou Dun?
reply:
## Conclusion

In the *Sanguozhi*, there is **no account of Zhuge Liang setting a fire ambush at Bowang**. The ambush was set by **Liu Bei himself**, and the "fire" was Liu Bei **burning his own camp** as a ruse to fake a retreat. The famous "Bowang Slope fire" is a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* invention.

## What the sources actually say

**1. Liu Bei (not Zhuge Liang) laid the ambush and burned his own camp.**

The *Xianzhu zhuan* (Record of the First Sovereign) states that Liu Biao "sent him to resist Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin and others at Bowang":

「使拒夏侯惇、于禁等於博望。久之，先主設伏兵，一旦自燒屯偽遁，惇等追之，為伏兵所破。」[1]

*"He was sent to resist Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin and others at Bowang. After a long time, the First Sovereign set an ambush; one morning he himself burned his camp and feigned flight. Dun and the others pursued him, and were broken by the ambush."*

So the subject throughout is 先主 (Liu Bei). The burning was of **Liu Bei's own camp** — a decoy — not a fire-trap set by Zhuge Liang.

**2. Li Dian's account gives the tactical detail.**

The *Li Dian* biography: "Liu Biao sent Liu Bei north to invade, reaching Ye; the Grand Ancestor sent Li Dian to follow Xiahou Dun and resist him."

「備一旦燒屯去，惇率諸軍追擊之，典曰：『賊無故退，疑必有伏。南道狹窄，草木深，不可追也。』惇不聽，與於禁追之，典留守。惇等果入賊伏里，戰不利，典往救，備望見救至，乃散退。」[5]

*"Liu Bei burned his camp and left in one morning. Dun led all the armies to pursue. Li Dian said: 'The enemy retreats without cause; I suspect there must be an ambush. The southern road is narrow, the grass and trees are thick — we must not pursue.' Dun would not listen, and pursued with Yu Jin, while Li Dian stayed to guard. Dun and the others indeed entered the enemy's ambush; the fighting went badly. Li Dian went to the rescue; Liu Bei, seeing the relief arrive, scattered and withdrew."*

This confirms the sequence: **burn camp → fake retreat → enemy pursues into the ambush → ambushers attack → relief force arrives → Liu Bei withdraws.**

## Inferred point

According to Pei Songzhi's note, Liu Bei first met Zhuge Liang only **the year before** his defeat in Jian'an 13:

「臣松之案：劉備以建安十三年敗，遣亮使吳……然則備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也。」[27]

*"Your servant Songzhi notes: Liu Bei was defeated in Jian'an 13 and sent Liang on a mission to Wu… Thus Liu Bei first met Liang in the year before the defeat of his army."*

Since Jian'an 13 is the year of the Red Cliffs campaign, this places their first meeting in Jian'an 12 — after the Bowang engagement described above. Combining this with facts [1] and [5], **by inference** the Bowang ambush was fought by Liu Bei on his own, before Zhuge Liang had joined him, so Zhuge Liang cannot have planned it.

## Background (not from the *Sanguozhi*)

The story of Zhuge Liang commanding the "fire attack at Bowang Slope" as his debut battle — with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei carrying out his orders and Xiahou Dun being lured into a burning valley — is the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*' version; the *Sanguozhi* records no such thing, and instead credits the ruse to Liu Bei himself, with Li Dian's warning and rescue as the only detailed tactical account.

q: One side had the advantage in troops and supplies; the other, in a prolonged standoff, was running short of grain. In the end the weaker side, acting on intelligence from a defector, raided the enemy's main grain depot and turned the battle around. Which battle was this, and who was the defector?
reply:
**Conclusion:** This was the **Battle of Guandu (官渡之戰)**, fought in the fifth year of Jian'an (建安五年 = 200 CE). The defector was **Xu You (許攸, courtesy name Ziyuan 子遠)**, a strategist on Yuan Shao's side.

**The setup — one side strong in men and grain, the other short of food in a long standoff:**

Yuan Shao's side had the numbers and the supplies. Yuan Shao's own adviser Ju Shou (沮授) summed up the asymmetry: 「北兵數衆而果勁不及南，南穀虛少而貨財不及北；南利在於急戰，北利在於緩搏。宜徐持久，曠以日月。」[11] — the northern army was numerous but the southern army's grain was scarce, so Yuan Shao should protract the standoff. On Cao Cao's side, the shortage was acute: 「公與紹相拒連月，雖比戰斬將，然衆少糧盡，士卒疲乏」[5], and Cao Cao even wrote to Xun Yu about pulling back to Xu because 「太祖軍糧方盡」[6].

**The defection and the raid:**

Xu You came over because his greed was not satisfied and, per one account, because Shen Pei had arrested his family: 「紹謀臣許攸貪財，紹不能足，來奔，因說公擊瓊等」[5]; and 「審配以許攸家不法，收其妻子，攸怒叛紹」[6]. He told Cao Cao exactly where Yuan Shao's grain was and that it was poorly guarded. In the *Cao Man Zhuan* (裴注引《曹瞞傳》), Xu You says: 「今袁氏輜重有萬餘乘，在故市、烏巢，屯軍無嚴備；今以輕兵襲之，不意而至，燔其積聚，不過三日，袁氏自敗也。」[1]

Cao Cao acted on it: 「公乃留曹洪守，自將步騎五千人夜往，會明至……士卒皆殊死戰，大破瓊等，皆斬之。」[5] The target was the depot at **Wu Chao (烏巢)**, guarded by Chunyu Qiong (淳于瓊). After the depot fell, Yuan Shao's army collapsed: 「紹衆大潰，紹及譚棄軍走，渡河」[5]. Cao Cao reported the outcome as 「與戰官渡……得斬紹大將淳于瓊等八人首，遂大破潰……凡斬首七萬餘級」[12].

**Inference (based on the facts above):** Yuan Shao held the advantage in manpower and grain, while Cao Cao was, by his own admission in the letters to Xun Yu, short of food and considering withdrawal. Xu You, an insider, supplied the location and the weak guard of the grain depot; Cao Cao's night raid on Wu Chao destroyed that depot. Since the destruction of the grain reserve removed the very advantage Yuan Shao had been relying on to outlast Cao Cao, it is reasonable to infer that the raid — and the intelligence that enabled it — was the turning point that reversed the campaign.

**Note on the defector's later fate:** The *Wei Lüe* (裴注引《魏略》) says Xu You had known both Yuan Shao and Cao Cao since youth, and that after Yuan Shao's defeat he grew arrogant and taunted Cao Cao with his own childhood name: 「某甲，卿不得我，不得冀州也」[3], which Cao Cao resented; Xu You was eventually arrested after boasting at Ye's east gate [3]. This is separate from his role at Guandu.

q: This man first served Yüan Shao and later went over to Ts'ao Ts'ao. He fought in Han-chung, defeated Ma Su at Chieh-t'ing, and finally died at Mu-men while pursuing the Shu army. Who was he?
reply:
The man was **Zhang He (張郃), courtesy name Junyi (雋乂)**, of Mo County in Hejian. Here is the evidence from the《三国志》.

**Served Yuan Shao, then went over to Cao Cao**
His biography begins: 「張郃字雋乂，河間鄚人也。漢末應募討黃巾，爲軍司馬，屬韓馥。馥敗，以兵歸袁紹。」[3] — after Han Fu's defeat he took his troops to Yuan Shao, who made him a Colonel. At Guandu his advice to rescue Chunyu Qiong was rejected, and after slander by Guo Tu: 「郃懼，乃歸太祖。」[3] (Cao Cao welcomed him, comparing him to "Weizi leaving Yin and Han Xin joining Han") [5].

**Fought in Hanzhong**
「太祖征張魯……至陽平，魯降，太祖還，留郃與夏侯淵等守漢中，拒劉備。」[5] He campaigned there, and after Xiahou Yuan's death the army made him commander: 「遂推郃爲軍主。郃出，勒兵安陳，諸將皆受郃節度，衆心乃定。」[11]

**Defeated Ma Su at Jieting**
「諸葛亮出祁山。加郃位特進，遣督諸軍，拒亮將馬謖於街亭。謖依阻南山，不下據城。郃絶其汲道，擊，大破之。」[10] The same is recorded in Zhuge Liang's and Ma Su's biographies: 「與郃戰于街亭。謖違亮節度，舉動失宜，大爲張郃所破」[2]; 「與魏將張郃戰於街亭，爲郃所破」[8].

**Died at Mumen pursuing the Shu army**
「諸葛亮復出祁山，詔郃督諸將西至略陽，亮還保祁山，郃追至木門，與亮軍交戰，飛矢中郃右膝，薨，諡曰壯侯。子雄嗣。」[13]

So all four points in your question match Zhang He's biography.

**A discrepancy worth noting (two versions in the sources):**
- The *Wei* biography and the *Weilüe* commentary say he died at **Mumen**: 「郃追至木門……飛矢中郃右膝，薨」[13]; 「蜀軍乘高布伏，弓弩亂發，矢中郃髀」— Pei Songzhi's note quotes《魏略》, and it adds that Sima Xuanwang (Sima Yi) ordered the pursuit despite Zhang He's objection: 「司馬宣王使郃追之……宣王不聽。郃不得已，遂進。」[14] (note: here the arrow hits the *thigh*, 髀, whereas the main text says the *right knee*, 右膝).
- The *Shu* record of the Later Ruler gives a different place: 「亮糧盡退軍，郃追至青封，與亮交戰，被箭死」[15].

I have cited each version as it stands rather than deciding between Mumen and Qingfeng.

**Inference (my own, from the facts above):** the sources agree that Zhang He died from an arrow wound while pursuing Zhuge Liang's retreating army; they disagree on the exact place (木門 vs 青封), on whether the wound was in the knee or the thigh, and the《魏略》alone says Sima Yi compelled the pursuit. Since these accounts differ, the safest conclusion is that he died in a pursuit ordered by the Wei command, struck by an arrow — without treating any single version as certain.

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The popular image of Zhang He as a general repeatedly outmaneuvered and finally "forced" to his death by Sima Yi's jealousy comes largely from《三国演义》and later tradition; the《三国志》records only the brief accounts quoted above.

q: Cao Cao took in Emperor Xian of Han and issued orders in the name of the Han central government. Compared with relying on military strength alone, what political advantage did this chiefly bring him?
reply:
## Conclusion

The chief political advantage was **legitimacy**: by taking in Emperor Xian, Cao Cao could act as the Han government rather than as one warlord among many — issuing orders, conferring offices, and waging war in the state's name. The《三国志》frames this not merely as a propaganda trick but as a triple gain: winning the populace, overawing the powerful, and drawing in talented men.

## Evidence

**1. The two advisers' arguments state the advantage explicitly.**

Mao Jie (毛玠) told Cao Cao:「宜奉天子以令不臣，脩耕植，畜軍資，如此則霸王之業可成也。」[20] — "You should support the Son of Heaven in order to command the insubordinate, improve farming, and store up military supplies; thus the enterprise of hegemon-king can be achieved."

Xun Yu (荀彧), in 建安元年 (= 196 CE), argued it was a threefold benefit:「誠因此時，奉主上以從民望，大順也；秉至公以服雄傑，大略也；扶弘義以致英俊，大德也。」[9] — "Sincerely seizing this moment to support the sovereign and follow the people's hopes is the supreme conformity; holding to perfect impartiality so as to subdue the heroes is the supreme strategy; upholding the great righteousness so as to draw in the outstanding is the supreme virtue." He added that even rebels could not then harm him, and that delay would let "the four quarters conceive their own designs."

**2. The concrete results.**

The 武帝紀 records that after the emperor was brought to 許,「天子假太祖節鉞，錄尚書事」and then「自天子西遷，朝廷日亂，至是宗廟社稷制度始立」[41] — the court's ancestral-temple and state-altar system was only re-established at this point. The 袁紹傳 notes:「會太祖迎天子都許，收河南地，關中皆附。」[45] — Cao Cao took the land south of the Yellow River and the Guanzhong region all submitted.

**3. Contemporaries treated the advantage as real and decisive.**

Pei Songzhi's note to the 武帝紀, quoting《獻帝春秋》, records a deserter from Yuan Shao's army saying:「田豐使紹早襲許，若挾天子以令諸侯，四海可指麾而定。」[17] — Tian Feng had urged Yuan Shao to strike at Xu first, for whoever "held the Son of Heaven to command the lords" could settle the empire at a gesture. The same《獻帝春秋》records Yuan Shao's own furious reaction:「曹操當死數矣，我輒救存之，今乃背恩，挾天子以令我乎！」[5] — "How often Cao Cao deserved death, and I saved him each time; now he repays the favor by holding the Son of Heaven to order me about!"

## Inference

Putting these facts together: Xun Yu's three points (people's hopes / subduing the heroes / attracting the able) map directly onto the recorded results —「收河南地，關中皆附」[45] is submission, and the re-establishment of court institutions [41] is the machinery of legitimacy. Because the emperor's commissions were now Cao Cao's to dispense (he was given 節鉞 and 錄尚書事 [41]), offices and titles could be used as rewards and bait. Yuan Shao's regret and Tian Feng's lost plan [17][45] suggest that contemporaries judged this a decisive edge over raw military strength — and Yuan Shao's own outburst [5] shows the orders he received under that name were felt as a real constraint on a rival who was militarily stronger.

This is a comparison drawn from the texts, not a claim that the texts give a causal verdict.

## One qualification from the sources

The advantage was contested. Zhou Yu (周瑜) of Wu, urging resistance, said:「操雖託名漢相，其實漢賊也。」[32] — "Cao Cao may falsely claim the name of Han Chancellor, but he is in truth a traitor to Han." So the legitimacy was a claim that did not convince everyone; the 周瑜傳 records it being rejected outright.

q: Before the Battle of Red Cliffs, Liu Bei was comparatively weak, while Sun Quan held the Jiangdong territory and a navy. Given this imbalance, why did Sun Quan still have an incentive to ally with Liu Bei rather than stand by and let Cao Cao destroy him?
reply:
## Conclusion

Sun Quan's incentive was not charity toward a weak neighbor. The records show three linked reasons: (1) standing aside was not a safe option — Cao Cao's demand was aimed at Wu itself, so Sun Quan had to fight anyway, and Liu Bei was the only available partner; (2) Liu Bei was not negligible — he still had roughly 20,000 men plus a river fleet and a claim on Jing province's people, precisely the things Sun Quan lacked on land; (3) Sun Quan's advisers argued that keeping Liu Bei alive multiplied Cao Cao's enemies while costing Sun Quan little, since Liu Bei could rally the Jing province populace that had submitted to Cao Cao only under duress.

## Evidence

**1. Standing aside was not on offer; Cao Cao's target was Wu.**

Cao Cao's letter to Sun Quan, recorded in Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Jiangbiao zhuan*: 「今治水軍八十萬眾，方與將軍會獵於吳。」[36] — "Now I have marshaled a water army of eight hundred thousand, and am about to go hunting with you in Wu." Sun Quan showed it to his officials, and 「莫不鄉震失色」[36] (none failed to turn pale with fright).

Lu Su's private argument to Sun Quan is the core of it: surrender was survivable for a subject, but not for a ruler — 「今肅可迎操耳，如將軍，不可也……將軍迎操，欲安所歸？」[16] — "I, Su, may welcome Cao; a man in your position may not… If you welcome Cao, where are you to go?" Lu Su had told Sun Quan years earlier that 「漢室不可復興，曹操不可卒除。為將軍計，惟有鼎足江東，以觀天下之釁」[50] ("the Han house cannot be revived, Cao Cao cannot be quickly removed; for you the only plan is to stand as one leg of a tripod in Jiangdong and watch for openings").

**2. Liu Bei was not a broken man — he brought troops and a fleet.**

Zhuge Liang's pitch to Sun Quan: 「豫州軍雖敗於長阪，今戰士還者及關羽水軍精甲萬人，劉琦合江夏戰士亦不下萬人」[11] — returning soldiers plus Guan Yu's marine armored troops made ten thousand, and Liu Qi's Jiangxia troops were no fewer than another ten thousand. The main *Xianzhu zhuan* likewise says Liu Bei joined Liu Qi's 「眾萬餘人」[1], and Guan Yu had been sent ahead with 「船數百艘」[46] (several hundred ships). Cao Cao himself treated Liu Bei as a peer: 「劉備，吾儕也」[6] ("Liu Bei is my equal").

**3. Liu Bei could deliver Jing province's people, which Sun Quan could not.**

Lu Su's memorial before Liu Biao's death: 「加劉備天下梟雄，與操有隙……及說備使撫表眾，同心一意，共治曹操，備必喜而從命」[14] — Liu Bei is a fierce hero of the realm with a grudge against Cao, so persuade him to pacify Liu Biao's following and "with one heart and one purpose, deal with Cao Cao together." And on whether to detain Liu Bei, Lu Su said no: 「將軍雖神武命世，然曹公威力實重，初臨荊州，恩信未洽，宜以藉備，使撫安之。多操之敵，而自為樹黨，計之上也。」[17] — Cao's power is still heavy; Sun Quan had just arrived in Jing province and had no恩信 there, so he should use Liu Bei to pacify it: "multiply Cao Cao's enemies and make a party for yourself — that is the best plan."

**4. Sun Quan's court also judged that resistance was feasible — i.e., an ally could tip the balance.**

Zhou Yu's assessment: Cao Cao's northern base was unsettled, with 「馬超、韓遂尚在關西，為操後患」; his men were giving up horses for boats, "本非中國所長"; it was deep winter with no fodder; and 「驅中國士眾遠涉江湖之間不習水土，必生疾病」[39]. He added the real numbers: 「彼所將中國人，不過十五六萬，且軍已久疲，所得表眾，亦極七八萬耳，尚懷狐疑」[21] — and 「夫以疲病之卒，御狐疑之眾，眾數雖多，甚未足畏」[21]. Zhuge Liang made the same point: 「北方之人，不習水戰；又荊州之民附操者，逼兵勢耳，非心服也」[2] (the Jing people submitted to Cao only under military pressure, not from conviction).

**5. Sun Quan's own stated reason.**

Sun Quan's answer to Zhuge Liang: 「非劉豫州莫可以當曹操者」[11] — "Apart from Liu Yuzhou, no one can stand up to Cao Cao." From Liu Bei's side, Liu Bei explained his own confidence that Sun Quan needed him: 「孤以仲謀所防在北，當賴孤為援」[34] ("I judged that Zhongmou's defense was directed north, and that he would rely on me as an outside support").

**6. The payoff afterward.**

Liu Bei and Zhou Yu pursued together [7]; 「先主遂收江南」[2] (Liu Bei then took the south of the Yangzi). Later Sun Quan let Liu Bei have Jing province on Lu Su's advice 「共拒曹公」, and Cao Cao, hearing of it, 「方作書，落筆於地」[15] (was writing a letter and dropped the brush). Sun Quan later listed this as one of Lu Su's two great services, though he also called lending the land "a shortcoming" [22]. Zhou Yu, for his part, saw the risk: 「劉備以梟雄之姿，而有關羽、張飛熊虎之將，必非久屈為人用者」[33], and proposed detaining him; Sun Quan refused because 「權以曹公在北方，當廣攬英雄，又恐備難卒制」[33] (Cao was in the north, so he should broadly recruit heroes — and he feared Liu Bei could not easily be controlled).

## Inference

Pulling the above together: surrender (or standing aside) did not offer Sun Quan a safe outcome, because Cao Cao's ultimatum was directed at Wu and Lu Su's logic — that a ruler who submits has nowhere to go — applied regardless of Liu Bei's fate [16][36]. Meanwhile resistance required land forces and local Jing support, which Liu Bei supplied [11][17][46]. And Cao Cao's army, per Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang, had identifiable weaknesses that a combined force could exploit [2][21][39]. From these facts it follows that allying with Liu Bei was not a favor to a weak man but the cheapest way for Sun Quan to add troops, ships, and Jing province legitimacy to a fight he had to wage anyway — which is exactly the "multiply Cao Cao's enemies, build your own party" calculus Lu Su stated [17]. The records do not contain a Sun Quan statement about "letting Liu Bei be destroyed"; that framing appears to be a modern reconstruction rather than a recorded motive.

A note on one source conflict: the *Wei shu* and *Jiuzhou chunqiu* (Pei Songzhi's note) report that Lu Su pretended to urge surrender to provoke Sun Quan, who "wanted to behead Su" [13]; Sun Sheng rejects this on the ground that the *Wu shu* and *Jiangbiao zhuan* say Lu Su argued against Cao from his first audience [13]. Pei Songzhi also notes the *Zhou Yu zhuan* credits the resistance plan solely to Zhou Yu while the *Zhuge Liang zhuan* credits Zhuge Liang, and concludes 「建計拒曹公，實始魯肅」[21] — the plan began with Lu Su.

q: This man did not personally lead the army that conquered Shu, yet he pushed the war of conquest forward while he controlled the Cao-Wei court. His son later replaced Cao-Wei and founded the Western Jin. Who was he?
reply:
The man was **Sima Zhao (司马昭)**, posthumously **Prince Wen of Jin (晋文王 / 晋文帝)**, the son of Sima Yi and father of Sima Yan, founder of the Western Jin.

**Evidence from the records**

He controlled the Cao-Wei court as Chancellor (相国) and directed the conquest of Shu without leading the conquering army himself:

- 「文王以蜀大將姜維屢擾邊陲，料蜀國小民疲，資力單竭，欲大舉圖蜀。」[12] — "King Wen, because the Shu general Jiang Wei repeatedly harassed the frontier and reckoning that Shu was a small state with an exhausted people and depleted resources, wished to undertake a great enterprise against Shu."
- The same passage records that in the autumn of Jingyuan 4 (景元四年), he issued the edict sending Deng Ai and Zhuge Xu with over 30,000 men each, while 「會統十餘萬眾，分從斜谷、駱谷入」[12] — Zhong Hui commanded the main force of over 100,000. The conquest was thus carried out by Zhong Hui and Deng Ai, not by Sima Zhao in person.
- 「四年秋，詔諸軍征蜀，大將軍司馬文王皆指授節度」[16] — "In the autumn of the fourth year, an edict ordered the various armies to march against Shu; the Grand General, King Wen of Jin, personally assigned all the dispositions." This is the sense in which he "pushed the war forward" from the court.
- He chose the commander himself: 「初，文王欲遣會伐蜀」[10] — "Initially, King Wen wished to send Zhong Hui to attack Shu."

His son replaced Cao-Wei:

- 「命撫軍大將軍新昌鄉侯炎為晉世子」[22] — Sima Yan was made Heir of Jin.
- 「秋八月辛卯，相國晉王薨。壬辰，晉太子炎紹封襲位，總攝百揆」[23] — "In the eighth month... the Chancellor, the Prince of Jin, died. On the next day, the Jin Heir Sima Yan inherited the fief and succeeded to the position, assuming general control of all affairs."
- Pei's note quoting the *Xiangyang Ji*: 「明年十二月而晉武帝即尊位」[20] — "In the twelfth month of the following year, Emperor Wu of Jin ascended the honored throne," i.e. Sima Yan took the throne and founded Jin.

**Years**

- The conquest of Shu was ordered in Jingyuan 4 = **263 CE** [era: 景元4年 = 263].
- Sima Zhao died and Sima Yan succeeded in Xianxi 2 = **265 CE** [era: 咸熙2年 = 265], the year Sima Yan took the throne.

**Inference (据此推断)**

The records show that the campaign of 263 was commanded in the field by Zhong Hui and Deng Ai, while Sima Zhao "personally assigned all the dispositions" from the court [16][12]; only afterward, when Zhong Hui reported Deng Ai for insubordination, did Sima Zhao move west himself, and by the time his army reached Chang'an Zhong Hui was already dead: 「軍至長安，會果已死」[10]. Combining these facts, it is consistent with the records to say that Sima Zhao drove the war of conquest forward through his control of the Wei court without personally commanding the army that took Shu.

q: While Kuan Yü was attacking Fan in the north, Sun Ch'üan's side seized Chiang-ling and other places in his rear. Why could Kuan Yü still collapse so quickly overall, even though he had won a major victory on the northern front?
reply:
## Conclusion

The short answer: Guan Yu's northern victory at Fan (樊) in 219 was won with his rear stripped bare, and Sun Quan's strike did not merely "take some places behind him" — it took his **base, his family, and his men's families** in a single stroke, while the northern front simultaneously turned against him. So the collapse was fast because it was structural, not because of one battle lost.

Below, the evidence, then a reasoned inference.

## The evidence

**1. The northern "victory" was already reversing.** Guan Yu flooded Yu Jin's seven armies and captured Yu Jin, and "羽威震華夏"[36]. But Cao Cao sent Xu Huang to relieve Cao Ren, and the result was: 「而曹公遣徐晃救曹仁，羽不能克，引軍退還」[36]. In the Wei annals: 「晃攻羽，破之，羽走，仁圍解」[1]. So when the rear blow came, Guan Yu was already an army in retreat, not a victorious one.

**2. Guan Yu had deliberately drained his own rear to push north — exactly as Lü Meng predicted.** Lü Meng's memorial: 「羽討樊而多留備兵，必恐蒙圖其後故也。蒙常有病，乞分士眾還建業，以治疾為名。羽聞之，必撤備兵，盡赴襄陽」[15]. And it worked: 「羽果信之，稍撤兵以赴樊」[15].

**3. Sun Quan's decision was made well in advance, and masked by flattery.** Lü Meng's plan was set before Guan Yu marched: 「蒙乃密陳計策曰……不如取羽，全據長江」[14]. Lu Xun, posing as an unthreatening replacement, wrote Guan Yu a groveling letter; 「羽覽遜書，有謙下自托之意，意大安，無復所嫌」[21]. Sun Quan also flatly refused to answer Quan Cong's memorial lest the plan leak: 「權時已與呂蒙陰議襲之，恐事洩，故寢琮表不答」[9].

**4. Wei and Wu were effectively coordinating — Wei wanted Wu to stab Guan Yu in the back.** Sima Yi and Jiang Ji advised Cao Cao: 「可遣人勸權躡其後，許割江南以封權，則樊圍自解」, and Cao Cao did so [36][4]. Sun Quan's envoy offered to serve Wei by attacking Guan Yu [31], and Dong Zhao had Xu Huang shoot copies of Sun Quan's letter into the siege lines, both to hearten the defenders and to make Guan Yu hesitate: 「羽果猶豫」[28]. Sun Quan's own troops were therefore expected and welcome.

**5. The two men guarding his rear defected immediately.** Mi Fang (南郡太守, at Jiangling) and Shi Ren (general, at Gong'an) had long resented Guan Yu's contempt and feared his threat to punish them on return: 「素皆嫌羽輕己……羽言『還當治之』，芳、仁咸懷懼不安。於是權陰誘芳、仁，芳、仁使人迎權」[36]. Lü Meng arrived and 「士仁、麋芳皆降」[15]. The record states their grudge plainly: 「與羽有隙，叛迎孫權」[12].

**6. The strike was a surprise, and it cost Guan Yu his whole foundation.** Lü Meng hid his troops in the hulls disguised as merchants and seized every riverside watch-post so that no warning reached Guan Yu: 「至羽所置江邊屯候，盡收縛之，是故羽不聞知」[15]. He then took the city, 「盡得羽及將士家屬」, treated the families well, and enforced discipline (even executing a soldier for taking a peasant's hat) [15].

**7. That is what dissolved the army.** Lü Meng treated Guan Yu's returning envoys lavishly and let them tour the city and carry letters home; 「咸知家門無恙，見待過於平時，故羽吏士無鬬心」[20]. The result: 「權已據江陵，盡虜羽士眾妻子，羽軍遂散」[36]; 「眾皆委羽而降」[20]. Guan Yu fled to Mai Cheng, and Zhu Ran and Pan Zhang cut off his road: 「即父子俱獲，荊州遂定」[20], 「斬羽及子平於臨沮」[36].

## Inference (marked as such)

Putting only the facts above together: (a) Guan Yu's base, families, and supply were all in Jiangling/Gong'an; (b) he had moved his reserve troops north on the strength of Lü Meng's feigned illness; (c) his watch-posts were destroyed so he learned of the attack too late; (d) the two rear commanders surrendered without a fight; (e) the northern front had already turned against him with Xu Huang's victory. From these, the collapse does not need a second defeat to explain it: **the moment Jiangling fell, his army's reason to fight — home and family — was gone, and he had no fortified base left to retreat to.** His field victory at Fan was in fact what made this possible, since it was the victory that let him pull his rear troops forward. Note that the record does not say the northern victory "caused" the rear attack; the two are best read as simultaneous developments that Wei and Wu deliberately arranged to coincide.

## Background (not from the Sanguozhi)

The following is not a record in the *Sanguozhi*: the dramatic framing in some later accounts of this episode as a single decisive "betrayal" is a simplification — the *Sanguozhi* presents it as a premeditated plan (Lü Meng's and Lu Xun's memorials), carried out with Wei's encouragement.

q: Identify the stratagem: Wang Yun used Diaochan to sow suspicion between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu, and in the end had Dong Zhuo killed by Lü Bu's hand. What is this stratagem usually called?
reply:
**结论：这个计谋通常叫「连环计」（也称「王允献貂蝉」「美人计」）。** 不过这是《三国演义》的说法，《三国志》里没有貂蝉这个人，也没有用貂蝉离间董卓、吕布这回事。

**《三国志》里实际的记载：**

董卓与吕布之间确实生了嫌隙，但起因不是貂蝉，而是一名叫「侍婢」的女子：

- 吕布原受董卓宠爱信任，二人誓为父子：「卓以布見信於原，誘布令殺原。布斬原首詣卓，卓以布為騎都尉，甚愛信之，誓為父子」[7]。
- 后来董卓因小事发怒，掷手戟打吕布，吕布躲开，从此暗恨董卓；又因替董卓守中阁时与其侍婢私通，心中不安：「卓性剛而褊……嘗小失意，拔手戟擲布……由是陰怨卓。卓常使布守中閤，布與卓侍婢私通，恐事發覺，心不自安」[8]。
- 真正去联络吕布做内应的，是司徒王允和尚书仆射士孙瑞，而不是靠献美女：「時允與僕射士孫瑞密謀誅卓，是以告布使為內應。布曰：『奈如父子何！』允曰：『君自姓呂，本非骨肉……』布遂許之，手刃刺卓」[1]。

**刺杀经过（初平三年四月）：**

「三年四月，司徒王允、尚書僕射士孫瑞、卓將呂布共謀誅卓……布使同郡騎都尉李肅等將親兵十餘人，偽著衞士服守掖門。布懷詔書。卓至，肅等格卓……布曰『有詔』，遂殺卓，夷三族」[3]。可见董卓是王允、士孙瑞、吕布三人合谋，由吕布亲手所杀。

**据此推断：** 由上引几条可知，《三国志》中董卓之死是王允等人趁吕布已对董卓心怀怨恨、又恐惧私通侍婢之事败露，才拉吕布做内应而成功的；吕布与董卓的不和早已存在，并不是王允用一个女子离间出来的。所谓「王允用貂蝉离间董卓与吕布」，在《三国志》里找不到对应记载。

**以下不是《三国志》的记载：**
问题里说的王允用貂蝉离间董卓、吕布，这套「连环计／美人计」的情节，《三国志》里没有记载（书中只有吕布与董卓侍婢私通一事，无「貂蝉」其人），可能出自《三国演义》或其他非正史的说法；「连环计」「王允献貂蝉」是小说、戏曲里对这一段故事的称法。

q: The Oath of the Peach Garden: after Liu Pei, Kuan Yü and Chang Fei swore brotherhood, what was the order of seniority among the three?
reply:
**结论**：所谓"桃园结义"以及由此排定的"刘备为长、关羽次之、张飞最幼"的固定排行，在《三国志》里没有记载。正史只记到两点：刘备与关、张二人"恩若兄弟"，以及关羽年长于张飞数岁、张飞以兄礼事关羽。刘备与关、张谁年长，《三国志》没有交代。

**依据（原文）**

1. 《关羽传》记三人的关系是"恩若兄弟"，并未结拜：
「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟。而稠人廣坐，侍立終日，隨先主周旋，不避艱險。」[1]
——刘备与关、张同床而眠，情谊如同兄弟；在人多的场合，二人整天侍立刘备身旁。

2. 《张飞传》明确写了关、张之间的长幼：
「張飛字益德，涿郡人也，少與關羽俱事先主。羽年長數歲，飛兄事之。」[2]
——张飞年少时与关羽一同跟随先主；关羽年长几岁，张飞把他当兄长侍奉。

**推断**：据以上两条，可以确定的是关、张之间关羽为长、张飞为幼（张飞"兄事之"）。至于刘备与关、张的长幼，正史在此处只说"恩若兄弟""侍立"，据此只能推断刘备处于主上、二人处于属下（"随先主周旋，不避艰险"），并不能据此判定刘备的年龄比关、张更大。

---

q: A Cao-Wei emperor left Luoyang to pay respects at the imperial tombs, and a senior minister who had long pleaded illness seized the chance to take control of the capital and force the other regent to surrender his power. What event was this, and who set it in motion?
reply:
**Short answer:** This is the Gaopingling Incident (高平陵之變), in the first month of the Cao-Wei era Zhengshi 10 / Jiaping 1, i.e. **249 CE**. The man who set it in motion was the Grand Tutor **Sima Yi (司馬懿, styled Zhongda)**, then titled 司馬宣王. The emperor was **Cao Fang (曹芳, the Prince of Qi)**, and the regent forced to give up power was the Grand General **Cao Shuang (曹爽)**.

**The setup — Sima Yi's long "illness"**

Cao Shuang and Sima Yi had both received Wei Mingdi's deathbed charge to assist the young ruler「與太尉司馬宣王並受遺詔輔少主」[2]. When Cao Shuang's party (He Yan, Ding Mi and others) pushed Sima Yi aside, Sima Yi withdrew by claiming illness:「宣王遂稱疾避爽」[10]. In the winter of Zhengshi 9, when Li Sheng came to take leave before going out as Inspector of Jingzhou, Sima Yi put on the act of a dying man:「宣王稱疾困篤，示以羸形。勝不能覺，謂之信然」[11].

**The coup**

In the first month of Zhengshi 10, the emperor went to worship at Gaopingling and Cao Shuang and his brothers all accompanied him:「十年正月，車駕朝高平陵，爽兄弟皆從。宣王部勒兵馬，先據武庫，遂出屯洛水浮橋」[11]. Sima Yi memorialized against Cao Shuang and had the Empress Dowager authorize it:「皇太後令勑臣如奏施行」[11]. The annals of the Prince of Qi record the same day:「嘉平元年春正月甲午，車駕謁高平陵。太傅司馬宣王奏免大將軍曹爽、爽弟中領軍羲、武衞將軍訓、散騎常侍彥官，以侯就第」[1]. Huan Fan fled to Cao Shuang and urged him to take the emperor to Xuchang and summon outside troops, but Cao Shuang hesitated and gave in:「爽於是遣允、泰詣宣王，歸罪請死，乃通宣王奏事。遂免爽兄弟，以侯還第」[4]. Sima Yi had sworn by the Luo River that only dismissal was intended:「以洛水爲誓。爽信之，罷兵」[13]. Cao Shuang was then destroyed with three clans wiped out:「皆與爽通姦謀，夷三族」[1].

**Dates:** the era tool gives 正始10年 = 249 CE and 嘉平1年 = 249 CE (the era was changed to Jiaping within that year).

**Inference:** since Sima Yi had long feigned illness and secretly prepared「宣王密爲之備」[10], and only moved once the emperor and Cao Shuang had left the capital for Gaopingling [11], it follows that the tomb visit gave him the opening he had been waiting for. Note that the sources differ on who initiated: the *Shishu* passage above (via Pei's note) has Sima Yi sending Xu Yun, Chen Tai and Yin Damu to talk Cao Shuang down [13], while the main text has Xu Yun and Chen Tai persuading Cao Shuang to surrender himself [4] — both agree Cao Shuang yielded without fighting.

**Background (not from the *Sanguozhi*):** 高平陵 (the tomb of Wei Mingdi) lies south of the Luo River on Mount Dashi, 90 li from Luoyang, per Pei's note citing Sun Sheng's *Wei Shiji*:「高平陵在洛水南大石山，去洛城九十里」[19].

q: Shu-Han's main base was Yi Province, and its northern expeditions had to haul grain across the mountains to the front. Why did 'winning a battle at the front' not necessarily mean 'being able to hold the newly gained territory for long'?
reply:
## Conclusion

In the *Sanguozhi*, Shu's northern campaigns show a repeated pattern: a battlefield success or a sudden enemy collapse (three commanderies switching sides, a Wei general killed) did **not** translate into lasting occupation, because the army's food supply — hauled from Yi Province across the Qinling mountains — ran out on a fixed clock. The sources state this explicitly from both sides.

## Evidence

**1. Wei commanders calculated Shu's retreat by counting its grain.**
Before Zhang He (張郃) went to relieve Chencang, he told Emperor Ming: 「郃知亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻」 and 「屈指計亮糧不至十日」[6]. The Wei court's whole strategy assumed Shu could not stay.

**2. Shu did in fact withdraw for lack of grain again and again, even right after a victory.**
- Chencang: 「冬，亮復出散關，圍陳倉，曹真拒之，亮糧盡而還」 — and only on the way home did he kill the pursuing Wang Shuang [7].
- 231 (建興九年): 「九年，亮復出祁山，以木牛運，糧盡退軍，與魏將張郃交戰，射殺郃」[4]; the *Houzhu zhuan* dates it: 「夏六月，亮糧盡退軍……與亮交戰，被箭死」[16]. So a dead Wei general and a "victory" came *during the withdrawal*, not before it.
- 230: Li Yan, in charge of transport, failed to keep the grain coming and recalled Zhuge Liang: 「秋夏之際，值天霖雨，運糧不繼，平遣參軍狐忠、督軍成籓喻指，呼亮來還；亮承以退軍」[21].
- 254 (延熙十六年): 「維率數萬人出石營，經董亭，圍南安。魏雍州刺史陳泰解圍至洛門，維糧盡退還」[37].

**3. The problem was structural, and Shu itself named it.**
Zhuge Liang at Wuzhang Plain: 「亮每患糧不繼，使己志不申，是以分兵屯田，為久駐之基」[4] — he had to farm on the spot precisely because the haul was unreliable. Earlier, when Liu Bei contested Hanzhong, Yang Hong described the mobilization: 「方今之事，男子當戰，女子當運」[24]. The route itself defeated armies: Cao Zhen's 230 invasion stalled when 「會大霖雨三十餘日，或棧道斷絕，詔真還軍」[13].

**4. The enemy could simply refuse battle and wait, or feed itself locally.**
- Sima Yi repeatedly refused engagement, so much so that his officers taunted him, 「公畏蜀如虎，奈天下笑何！」 and Emperor Ming had Xin Pi hold a tally to stop him fighting [10][5].
- Wei, by contrast, could tap local resources. Guo Huai, when 「隴右無穀，議欲關中大運」, instead 「以威恩撫循羌、胡，家使出穀，平其輸調，軍食用足」[8]. And in the 231 campaign, the Wei side reaped the Shanggui wheat: 「賴得此麥以爲軍糧」[1] — while Zhuge Liang had also cut and seized local wheat on the way [10].
- Shu's own later doctrine admits the logic: Jiang Wei proposed concentrating grain in Han/Lo cities so that an invader 「千里縣糧，自然疲乏」[34].

**5. Newly won territory was re-lost once the army left.**
After Jieting, three commanderies had gone over to Shu [14], but 「南安、天水、安定郡反應亮，郃皆破平之」[6]; Cao Zhen likewise 「三郡皆平」[13]. The defection lasted only as long as Shu's army was physically present.

## Inference

Putting the cited facts together: Shu's forces operated at the end of a mountain supply line (yang Hong's "women haul" mobilization [24], Cao Zhen's washed-out plank roads [13]), so their operating window was measured in days-to-weeks (Zhang He's "less than ten days" [6]). Whenever they ran out, they had to pull back regardless of what they had just accomplished — Wang Shuang killed while covering the retreat [7], Zhang He killed while covering the retreat [4][16]. A defected city or commandery, meanwhile, only stayed defected while a Shu army was nearby; once Shu withdrew, Wei re-subjugated it [6][13]. Therefore a battlefield win could not be converted into lasting control unless the win removed the *time limit* — which is exactly why Zhuge Liang turned to on-site 屯田 in 234 [4], and why the whole plan collapses without either local grain (which Wei denied him [1][8]) or a secure, short supply line. Hence "winning at the front" and "holding the new ground" were governed by different clocks: the battle by hours, the occupation by harvests.

One caveat: the sources do not give a single campaign in which Shu both won decisively and then held the ground for a long period, so this conclusion is drawn from the repeated pattern of grain-driven withdrawals, not from a stated principle in the text.

q: Identify the person: when Cao Cao was routed at Wancheng, who held the camp gate and fought to the death to cover Cao Cao's retreat?
reply:
**The person was Dian Wei 典韦.**

Dian Wei held the camp gate at Wancheng (宛城, in present-day Nanyang, Henan) and fought to the death so that Cao Cao could get away. The account is in his biography in the *Wei shu*:

- When Cao Cao marched against Jing Province and reached Wan, Zhang Xiu came out to surrender. Cao Cao feasted Zhang Xiu and his officers, and Dian Wei stood behind him holding a great axe: 「太祖行酒，韋持大斧立後，刃徑尺，太祖所至之前，韋輒舉斧目之。竟酒，繡及其將帥莫敢仰視」[10].
- Over ten days later Zhang Xiu revolted and raided Cao Cao's camp; Cao Cao went out to fight, was worsted, and withdrew with light cavalry. Dian Wei fought in the gate so the enemy could not get in: 「後十餘日，繡反，襲太祖營，太祖出戰不利，輕騎引去。韋戰於門中，賊不得入」[10].
- The soldiers then scattered and poured in through other gates. With only about ten men left, all fighting to the death and each worth ten, Dian Wei kept them off with a long halberd; his men were nearly all killed or wounded. Wounded in dozens of places, he fought hand to hand, killed two enemies by tucking one under each arm, then charged again and killed several more until his wounds burst open: 「韋被數十創，短兵接戰，賊前搏之。韋雙挾兩賊擊殺之，餘賊不敢前。韋復前突賊，殺數人，創重發，瞋目大罵而死」[10].
- Only after he died did the enemy dare to come forward, cut off his head and pass it around: 「賊乃敢前，取其頭，傳觀之，覆軍就視其軀」[10].

Cao Cao, having fallen back to Wuyin, wept when he heard of Dian Wei's death, had his body recovered by a side road, mourned him in person, and sent him home for burial at Xiangyi; he later appointed Dian Wei's son Dian Man 典滿 as a gentleman attendant, and Emperor Wen made Dian Man a commandant and granted him the title of marquis within the passes [10].

For context on the defeat itself, the *Wudi ji* records it under the second year of Jian'an (spring, first month): Zhang Xiu surrendered and then revolted, Cao Cao's army was beaten, he was hit by a stray arrow, and his eldest son Cao Ang and his nephew Cao Anmin were killed [2]. The *Zhang Xiu* biography adds that Cao Cao had taken Zhang Xiu's (uncle Zhang Ji's) wife, which embittered Zhang Xiu [1]; Pei Songzhi's commentary, citing the *Fu zi* and the *Wu shu*, gives further explanations of why Zhang Xiu turned on him [6].

Note: the *Sanguozhi* text does not itself spell out "to cover Cao Cao's retreat" as Dian Wei's stated purpose — it says he fought in the gate and the enemy could not enter, and he died fighting. The inference that this covered Cao Cao's escape is reasonable (Cao Cao did get away with light cavalry while Dian Wei held the gate), but it is an inference from the account rather than a phrase in the text.

q: Changban: who rescued the infant A'dou at Changban Slope? And who stood on Changban Bridge and scared off Cao Cao's army with his shouts?
reply:
**Short answer:** Zhao Yun (趙雲) rescued the infant A'dou; Zhang Fei (張飛) held the bridge at Changban and frightened off Cao Cao's pursuers.

**Zhao Yun rescued A'dou and Lady Gan**

The *Sanguozhi* biography of Zhao Yun records:

「及先主為曹公所追於當陽長阪，棄妻子南走，雲身抱弱子，即後主也，保護甘夫人，即後主母也，皆得免難。」[1]

"When the Former Lord was pursued by Lord Cao at Changban in Dangyang and abandoned his wife and children to flee south, Yun himself carried the young child — that is, the Later Lord — and protected Lady Gan, the Later Lord's mother; both escaped the disaster." [1]

Lady Gan's own biography confirms the rescue:

「值曹公軍至，追及先主於當陽長阪，於時困偪，棄后及後主，賴趙雲保護，得免於難。」[4]

"When Lord Cao's army arrived and caught up with the Former Lord at Changban in Dangyang, the situation was desperate; he abandoned the Empress and the Later Lord, and they escaped the disaster only through Zhao Yun's protection." [4]

The Later Lord's own edict (quoted in Pei Songzhi's note from the *Yun Bielu* 雲別傳) later praised this: 「當陽之役，義貫金石，忠以衛上」[5] — "At the battle of Dangyang his righteousness pierced metal and stone, his loyalty guarded his sovereign."

**Zhang Fei held the bridge and scared off the pursuers**

Zhang Fei's biography records:

「先主聞曹公卒至，棄妻子走，使飛將二十騎拒後。飛據水斷橋，瞋目橫矛曰：『身是張益德也，可來共決死！』敵皆無敢近者，故遂得免。」[12]

"When the Former Lord heard that Lord Cao had arrived suddenly, he abandoned his wife and children and fled, ordering Fei to take twenty horsemen and hold the rear. Fei took position by the water and broke the bridge, glared with eyes wide and leveled his spear, saying: 'I am Zhang Yide — come and fight me to the death!' None of the enemy dared approach him, and so they got away." [12]

The Former Lord's biography gives the same setting: 「曹公將精騎五千急追之，一日一夜行三百餘里，及於當陽之長坂。先主棄妻子，與諸葛亮、張飛、趙雲等數十騎走」[10] — Cao Cao led 5,000 elite cavalry in forced pursuit, covering over 300 *li* in a day and a night, and caught him at Changban in Dangyang; the Former Lord abandoned his family and fled with Zhuge Liang, Zhang Fei, Zhao Yun and a few dozen riders.

**Note on the two episodes being one event**

The two stories come from the same pursuit. The *Sanguozhi* does not say Zhang Fei's stand and Zhao Yun's rescue happened at exactly the same spot or in a stated sequence; the records place both at Changban (長坂) during the same flight. The claim that Zhang Fei, standing on the bridge and shouting, single-handedly halted Cao Cao's army is essentially the *Sanguozhi* account (twenty riders, broken bridge, no one daring to approach) [12]; the more elaborate version in which he shouted and a Cao general died of fright is not in the *Sanguozhi*.

以下不是《三国志》的记载:

The dramatic tale of Zhang Fei's shout killing Xiahou Jie (夏侯傑) outright, and the vivid scene of Zhao Yun charging through the enemy lines with A'dou tucked in his breastplate, come from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国演义》) and popular storytelling; the *Sanguozhi* records only that Zhao Yun carried the child and protected Lady Gan, and that Zhang Fei broke the bridge and no enemy dared close with him.

q: Sequence of episodes: put the following in the order in which they occur in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*: A. The Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage  B. The Battle of Guandu  C. The Oath of the Peach Garden  D. The Battle of Red Cliffs
reply:
##结论

按《三国演义》的叙事顺序，四个情节依次是：

**C. 桃园结义 → B. 官渡之战 → A. 三顾茅庐 → D. 赤壁之战**

即：C → B → A → D。

## 依据（《三国志》原文）

**C. 结义/起兵最早。** 刘备在涿郡乡里聚众时，关羽、张飞已跟随他：「先主於鄉里合徒眾，而羽與張飛為之禦侮」「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟」[1]；张飞传亦称「少與關羽俱事先主」[2]。此事在时间上早于下面各事，属刘备起家之初。

**B. 官渡之战在汉献帝建安五年（公元 200 年）。**「建安五年，曹公與袁紹相拒於官渡」[14]；「五年，與紹連戰。太祖保官渡，紹圍之」[20]；曹操纪亦载是年「九月，公還許，分兵守官渡……十二月，公軍官渡」[12]。建安五年即公元 200 年（据年号换算）。

**A. 三顾茅庐在建安十三年（公元 208 年）之前一年。** 诸葛亮传：「由是先主遂詣亮，凡三往，乃見」[27]；同传后文亦作「乃三顧亮於草廬之中」[24]。裴松之按语推算：「劉備以建安十三年敗，遣亮使吳……然則備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也」[46]，即建安十二年。

**D. 赤壁之战在建安十三年（公元 208 年）。**「先主遣諸葛亮自結於孫權，權遣周瑜、程普等水軍數萬，與先主并力，與曹公戰於赤壁，大破之，焚其舟船」[37]；周瑜传亦载黄盖火攻、曹军败退「還保南郡」[39]。建安十三年即公元 208 年（据年号换算）。

## 推断

据以上事实：结义/起兵发生在刘备初起之时，早于建安五年[1][2]；官渡在建安五年（200 年）[12][14][20]；三顾在建安十二年（赤壁前一年）[46]；赤壁在建安十三年（208 年）[37]。据此推断，四事的先后顺序为：结义 → 官渡 → 三顾 → 赤壁。这与《三国演义》的叙述顺序一致。

## 以下不是《三国志》的记载：

问题里说的「桃园结义」（在桃园中结拜为兄弟）《三国志》里没有记载，可能出自《三国演义》或其他非正史的说法；《三国志》只说刘备与关、张「寢則同床，恩若兄弟」，并未记载结拜的仪式、地点与誓词。

q: The chained ships: before the Battle of Red Cliffs, who advised Ts'ao Ts'ao to link his warships together with iron chains? Why did this arrangement magnify the damage done by the fire attack?
reply:
## 结论

**《三国志》里没有记载是谁劝曹操把战船连锁起来的。** 正文只记曹操的战船"首尾相接"这一事实，是吴将**黄盖**（Huang Gai）在战前观察到、并据此提出火攻的。至于"某人向曹操献连环计"，尤其是"庞统献连环计"，在《三国志》中查不到，是《三国演义》的说法。

## 依据

黄盖的话，见《周瑜传》正文：

「瑜部將黃蓋曰：『今寇眾我寡，難與持久。然觀操軍船艦，首尾相接，可燒而走也。』」[11]

也就是说，**黄盖是提出火攻的人**（《黄盖传》也印证：「建安中，隨周瑜拒曹公於赤壁，建策火攻，語在〈瑜傳〉」[34]），但"首尾相接"是他在战场上看到的曹操一方的布阵状态，并不是他建议曹操这么做的；《三国志》没有交代曹操为何、听谁之劝把船连在一起。

火攻的执行过程，见《周瑜传》正文：

「乃取蒙沖鬥艦數十艘，實以薪草，膏油灌其中。裹以帷幕，上建牙旗，先書報曹公，欺以欲降。……蓋放諸船，同時發火。時風盛猛，悉延燒岸上營落。頃之。煙炎張天，人馬燒溺死者甚眾，軍遂敗退，還保南郡。」[11]

裴注引《江表传》补充：

「時東南風急……去北軍二里餘，同時發火，火烈風猛，往船如箭，飛埃絕爛，燒盡北船，延及岸邊營柴。瑜等率輕銳尋繼其後，雷鼓大進，北軍大壞，曹公退走。」[35]

另一说（裴注引《山阳公载记》）则把烧船归于刘备：「公船艦爲備所燒，引軍從華亭道步歸……」[12]，并附孙盛的异议。两说不同，此处并列，不作裁决。

## 为什么连锁会放大火攻的损失（以下为推断）

据上文几条事实可以推出：

1. 曹军船舰「首尾相接」，即彼此紧靠连成一片 [11]；
2. 黄盖放火后「同時發火」「火烈風猛」，风助火势 [11][35]；
3. 结果是「燒盡北船，延及岸邊營柴」，连岸上营寨也被延烧 [35]。

由此可知：船既首尾相连，一艘着火便无法各自解开驶离，火会顺着相连的船身迅速蔓延到整个船队，并进而烧到岸上的营寨；加之当时东南风急，火势更猛，所以「人馬燒溺死者甚眾」[11]。火势能被放大，关键正在于船被连成一体、无法分散避险。

## 以下不是《三国志》的记载：

问题里"有人劝曹操把战船用铁链连起来"（通常指庞统献连环计）这一情节，《三国志》里没有记载，可能出自《三国演义》或其他非正史的说法。正史只记曹军船舰首尾相接、黄盖据此建策火攻 [11]；庞统在《三国志》中的事迹是劝刘备取益州、随刘备入蜀，并无向曹操献连环计之事 [21][22][26]。

q: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats: what weather conditions did Zhuge Liang take advantage of when he borrowed the arrows, and why did those conditions help him carry out the plan?
reply:
## Conclusion

《三国志》(including Pei Songzhi's commentary) contains **no record of Zhuge Liang "borrowing arrows with straw boats."** The closest recorded incident belongs to **Sun Quan**, at Ruxu, and the only weather element the histories attach to it is the **rising spring floodwater (春水方生)** — not fog. The fog, the straw bundles, and Zhuge Liang's role are all from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*.

## What the histories do say

**The setting (Ruxu, 建安 18 = 213 CE):**
- 「十八年正月，曹公攻濡須，權與相拒月餘。」[38] — In the first month, Cao Cao attacked Ruxu; Sun Quan resisted him for over a month. (建安十八年 = 213 CE, per the era conversion.)

**The arrow incident (Pei note quoting the *Weilüe*):**
- 「魏略曰：權乘大船來觀軍，公使弓弩亂發，箭著其船，船偏重將覆，權因回船，復以一面受箭，箭均船平，乃還。」[12] — Sun Quan rode a large ship to observe Cao Cao's army; Cao Cao had crossbows fire wildly, arrows struck his ship, the ship became lop-sided and nearly capsized, so Sun Quan turned the ship about and let the other side take arrows, and once the arrows were even the ship was level, and only then did he return.

**The weather element (Pei note quoting the *Wuli*):**
- 「權爲箋與曹公，説：『春水方生，公宜速去。』」[12] — Sun Quan wrote to Cao Cao: "The spring waters are just now rising; you should leave quickly."

## Answering the question as asked

- **What weather did he use?** According to the histories, the only weather condition tied to this affair is **the rising spring river water (春水方生)** [12]. No fog is mentioned in connection with it.
- **Why would it help?** Based on the sources above: the *Weilüe* account shows the plan did not depend on concealment at all — Cao Cao's men shot voluntarily, and Sun Quan's problem was that the accumulating arrows made the ship lop-sided. The recorded solution was to turn the ship so the other side received arrows until 「箭均船平」 ("the arrows were even and the ship was level") [12]. The rising spring water [12] fits the same campaign in which Cao Cao ultimately withdrew [38], so on the evidence the useful "condition" was the spring flood, not a fog bank. (This is my inference from the cited passages; the histories never state that the flood was used to gather arrows.)

## Background (not from the *Sanguozhi*)

The following is not a record from the *Sanguozhi*: the story of Zhuge Liang "borrowing arrows with straw boats" — including the thick fog on the river and the straw men used to collect the arrows — has no such record in the *Sanguozhi*; it is a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* / popular tradition version. In the histories the analogous deed is attributed to Sun Quan, and the fog is not mentioned.

q: Empty Fort Strategy: in the novel, where does Zhuge Liang use the Empty Fort Strategy, and which Wei commander leads the army that comes against him?
reply:
## Short answer

The Empty Fort Strategy (空城計) is **not in Chen Shou's main text of the *Sanguozhi***. The earliest version of the story is preserved in **Pei Songzhi's annotation**, quoting **Guo Chong's《三事》** — and there the place is **Yangping (陽平), in Hanzhong**, not Xicheng; the Wei commander is **Sima Yi (司馬懿 / 晉宣帝)**, whom Zhuge Liang's men had left with a token force. In the Romance, the episode is the famous scene at Xicheng with Zhuge Liang playing the qin; the *Sanguozhi* knows nothing of that setting. Pei Songzhi himself rejects the whole story as chronologically impossible.

## What the sources actually say

**The story as Pei Songzhi quotes it (Guo Chong's《三事》)**

- Zhuge Liang was at Yangping and had sent Wei Yan and the other armies east, keeping only 10,000 men to hold the city: 「亮屯于陽平，遣魏延諸軍並兵東下，亮惟留萬人守城」[13].
- Sima Yi came against him with 200,000 troops: 「晉宣帝率二十萬眾拒亮」[13].
- Zhuge Liang ordered the banners lowered, the drums silenced, and the four gates thrown open: 「敕軍中皆臥旗息鼓，不得妄出菴幔，又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒」[13].
- Sima Yi, knowing Zhuge Liang to be cautious, suspected an ambush and withdrew toward the hills: 「宣帝常謂亮持重，而猥見勢弱，疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山」[13].

So the Wei commander in this version is **Sima Yi**, and the place is **Yangping**. Note that in Guo Chong's version there is **no qin-playing** — that is a later, Romance embellishment.

**Pei Songzhi's rebuttal**

The annotation appends a refutation: Yangping is in Hanzhong, and when Zhuge Liang first camped at Yangping, Sima Yi was still Inspector of Jingzhou, stationed at Wan; he only confronted Zhuge Liang in Guanzhong after Cao Zhen's death, and there was no battle at Yangping before or after: 「案陽平在漢中。亮初屯陽平，宣帝尚為荊州都督，鎮宛城，至曹真死後，始與亮於關中相抗禦耳……此之前後，無復有於陽平交兵事」[13].

The rebuttal also cites Wei Yan's biography to show Zhuge Liang would never have let Wei Yan take a large force away while keeping a weak guard himself: 「亮尚不以延為萬人別統，豈得如沖言，頓使將重兵在前，而以輕弱自守乎？」[13]. Pei concludes that Guo Chong's account is fabricated, partly because Guo Chong was telling these stories to Sima Yi's own son, Prince of Fufeng: 「故知此書舉引皆虛」[13].

**Pei's own verdict on Guo Chong's five stories** is stated earlier: 「臣松之以為亮之異美，誠所願聞，然沖之所說，實皆可疑，謹隨事難之如左」[27] — Pei says the stories are all suspect and refutes them one by one.

**Other than this annotation, my searches of the *Sanguozhi* (Zhuge Liang's biography, the Later Ruler's annals, the Ming Emperor's annals, and the relevant Pei annotations) turned up no "empty city" episode.** The main text's Hanzhong campaign has Zhuge Liang at Yangping as a **camp/position**, not as an empty-fort bluff: 「五年春，丞相亮出屯漢中，營沔北陽平石馬」[6].

## Inference

From the sources above: the *Sanguozhi* main text records no empty-fort trick at all; the only early version is Guo Chong's, in which the Wei commander is Sima Yi and the place is Yangping. Since Pei Songzhi shows that Sima Yi was not in the Guanzhong theater at the time Zhuge Liang was camped at Yangping, the Guo Chong version cannot be squared with the chronology — so the "Empty Fort Strategy" as a real event is, on the *Sanguozhi*'s own evidence, doubtful. (This is an inference from the sources, not a statement of the sources.)

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The Empty Fort Strategy as an actual battle — with Zhuge Liang sitting on the city wall playing the qin while Sima Yi's army withdraws — is the《三国演义》version, not a *Sanguozhi* record; the *Sanguozhi* text has no such episode, and the only old version of the story, quoted in Pei Songzhi's annotation from Guo Chong, differs from the novel both in place (Yangping rather than Xicheng) and in having no qin-playing, and Pei Songzhi rejects it outright.

q: Identify the posthumous ruse: in the saying 'a dead Zhuge frightens off a living Zhongda', who is 'Zhongda'? In the novel, how does the Shu army make him retreat?
reply:
## Conclusion

**"Zhongda" (仲达) is Sima Yi 司马懿** — Zhongda was his courtesy name (字). The alias table lists him as "司马懿, 字仲达," also called 司马宣王 / 晋宣帝 [who].

**How the Shu army made him withdraw (as recorded in the Sanguozhi material):** after Zhuge Liang died, Yang Yi's troops marched out in order; when Sima Yi pursued, **Jiang Wei ordered Yang Yi to turn the banners about and beat the drums, as if about to attack Sima Yi** — and Sima Yi then pulled back, not daring to press close.

## The evidence

The saying itself and the ruse come from **Pei Songzhi's annotation to the Zhuge Liang biography, quoting 《汉晋春秋》** — not from Chen Shou's main text:

> 「楊儀等整軍而出，百姓奔告宣王，宣王追焉。姜維令儀反旗鳴鼓，若將向宣王者，宣王乃退，不敢偪。於是儀結陳而去，入谷然後發喪。宣王之退也，百姓為之諺曰：『死諸葛走生仲達。』或以告宣王，宣王曰：『吾能料生，不便料死也。』」[12]

*Translation: Yang Yi and the others drew up their army and marched out; the common people ran to tell Sima Xuanwang, who pursued. Jiang Wei ordered Yang Yi to turn the banners and sound the drums, as if about to march on Sima Xuanwang; Sima Xuanwang then withdrew and did not dare press him. Yang Yi formed his ranks and left, and only after entering the valley did they announce the death. When Sima Xuanwang withdrew, the people made a saying of it: "A dead Zhuge frightens off a living Zhongda." Someone told Sima Xuanwang, who said: "I can reckon with the living; I cannot reckon with the dead."*

So: "Zhongda" = Sima Yi, and the "ruse" in the record is **the reversed banners and beating drums**, carried out by Yang Yi on Jiang Wei's order, plus the **withholding of the death announcement until the army was safely inside the valley** (「入谷然後發喪」[12]).

## Supporting facts

- The context is the summer/autumn of Zhuge Liang's last campaign. Chen Shou's main text: 「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出，以流馬運，據武功五丈原，與司馬宣王對於渭南……其年八月，亮疾病，卒于軍，時年五十四。」[39] (Jianxing 12 = **234 AD** [era]; Zhuge Liang died in the eighth month, aged 54.)
- The Wei side's record is simply that his army withdrew: 「司馬宣王與亮相持，連圍積日，亮數挑戰，宣王堅壘不應。會亮卒，其軍退還。」[10]
- Yang Yi concealed the death and withdrew: 「亮適卒，秘不發喪」[7].
- Sima Yi is referred to throughout as 宣王 (Sima Xuanwang), which is how the same man appears in these passages [who].

## Inference (marked as such)

From [12] and [39] together: the withdrawal succeeded **because the death was kept secret and the army marched out in order behind a show of force** — turning the banners and beating the drums mimicked an advance, and Sima Yi, who had just spent a hundred-odd days refusing battle against Zhuge Liang, had no way to tell a live Zhuge Liang from a dead one. That is precisely what his own remark concedes: 「吾能料生，不便料死也」[12]. This is my reading of the evidence, not a statement the text makes.

Note also that Pei Songzhi himself rejects a rival version in 《魏书》 that has Zhuge Liang "vomiting blood and fleeing" (「亮糧盡勢窮，憂恚歐血」[1]), arguing that Sima Yi had no such victory: 「夫以孔明之略，豈為仲達歐血乎？」[1] (裴松之按). So the sources disagree about the circumstances, and the "frightened off" episode rests on Xi Zuochi's 《汉晋春秋》.

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The version in which the Shu army scares Sima Yi off with a wooden image/statue of Zhuge Liang 《三国志》里没有记载, 可能出自《三国演义》或其他非正史的说法. 《三国志》和裴注所记的退敌办法, 是姜维令杨仪反旗鸣鼓, 以及秘不发丧、结阵入谷.

q: In the late Eastern Han, was a 'Grand Administrator' (taishou) normally the chief official of a province, a commandery or a county?
reply:
**Short answer: a commandery (jun 郡).** In the *Sanguozhi*, a Grand Administrator (taishou 太守) is the chief official of a commandery — not of a province (zhou 州) and not of a county (xian 縣). The chief of a province was the Inspector (cishi 刺史) or Governor (zhoumu 州牧), and the chief of a county was the Prefect/Chief (ling 令 / zhang 長).

**Evidence**

1. Grand Administrators are always named as heads of a *jun* (commandery), and are classed as the "two-thousand-bushel" officials:
「魏郡太守陳國吳瓘、清河太守樂安任燠、京兆太守濟北顏斐、弘農太守太原令狐邵、濟南相魯國孔乂……咸為良二千石。」[1] — "Administrator of Wei Commandery… Administrator of Qinghe… all fine two-thousand-bushel officials."

2. A county chief is distinct from, and subordinate to, the Grand Administrator. In the *Shishuo*-style description of provincial administration, Xiahou Xuan complains that "the long officials" (i.e., county-level chiefs) are made rulers of the people, "and on top of them the commandery governors are piled, and then the Inspectors piled on again":
「今之長吏，皆君吏民，橫重以郡守，累以刺史。」[16]
He proposes abolishing the commandery layer and letting the Inspector supervise directly, and says the commandery staff's job is to oversee the counties, with the commandery receiving what the counties accomplish:
「宜省郡守，但任刺史……又幹郡之吏，職監諸縣……郡受縣成……」[20]
If the commandery governors were removed, "the counties would all report directly" —「若省郡守，縣皆徑達」[20].

3. The Inspector/Governor is described as presiding over the *commandery* level, not the county level:
「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外，非若曩時司察之而已。」[23] — "Since the late Han, the Inspectors have overseen all the commanderies."
And Sima Yi notes that in Qin times there was no Inspector, "only commandery governors and long officials":
「秦時無刺史，但有郡守長吏。」[21]

4. Other passages show the Grand Administrator's jurisdiction is "a single commandery": Wang Guan says, "How could I, for the Grand Administrator's private interest, betray the people of one commandery?" —「豈可為太守之私而負一郡之民乎？」[11]. And in the same passage a county office (Prefect of Xuwen 徐聞令) is listed alongside commandery-level Grand Administrators (合浦太守, 九真太守), showing the two tiers as different: 「表壹領合浦太守，次弟徐聞令䵋領九真太守」[4].

**So the hierarchy reflected in the text is: Inspector/Governor (州) → Grand Administrator (郡) → Prefect/Chief (縣).** The Grand Administrator sits at the commandery level.

**A caveat on wording:** the sources do note that in this period the Inspector's role had changed from a purely supervisory one to one that "governed all the commanderies" and handled administration abroad —「刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外」[23]. That describes the Inspector's expanded role at the *province* level; it does not make the Grand Administrator a provincial office.

q: Huarong Trail: in the novel, why does Guan Yu let Cao Cao go at Huarong Trail? What conflict within his character does this episode bring out?
reply:
## Conclusion

The Huarong Trail episode as the novel tells it — Guan Yu, having sworn a military oath to capture Cao Cao, lets him go out of gratitude — **is not in the *Sanguo zhi***. What the *Sanguo zhi* does contain is (1) the record that Cao Cao did retreat through Huarong Trail, but pursued by **Liu Bei**, not by Guan Yu; and (2) the material that the novel drew on for the "debt of gratitude" theme: Guan Yu's own declaration that he owed Cao Cao a debt he must repay before leaving, and Cao Cao's decision to let Guan Yu go rather than pursue him. The inner conflict the novel dramatizes — personal righteousness (*yi* 義) and gratitude toward Cao Cao versus loyalty to Liu Bei and military duty — can be read out of the *Sanguo zhi*, but the *Sanguo zhi* never stages it at Huarong Trail.

## What the *Sanguo zhi* actually records

**1. The retreat through Huarong Trail — the pursuer is Liu Bei, not Guan Yu.**

Pei Songzhi's note quoting the *Shanyang gong zaiji*:

> 「公船艦爲備所燒，引軍從華容道步歸，遇泥濘，道不通，天又大風，悉使羸兵負草填之，騎乃得過。羸兵爲人馬所蹈藉，陷泥中，死者甚衆。軍旣得出，公大喜，諸將問之，公曰：『劉備，吾儔也。但得計少晚；向使早放火，吾徒無類矣。』備尋亦放火而無所及。」[17]

(Pei's note cites the *Shanyang gong zaiji*: Cao Cao's ships were burned by Liu Bei; he led his army back on foot by the Huarong road, hit mud, had the weak soldiers carry grass to fill it; many died. Once out, he was delighted and said, "Liu Bei is my match; his plan was just a little late — had he set fire earlier, we would have had no survivors." Liu Bei then set fire, but too late.)

So in this account Cao Cao *does* march out through Huarong Trail — but the one who tries to burn him out is Liu Bei, and there is no Guan Yu waiting in ambush, no oath, no release.

**2. Guan Yu's debt to Cao Cao and his declared intention to repay it.**

In the Guan Yu biography, after Cao Cao captured him at Jian'an 5:

> 「曹公禽羽以歸，拜為偏將軍，禮之甚厚。」[2]

> 「吾極知曹公待我厚，然吾受劉將軍厚恩，誓以共死，不可背之。吾終不留，吾要當立效以報曹公乃去。」[2]

> 「及羽殺顏良，曹公知其必去，重加賞賜。羽盡封其所賜，拜書告辭，而奔先主於袁軍。左右欲追之，曹公曰：『彼各為其主，勿追也。』」[2]

(Cao Cao captured Guan Yu, made him a General of the Household and treated him very well. Guan Yu said: "I know full well Cao Cao treats me generously, but I have received Lord Liu's deep kindness and swore to die with him; I cannot betray him. I will not stay — but I must first render some service to repay Cao Cao before I go." After Guan Yu killed Yan Liang, Cao Cao knew he would leave, gave him more gifts; Guan Yu sealed it all up, sent a letter of farewell, and went to Liu Bei. Cao Cao's men wanted to pursue; Cao Cao said, "Each serves his own lord; do not pursue.")

**3. The theme of mutual "righteousness."**

Pei's note quoting the *Fuzi*:

> 「太祖曰：『事君不忘其本，天下義士也。』」[3]

Pei Songzhi's own comment (not a quoted book):

> 「臣松之以為曹公知羽不留而心嘉其志，去不遣追以成其義……斯實曹公之休美。」[47]

(Pei Songzhi's note: Cao Cao knew Guan Yu would not stay, yet admired his resolve, and did not pursue, thus completing Guan Yu's righteousness — this was truly Cao Cao's virtue.)

And Chen Shou's appraisal:

> 「羽報效曹公，飛義釋嚴顏，並有國士之風。然羽剛而自矜，飛暴而無恩，以短取敗，理數之常也。」[5]

(Chen Shou: "Guan Yu repaid Cao Cao's kindness, Zhang Fei released Yan Yan out of righteousness — both had the manner of a true knight (*guoshi*). But Guan Yu was firm and self-proud…")

**4. The other, harder side of Guan Yu.**

Pei's note quoting the *Shu ji*:

> 「初，劉備在許，與曹公共獵。獵中，眾散，羽勸備殺公，備不從。及在夏口……羽怒曰：『往日獵中，若從羽言，可無今日之困。』」[34]

(The *Shu ji*: earlier, when Liu Bei was in Xu and hunted with Cao Cao, the party scattered; Guan Yu urged Liu Bei to kill Cao Cao, and Liu Bei refused. Later at Xiakou, Guan Yu angrily said, "Had you followed me at the hunt, we would not have this trouble today.")

And on his temperament:

> 「羽善待卒伍而驕於士大夫」[39]

(Guan Yu treated his soldiers well but was arrogant toward the gentry-officials.)

## Inference (what can and cannot be concluded)

From the facts above one can infer the *shape* of the conflict the novel exploits, but not the episode itself:

- The *Sanguo zhi* gives Guan Yu a **real, stated debt to Cao Cao** ("I must render service to repay Cao Cao before I go" [2]) and shows Cao Cao **choosing not to pursue him** so as to "complete his righteousness" [47]. The novel's letting-go at Huarong Trail is a mirror image of this: the same debt, now paid back in the opposite direction.
- The *Sanguo zhi* also gives Guan Yu the **opposite impulse** — urging Liu Bei to kill Cao Cao at the hunt, and angrily recalling it at Xiakou [34]. So the tension between "gratitude toward Cao Cao" and "duty to kill Cao Cao for Liu Bei" is genuinely present in the sources; the novel simply makes it collide in one scene.
- The *Sanguo zhi*'s characterization of Guan Yu as 「剛而自矜」[5] and 「驕於士大夫」[39] fits the novel's version of him: a man whose personal sense of honor overrides the military order he has given, and who then accepts the consequence rather than excuse himself.

**What cannot be concluded from the *Sanguo zhi*:** that Guan Yu was at Huarong Trail at all, that he made a military oath to capture Cao Cao, or that Cao Cao pleaded with him. Those are the novel's additions, and the *Sanguo zhi* records the Huarong retreat with **Liu Bei** as the pursuer [17].

## Background

以下不是《三国志》的记载:

The story that Guan Yu intercepted and released Cao Cao at Huarong Trail is not recorded in the *Sanguo zhi*; it comes from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国演义》) and related popular tradition. The *Sanguo zhi* records only that Cao Cao withdrew by the Huarong road and that Liu Bei pursued and set fire too late [17].

The way the novel frames it — Guan Yu torn between repaying Cao Cao's old kindness and keeping faith with Liu Bei, and choosing *yi* at the cost of his own oath — is a literary elaboration on the theme Chen Shou already names in his appraisal, 「羽報效曹公……有國士之風」[5], combined with the record that Cao Cao himself had once let Guan Yu go, saying 「彼各為其主，勿追也」[2].

(The place name "Huarong" (華容) is not given a modern location in the material I retrieved.)

q: Arrange 'county, province, commandery' from highest to lowest according to the usual local administrative hierarchy of the late Eastern Han.
reply:
## Conclusion

From highest to lowest, the usual late Eastern Han local hierarchy was:

**province (州 zhōu) → commandery (郡 jùn) → county (县 xiàn)**

i.e. **province > commandery > county**.

## Evidence from the sources

The *Sanguozhi* consistently places the province above the commandery and the commandery above the county.

1. The province's chief (Inspector 刺史 or Governor 州牧) sits above the commandery's chief (Administrator 太守). In Xiahou Xuan's memorial arguing for cutting out a tier, he says the present arrangement stacks offices on top of each other:

「今之長吏，皆君吏民，橫重以郡守，累以刺史。」[1]

(His proposal is 「宜省郡守，但任刺史」[11] — "abolish the commandery administrators and keep only the Inspectors" — which only makes sense if the Inspector ranks above the Administrator.)

2. The commandery in turn oversees the counties:

「又幹郡之吏，職監諸縣」[11] — "the officials who manage the commandery have the duty of supervising the various counties."

3. The same order appears when offices are listed together. In Zhuge Liang's memorial on mourning grades for Liu Bei's death:

「其郡國太守、相、都尉、縣令長，三日便除服。」[36] — Administrators (太守) and Chancellors (相) of commanderies and kingdoms, and Commandants (都尉), together with county Prefects and Chiefs (縣令長), are listed as two successive tiers.

4. The title pairs show the same ranking: a man is made Administrator (太守) of a commandery, or Prefect/Chief (令/長) of a county. E.g. Shi Xie's brothers: 「燮乃表壹領合浦太守，次弟徐聞令䵋領九真太守」[16] — Shi Yi as Administrator of Hepu, his younger brother, the Prefect of Xuwen, as Administrator of Jiuzhen.

5. Shi Zong's account of the southern frontier likewise moves through the tiers 「州縣」 (province/county) and speaks of 「長吏」 governing counties under commanderies [12].

So the ranking is: **province (州, governed by 刺史/州牧) → commandery (郡, governed by 太守) → county (县, governed by 令 or 長)**.

Note: the *Sanguozhi* itself does not present a formal "table of ranks"; the conclusion above is drawn from the way these offices are listed and subordinated in the passages cited (for instance, only if the province outranks the commandery does it make sense to say 「省郡守，但任刺史」[11]).
