q: Both the 'Inspector' (cishi) and the 'Governor' (zhoumu) were offices tied to the province. What was the Inspector's original main function? And why can't every Inspector of the late Eastern Han simply be regarded as an official with supervisory powers only?
reply:
## Short answer

The Inspector (cishi 刺史) began as a **supervisory** office: an official sent out from the central government in the guise of a censor (御史) to police the commanderies and their ranking administrators, bound by the "six articles" (六條) and with no fixed seat of government. But from the late Eastern Han on, in actual practice Inspectors already "commanded the commanderies and exercised government abroad," raised troops, and held territory — so they cannot all be treated as mere supervisory officers. The creation of the Pastor/Governor (zhoumu 州牧) around 188 was precisely an attempt to give this de facto power a formal title.

## 1. The Inspector's original function: supervision

The clearest statement is Sima Yi's reply to Xiahou Xuan: 「秦時無刺史，但有郡守長吏。漢家雖有刺史，奉六條而已，故刺史稱傳車，其吏言從事，居無常治，吏不成臣，其後轉更爲官司耳。」[9] — "In Qin times there was no Inspector, only commandery governors and senior officials. The Han did have Inspectors, but they merely carried out the six articles; hence the Inspector was called 'carriage-and-team' (i.e. a traveling officer), his staff were called 從事, he had no fixed seat, and his subordinates were not his subjects — only later did the office turn into a regular bureau."

Jia Kui spells out the same origin: 「州本以御史出監諸郡，以六条詔書察長吏二千石已下，故其狀皆言严能鹰扬有督察之才，不言安静寬仁有恺悌之德也。」[3] — "The province (zhou) originally consisted of a censor going out to supervise the commanderies, using the six-article edict to inspect the long officials of 2,000-bushel rank and below; that is why their evaluations all speak of stern competence and hawk-like talent for inspection, and never of quiet benevolence and kindly virtue."

Xiahou Xuan traces the whole layered system to Qin/Han distrust: 「始自秦世，不師聖道，私以御職，姦以待下；懼宰官之不脩，立監牧以董之，畏督監之容曲，設司察以糾之」[8] — "From Qin on, not following the way of the sages, they used office for private ends and treated subordinates with guile; fearing the stewards would not keep order, they set up overseers to direct them, and fearing the overseers would tolerate crookedness, they set up inspectors to correct them."

So: the Inspector was a traveling supervisory official — no fixed seat (「居無常治」), his staff were 從事 rather than his own subjects (「吏不成臣」), his writ was the 六條, and his charge was the commandery-level 2,000-bushel officials.

## 2. Why late-Han Inspectors cannot all be called supervisory-only

The Wei history's verdict states the change outright: 「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外，非若曩時司察之而已。」[2] — "From the late Han on, Inspectors commanded the commanderies and exercised government abroad; they were not, as in former times, merely inspectors."

Concrete cases in the records:

- **Inspectors raising armies and taking part in the coalition.** In 初平元年, among those who rose together against Dong Zhuo and made Yuan Shao their leader were 「冀州牧韓馥、豫州刺史孔伷、兖州刺史劉岱」[40] — the 豫州 and 兖州 *Inspectors*, alongside the 冀州 *Pastor*. An office confined to censorial duties does not raise tens of thousands of troops.
- **An Inspector fighting for and holding a province.** Liu Biao: 「靈帝崩，代王叡爲荊州刺史。是時山東兵起，表亦合兵軍襄陽。」[46] He then took the field against Yuan Shu and Sun Jian, and Li Jue and Guo Si made him 荊州牧 with 鎮南將軍 and 假節[48] — the man was a military warlord before he was a Pastor.
- **Inspectors as victims of violence.** 「并州殺刺史張壹，涼州殺刺史張壹、涼州殺刺史耿鄙」[6] (並州 killed its Inspector Zhang Yi, Liangzhou killed its Inspector Geng Bi) — people were not murdering their Inspectors over supervision alone; these were regional power struggles.
- **Pastor as the formalized version of the same power.** Liu Yan's proposal: 「刺史、太守，貨賂為官，割剝百姓，以致離叛。可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏。」[12] — "Inspectors and administrators have bought office with bribes and fleeced the people, so that they have broken away; select officials of clean reputation and weight as Pastors to pacify the realm." He then 「出為監軍使者，領益州牧」[6] — going out as Army-Supervising Commissioner and holding the Pastorate of Yizhou. The 《續漢書》 lists the wave: 「用劉虞為幽州，劉焉為益州，劉表為荊州，賈琮為冀州……或從列卿尚書以選為牧伯，各以本秩居任。」[13]

## 3. Inference (clearly marked as such)

Basing only on the above: (a) the office's original mandate was supervisory, bound to the 六條 and the 2,000-bushel commandery officials, with no fixed seat; (b) the sources state that "from the late Han on" Inspectors "commanded the commanderies and exercised government abroad"; and (c) the records show specific Inspectors mustering armies, holding provinces, being killed by their provinces, and being converted into Pastors. From these it follows that by the late Han the title *cishi* no longer tells you what a man actually did: some might still be exercising supervision, but others were territorial military governors in all but name. Hence one cannot treat every late-Han Inspector as an official with supervisory powers only. (Whether any *given* Inspector functioned as a supervisor or a warlord has to be checked case by case; the sources do not license a blanket judgment either way.)

## Background (not from the *Sanguozhi*)

以下不是《三国志》的记载: A 刺史 (Inspector) was nominally of lower rank than a 太守 of 2,000-bushel grade, which is why a supervisory rather than a commanding role was originally assigned to it; a 州牧 (Pastor/Governor) ranked above the commandery administrators and combined civil and military authority over a whole province. These are general descriptions of the two offices, not reports of any particular man.

q: Chu-ko Liang was Chancellor of Shu-Han and also held the charge of 'Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat' (lu shangshu shi). Taking part in and overseeing what kind of business did that charge chiefly mean?
reply:
## Conclusion

"Recording the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat" (錄尚書事, lu shangshu shi) was not a separate department of its own; it meant **superintending (錄) the business of the 尚書 (Imperial Secretariat / 尚書臺)** — the office that handled the documents, memorials and edicts flowing in and out of the throne, "综理万机," i.e. the routine day‑to‑day state business. So the charge chiefly meant taking part in and overseeing the **handling of government documents and memorials (文書、奏事) and thereby of the whole machinery of civil administration**, which is exactly why Zhuge Liang's tenure is described as "政事無巨細，咸決於亮."

## Evidence from the texts

**1. The office itself.** Zhuge Liang received the post together with the chancellorship:

> 「備稱尊號，拜亮為丞相，錄尚書事。」[58]
> 「亮以丞相錄尚書事，假節。」[2]

**2. What the 尚書 does — "出纳帝命."** In Wang Lang's memorial the 尚書 is explained by analogy with the ancient 納言 (Receiver of Words):

> 「然後惟龍爲納言，猶今尚書也，以出內帝命而已。」[16]

So the 尚書's business is receiving and issuing the emperor's commands — the documents and edicts.

**3. The 尚書 "综理万机."** Cheng Xiao's memorial describes the division of labor at court:

> 「內有侍中尚書綜理萬機，司隸校尉督察京輦，御史中丞董攝宮殿。」[21]

The 侍中 and 尚書 are the ones who "综理万机" — coordinate and manage the myriad affairs — as against the censorial officers who police the capital and the palace.

**4. "錄尚書事" glossed in a Cao-Wei edict.** When Cao Pi went to the Yangtze, he assigned Sima Yi to "record the documents of the rear secretariat" and Cao Xiu to "record the affairs of the traveling secretariat":

> 「撫軍當留許昌，督後諸軍，錄後臺文書事；鎮軍隨車駕，當董督衆軍，錄行尚書事。」[26]

Here "錄…尚書事" is expressly tied to 文書 (documents) — the secretariat's paper business — for both the rear and the traveling court.

**5. "尚書事" = the documents that reach the secretariat.** Pei Songzhi quotes Hua Qiao's 《譜叙》:

> 「時同寮諸郎共平尚書事……尚書事至，或有不便，故遺漏不視。」[18]

The 郎 officials "平尚書事" — deliberate on the secretariat's business — and "尚書事至" means the secretariat's documents arrive. So "尚書事" is precisely the flow of documents/memorials.

**6. Why the post carried power: control of the flow of memorials.** Of Cao Shuang, who also held 錄尚書事:

> 「外以名號尊之，內欲令尚書奏事，先來由己，得制其輕重也。」[37]

The point of controlling the secretariat was that the 尚書's 奏事 (memorials to the throne) would pass through one's own hands first, so one could "制其輕重" — decide what went up and how.

**7. The result in Zhuge Liang's case.** Having the secretariat business, he decided everything:

> 「政事無巨細，咸決於亮。」[12]

### Inference

Putting these together (据此推断): since the 尚書 were defined as the ones who "出纳帝命" [16] and "综理万机" [21]; since "錄…尚書事" is equated with "錄…文書事," i.e. supervising the secretariat's documents [26]; and since the purpose of holding it was that "尚書奏事，先來由己" [37] — the charge of 錄尚書事 chiefly meant taking part in and overseeing the **processing of state documents and memorials through the Imperial Secretariat**, and with them the everyday civil government that those documents carried. That is why in Zhuge Liang's case the outcome was that "政事無巨細，咸決於亮" [12].

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载: 尚書 (the Imperial Secretariat, later 尚書省) was the central office through which memorials were submitted to the throne and edicts were issued; its head was the 尚書令, with 僕射 as deputy, and 錄尚書事 was a title for a senior minister placed over the whole secretariat.

q: Which present-day city roughly corresponds to Jianye of the Three Kingdoms period? What is the city that served as Shu-Han's capital called today?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Jianye (建業) of the Three Kingdoms period corresponds to present-day **Nanjing, Jiangsu Province**; Shu-Han's capital Chengdu (成都) is present-day **Chengdu, Sichuan Province**.

**Evidence for Jianye**

Sun Quan first moved his seat of government to Moling, then renamed it Jianye:

「十六年，權徙治秣陵。明年，城石頭，改秣陵爲建業。」[5]
(In the 16th year [of Jian'an], Sun Quan moved his administrative seat to Moling. The next year he built a walled town at Shitou and changed Moling's name to Jianye.)

He later moved the capital away and then back:

「秋九月，權遷都建業，因固府不改館」[4]
(In the ninth month of autumn, Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye, keeping the existing offices and not rebuilding the palaces.)

**Evidence for Chengdu**

When Liu Bei took the throne, he did so at Chengdu:

「即皇帝位於成都武擔之南。」[18]
(He ascended the imperial throne south of Wudan in Chengdu.)

And when Liu Shan succeeded him, the seat remained Chengdu:

「五月，後主襲位於成都，時年十七」[11]
(In the fifth month, the Later Ruler succeeded to the position in Chengdu, being seventeen years old.)

**Inference:** Since the source records Moling being renamed Jianye and Sun Quan subsequently making Jianye his capital, and since Jianye is identified with the place called Moling, the Jianye of Wu is the same site as Moling — i.e., modern Nanjing. Likewise, both Liu Bei's accession and Liu Shan's succession are recorded as taking place at Chengdu, so Chengdu was the Shu-Han capital throughout that period.

The following is not from the Records of the Three Kingdoms: Jianye (建業, earlier Moling) is in present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu Province. Chengdu (成都) is present-day Chengdu, Sichuan Province.

q: Which cities normally served as the capitals of Ts'ao-Wei, Shu-Han and Sun-Wu respectively? For Wu, give the capital used over the long term after Sun Ch'üan moved the court.
reply:
## Short answer

- **Ts'ao-Wei (曹魏): 洛陽 (Luoyang)** — Cao Pi, having taken the throne at Fanyang, in the twelfth month "began building the Luoyang palace" and arrived at Luoyang.
- **Shu-Han (蜀漢): 成都 (Chengdu)** — Liu Bei took the imperial throne south of the Wu Dan in Chengdu; Liu Shan likewise succeeded there.
- **Sun-Wu (孫吳): 建業 (Jianye)** — Sun Quan moved the court from Wuchang to Jianye in the ninth month of Huanglong 1 (= 229 CE), and this was Wu's capital thereafter.

## Evidence

**Wei — Luoyang.** After ascending the altar at Fanyang and taking the throne, Cao Pi in the twelfth month of Huangchu 1 (= 220 CE) turned to the palace and capital: 「十二月，初營洛陽宮，戊午幸洛陽。」[1] (In the twelfth month he first built the Luoyang palace; on the *wuwu* day he arrived at Luoyang.) Earlier, while Cao Cao controlled the Han emperor, the court had been settled at Xu: 「洛陽殘破，董昭等勸太祖都許……九月，車駕出轘轅而東」[2] (Luoyang was in ruins, so Dong Zhao and others urged Cao Cao to make Xu the capital… in the ninth month the imperial carriage went east through Huanyuan). Note that this is the Han emperor's seat under Cao Cao, before the Wei state existed.

**Shu-Han — Chengdu.** When Liu Bei proclaimed himself emperor: 「即皇帝位於成都武擔之南。」[12] (He took the imperial throne south of the Wu Dan in Chengdu.) On his death, 「五月，後主襲位於成都」[13] (in the fifth month the Later Ruler succeeded to the throne in Chengdu).

**Wu — Jianye.** Sun Quan first shifted his seat to Moling and then renamed it: 「十六年，權徙治秣陵。明年，城石頭，改秣陵爲建業。」[30] (In the sixteenth year Sun Quan moved his administration to Moling; the next year he walled Shitou and changed Moling's name to Jianye.) While he was King of Wu he moved to E, renaming it Wuchang: 「權自公安都鄂，改名武昌」[26]. Then, as emperor, he moved back east: 「秋九月，權遷都建業，因固府不改館，徵上大將軍陸遜輔太子登，掌武昌留事。」[22] (In the autumn, the ninth month, Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye, using the existing offices without building new palaces, and summoned the General-in-Chief Lu Xun to assist the Heir-Apparent Sun Deng and take charge of the Wuchang rear.) The Huanglong 1 in which he had taken the throne is 229 CE; the move to Jianye is recorded immediately after, under the same Huanglong 1 [22][34]. That the move was remembered as a landmark is confirmed elsewhere: 「黃龍元年，權遷都建業」[24], and Pei note quoting the *Jiangbiao zhuan*: 「初，權移都建業，大會將相文武」[27] (*Jiangbiao zhuan*: at first, when Sun Quan moved the capital to Jianye, he held a great assembly of civil and military officers).

**Inference.** Since Sun Quan's court is recorded at Wuchang (Huangchu 2, i.e. the year he was enfeoffed as King of Wu) [26], then at Jianye from Huanglong 1 (229 CE) [22][24], and since later references to the Wu court (e.g. Sun Shao's audience after 「權還建業」[25]) still place it at Jianye, it follows that Jianye, not Wuchang, was Wu's long-term capital after the move. Wuchang continued to exist as a secondary holding (Lu Xun was left in charge of Wuchang affairs [22]).

---

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:**

- 洛陽 (Luoyang, the Wei capital) is in present-day Henan province.
- 成都 (Chengdu, the Shu-Han capital) is in present-day Sichuan province.
- 建業 (Jianye, the Wu capital) is in present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu province; 武昌 (Wuchang, Sun Quan's earlier seat) is in present-day Ezhou, Hubei province.

q: In the title 'Marquis of Hanshou Village' (Hanshou tinghou), is 'Marquis' an office or a rank of nobility? Did Guan Yu's receiving this title mean that he served as Prefect of Hanshou county?
reply:
## Conclusion

**"Marquis" (侯) here is a rank of nobility (爵), not an office (官).** In the *Sanguozhi* Guan Yu is enfeoffed (封) as 漢壽亭侯, whereas his actual posts are separately "appointed" (拜) or "made" (以…為) — the text keeps the two verbs and the two kinds of title apart. And **no, the title did not make him Prefect of Hanshou county**: Guan Yu's recorded offices never include Hanshou, and the 亭侯 title was a hereditary fief‑rank (his son inherited it), which is not how an office works.

## Evidence from the source

**1. The enfeoffment itself is a 封, distinct from his office, which is a 拜.**
- 「曹公禽羽以歸，拜為偏將軍」 … 「曹公即表封羽為漢壽亭侯」 [36] — Cao Cao captured Guan Yu and *appointed* (拜) him 偏將軍, then *memorialized to enfeoff* (表封) him as 漢壽亭侯.
So within one passage, 偏將軍 is an appointment and 漢壽亭侯 is an enfeoffment. Cao Cao enfeoffed him in the Han emperor's name (表封), after Guan Yu killed Yan Liang at Baima.

**2. His actual offices are listed elsewhere, and none of them is Hanshou.**
- 「以羽為襄陽太守、蕩寇將軍，駐江北」；「拜羽董督荊州事」 [36] — he was made Administrator of Xiangyang and General Dangkou, and later charged with supervising Jingzhou affairs.
- Earlier: 「以羽、飛為別部司馬」 and 「使羽守下邳城，行太守事」 [36] — separate-rank Sima; acting Administrator of Xiapi.
These are the administrative/military posts; the marquisate is not among them.

**3. The marquisate was a hereditary noble rank with a fief, which an office is not.**
- 「追諡羽曰壯繆侯。子興嗣。」 [36] — Guan Yu was posthumously titled 壯繆侯, and his son Guan Xing *inherited* (嗣) it; the title then passed to Guan Tong and Guan Yi.
- A parallel case shows the fief carried households: 「紹封攸孫彪爲陵樹亭侯，邑三百戸」 [11] — Xun Biao was enfeoffed as 陵樹亭侯 with 300 households of fief.

**4. 亭侯 is explicitly classified as a rank of nobility, and graded below 鄉侯 and 縣侯.**
- 「昭儀比縣侯；昭華比鄉侯；脩容比亭侯；脩儀比關內侯」 [16] — the palace ranks are compared to 縣侯, 鄉侯, 亭侯, 關內侯, i.e. grades of 爵.
- 裴松之按： 「然漢高祖時封皆列侯，未有鄉亭之爵」 [28] — Pei Songzhi himself calls 鄉侯/亭侯 a 「爵」 (rank of nobility).
- 裴注引《魏書》： 「置名號侯爵十八級，關中侯爵十七級……與舊列侯、關內侯凡六等」 [20] — the marquis ranks form a graded system of 爵, and it notes the new ones 「皆不食租」 (did not collect rent), implying the old 列侯/亭侯 did have 食邑.
- A shift between grades of the same kind of title: 「封高鄉亭侯……徙封安乐鄉侯，邑六百户」 [17] — a 亭侯 moved up to 鄉侯.

## Inference

Putting these together: (a) the text marks 漢壽亭侯 with 封, while Guan Yu's posts are marked 拜/以…為 [36]; (b) the title was inherited by his son [36] and other 亭侯 are recorded with 食邑 [11]; (c) 亭侯 is listed among the 爵 grades [16][20][28]. Since offices are neither inherited nor described as 食邑, and since Guan Yu's actual offices (別部司馬, acting Administrator of Xiapi, Administrator of Xiangyang, General Dangkou, supervisor of Jingzhou) never include Hanshou [36], it follows that 漢壽亭侯 was a noble fief‑title — a marquisate attached to the place called Hanshou (漢壽亭) — and **not** a post as Prefect (令/長) or Administrator (太守) of Hanshou. He drew a noble rank and fief, not an administrative appointment over that place.

One caution on the place name: the *Sanguozhi* does record a Hanshou county — 「潘濬字承明，武陵漢壽人也」 [42] — i.e. Hanshou was a county in Wuling commandery. That the name existed as a county does not mean Guan Yu governed it; the source gives him no Hanshou office, and the 亭侯 form is a fief‑rank designation rather than a governorship.

q: When Liu Shan surrendered to Teng Ai, how many households and how many people did the registers he sent over give for Shu-Han in total? How many soldiers and how many officials?
reply:
**Short answer:** According to Pei Songzhi's annotation to the *Record of the Later Ruler* (《後主傳》), quoting Wang Yin's 王隱《蜀記》, the register (士民簿) that Liu Shan (劉禪) sent to Deng Ai (鄧艾) recorded: **280,000 households; 940,000 men and women; 102,000 armored troops; and 40,000 officials.**

**Evidence**

The main text (Chen Shou) records the surrender itself, but the actual figures come from the Pei note:

- The surrender: 「劉禪遣使奉皇帝璽綬，為箋詣艾請降」[2]; and 「艾至城北，後主興櫬自縛，詣軍壘門」[4].
- The register, 裴注引王隱《蜀記》: 「又遣尚書郎李虎送士民簿，領戶二十八萬，男女口九十四萬，帶甲將士十萬二千，吏四萬人，米四十餘萬斛，金銀各二千斤，錦綺採絹各二十萬匹，餘物稱此」[6].

So the register that Pei Songzhi quotes gives:

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Households (戶) | 280,000 |
| Men and women (男女口) | 940,000 |
| Armored officers and men (帶甲將士) | 102,000 |
| Officials (吏) | 40,000 |

**Note on the source:** these numbers are not in Chen Shou's main text; they are preserved in **裴注引王隱《蜀記》** [6], i.e. Pei Songzhi's annotation quoting Wang Yin's *Shu Ji*. For comparison, when Wu (吳) fell, 裴注引《晉陽秋》 gives 「戶五十二萬三千，吏三萬二千，兵二十三萬，男女口二百三十萬」[12].

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The later, much-cited figures of "280,000 households / 940,000 persons" for Shu-Han are exactly these *Shu Ji* numbers as transmitted through Pei's annotation; other numbers sometimes seen in later works may derive from different sources.

q: When Sun Hao surrendered, how many households and how many people of Wu did Wang Jun take over? How many soldiers and how many officials?
reply:
**结论：** 按裴松之注所引《晋阳秋》的记载，王濬接收吴国图籍，共得**户五十二万三千**、**男女口二百三十万**、**兵二十三万**、**吏三万二千**（另有州四、郡四十三、县三百一十三，以及米谷二百八十万斛、舟船五千余艘、后宫五千余人）。

**依据：** 《三国志·吴书·三嗣主传》孙皓投降一段，正文记王濬最先到达、接受孙皓投降：

「壬申，王濬最先到，於是受皓之降，解縛焚櫬，延請相見。」[1]

这一段下的裴注引《晋阳秋》给出了您问的数目：

「《晉陽秋》曰：濬收其圖籍，領州四，郡四十三，縣三百一十三，戶五十二萬三千，吏三萬二千，兵二十三萬，男女口二百三十萬，米穀二百八十萬斛，舟船五千餘艘，後宮五千餘人。」[7]（裴注引《晋阳秋》）

所以：
- 户：五十二万三千
- 人口（男女口）：二百三十万
- 兵：二十三万
- 吏（官吏）：三万二千

**说明（推断）：** 据此推断，这些数字是王濬入建业后清点接收吴国官府簿籍所得的统计，其中「户」「男女口」「兵」「吏」是分别开列的几类，兵、吏似不计入「男女口」之内；不过《晋阳秋》只列数字，并未说明彼此是否互相包含，这一点无法从原文确定。

以上数目出自裴注所引《晋阳秋》，不是陈寿正文；正文本身只记王濬受降、孙皓西迁洛阳等事，未列这些统计数字。

q: Can the 'Jing Province' of the late Eastern Han be equated directly with today's Jingzhou city in Hubei? Explain how the two differ as geographical concepts.
reply:
No — the "Jing Province" (荊州) of the late Eastern Han cannot be equated with today's Jingzhou city. The Han-era Jing Province was a province-level unit (州) made up of many commanderies; today's Jingzhou is a single prefecture-level city occupying only a small part of the old province's territory (roughly the old Nan Commandery/Jiangling area).

**1. Han Jing Province was a 州 comprising several commanderies (郡), not a single city.**

A passage in Pei's commentary quoting Sima Biao's *Zhanlüe* has Kuai Yue advise Liu Biao:

「南據江陵，北守襄陽，荊州八郡可傳檄而定」[35] — "Hold Jiangling in the south, hold Xiangyang in the north, and the eight commanderies of Jing Province can be settled with a single proclamation." So Jing Province contained eight commanderies.

The commanderies named in the sources include Changsha, Lingling, Guiyang, Wuling and Nan (南郡):

- 「遂分荊州、長沙、江夏、桂陽以東屬權，南郡、零陵、武陵以西屬備」[22] — "So Jing Province was divided: Changsha, Jiangxia and Guiyang east of [the line] went to Sun Quan; Nan Commandery, Lingling and Wuling west of it went to Liu Bei."
- A parallel passage in the *Xianzhu zhuan* gives the same partition: 「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」[24].

So the Han Jing Province was a multi-commandery province, not one city.

**2. Its seat moved and the province was administered as a whole.**

Liu Biao governed it as 荊州牧/刺史 with his base at Xiangyang:

「靈帝崩，代王叡為荊州刺史……表亦合兵軍襄陽」[2] — "After Emperor Ling died, he replaced Wang Rui as Inspector of Jing Province… Liu Biao too gathered troops and camped at Xiangyang."

At his death his son Liu Cong was still at Xiangyang: 「表卒，其子琮代，屯襄陽」[6]. Later Liu Bei held the office of 荊州牧 and camped at Gong'an: 「備領荊州牧，屯公安」[25].

**3. The province was repeatedly re-divided as a political unit.**

Cao Pi's reign record shows the province being split into Jing and Ying provinces:

「以荊、揚、江表八郡為荊州，孫權領牧故也；荊州江北諸郡為郢州」[14] — "The eight commanderies of Jing, Yang and south of the Yangtze were made into Jing Province, because Sun Quan held the office of pastor; the commanderies of Jing Province north of the Yangtze were made into Ying Province."

This again shows "Jing Province" was a shifting administrative region, not a fixed city.

**4. Nan Commandery's seat, Jiangling, is the part that roughly corresponds to today's Jingzhou.**

Jiangling was the seat of Nan Commandery and a key strongpoint: Cao Cao left 「曹仁、徐晃於江陵」[31], and Guan Yu sent boats to rendezvous at Jiangling: 「別遣羽乘船數百艘會江陵」[37]. Sun Quan's forces took it: 「蒙據江陵，撫其老弱」[38].

**Inference:** From these facts — that Jing Province was a province (州) of eight commanderies [35], that those commanderies included Nan, Jiangxia, Changsha, Lingling, Guiyang and Wuling [22][24], and that its administrative seats shifted between Xiangyang and Jiangling [2][6][25] — it follows that Han Jing Province covered a very large area far beyond any single modern city, and that today's Jingzhou city corresponds only to its old Nan Commandery/Jiangling core, not to the province as a whole. This is an inference from the cited passages, not a statement the *Sanguozhi* itself makes.

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:**
Today's Jingzhou city (荊州市) is in Hubei Province, and the Han-era Jiangling/Nan Commandery area lay in the region of present-day Jingzhou, Hubei. "州" in the Han sense was a province-level division, larger than and different from a modern city.

q: Jiange chiefly controls traffic between which two regions? Why is it so well suited to defense?
reply:
## Short answer

In the *Sanguozhi*, Jiange (劍閣) is the mountain pass on the road linking **Hanzhong (漢中) in the north** with **the Shu heartland around Chengdu (成都) / the Fu–Mianzhu corridor in the south** — i.e. the gateway between the Wei-held north (Hanzhong and, beyond it, Guanzhong) and the Chengdu plain. It was so well suited to defense because it is a narrow defile that a garrison could block: Jiang Wei "arrayed camps and held the defile," and Zhong Hui's large army could not get through and was already discussing withdrawal.

## Evidence from the text

**1. It sits on the Hanzhong–Chengdu road.** When Zhong Hui's armies entered Hanzhong, Jiang Wei pulled back, and he and Zhang Yi, Dong Jue and the others "all retreated to hold Jiange in order to resist Zhong Hui":

> 「維聞鍾會諸軍已入漢中，引退還……皆退保劍閣以拒會。」[9]

Deng Ai's memorial shows what lay on the far side of the pass — the road to Fu (涪) and Chengdu, about 300 li away:

> 「從陰平由邪徑經漢德陽亭趣涪，出劍閣西百里，去成都三百餘里，奇兵衝其腹心。」[2]

So the pass stands between Hanzhong (north) and the Fu–Chengdu plain (south).

**2. It was defensible because it is a narrow defile held by a garrison.** Jiang Wei "did not answer the letter, and arrayed his camps to hold the defile; Zhong Hui could not overcome him, and his grain transport was far off, so he was about to discuss returning":

> 「維不答書，列營守險。會不能克，糧運縣遠，將議還歸。」[23]

The Zhong Hui biography likewise records that the attack on Jiange failed:

> 「進攻劍閣，不克，引退，蜀軍保險拒守。」[4]

And Pei Songzhi's note stresses the same point — that as long as Jiang Wei held Jiange, Zhong Hui could not advance:

> 「維與諸將列營守險，會不得進，已議還計。」[10]

**3. The only way past it was a detour.** Zhong Hui sent Tian Zhang "from west of Jiange" out to Jiangyou [4], and Deng Ai ultimately broke the deadlock by taking the side road through Yinping rather than forcing the pass [2][23] — which shows that the direct route ran through Jiange and could not simply be bypassed.

## Inference (my reasoning, not stated directly in the text)

From the facts above: (a) Zhong Hui's armies came into Hanzhong and then moved on Jiange [9]; (b) Deng Ai says that west of Jiange lies the road to Fu and Chengdu, 300-odd li away [2]; and (c) a defending force "arrayed camps and held the defile," while the attacking army "could not overcome him" and "could not advance" [23][10]. Putting these together, the pass controls the north–south route between Hanzhong and the Chengdu plain, and it favors the defender because the road is constricted there — a small force blocking the defile can stop a much larger one, which is why a detour (Zhong Hui sending Tian Zhang west of Jiange; Deng Ai's Yinping side road) was needed to get around it [2][4][23].

*Note on dates:* the fall of Jiange belongs to the Shu Jingyao 6 / Wei Jingyuan 4 campaign, which the era tool gives as AD 263.

q: Is Hanzhong north or south of the Qinling mountains? Why was it such an important region for Shu-Han, both for defending against attack from the north and for sending armies northward?
reply:
## Hanzhong lies **south** of the Qinling range

**Conclusion:** In the *Sanguozhi*'s own directional language, the Qinling (秦嶺) sits *between* the Guanzhong plain/Chang'an to the north and Hanzhong to the south, so Hanzhong is on the southern side of the Qinling. It was decisive for Shu-Han in both directions: as the "throat" through which any northern army must come to reach the Shu heartland, and as the only practical springboard from which Shu could strike north.

### 1. Which side of the Qinling?

The records show the Qinling as the barrier you cross to get from Chang'an down into Hanzhong:

- When Cao Cao moved against Hanzhong, 「王自長安出斜谷，軍遮要以臨漢中，遂至陽平」[15] — the king went out from Chang'an through the Xie Valley and advanced on Hanzhong. (Chang'an is on the north side of the Qinling; he moves through the range to reach Hanzhong.)
- Cao Zhen's projected invasion of Shu went 「從子午道南入」[36] — "south" through the Ziwu road into Hanzhong.
- Conversely, Wei Yan's plan to strike Chang'an from Hanzhong was to go 「直從褒中出，循秦嶺而東，當子午而北，不過十日可到長安」[21] — out from Bao**zhong** (in Hanzhong), east along the Qinling, then *north* through Ziwu to Chang'an.

So from Hanzhong you go **north** to reach the Guanzhong plain, and from Chang'an you go **south** into Hanzhong — Hanzhong is the southern side of the Qinling. Liu Bei's own movement into the Hanzhong front is likewise described as going south across the Mian River: 「二十四年春，自陽平南渡沔水，緣山稍前」[4].

### 2. Why it mattered for **defending** Shu

The Shu men themselves called it the state's lifeline:

- Yang Hong: 「漢中則益州咽喉，存亡之機會，若無漢中則無蜀矣，此家門之禍也」[3] — "Hanzhong is the throat of Yizhou, the hinge of survival; without Hanzhong there is no Shu."
- Huang Quan: 「若失漢中，則三巴不振，此為割蜀之股臂也」[53] — losing Hanzhong would cripple the Three Ba and cut off Shu's thigh and arm.

And the whole Shu defense system was built around it. Liu Bei left Wei Yan as 督漢中 to hold it [18], and the standard method was to block the passes so the enemy could not get through: 「先主留魏延鎮漢中，皆實兵諸圍以御外敵。敵若來攻，使不得入」[7]. When Cao Shuang attacked, Wang Ping and Liu Min held Xingshi and the Wei army had to withdraw [20][26]; later Jiang Wei redesigned the plan to pull the garrisons back to Han and Le cities and let the enemy exhaust himself on the mountain roads [7]. The point is the same: the Qinling passes are narrow, and whoever holds Hanzhong's mouths can shut them.

Even the Wei side acknowledged this. Liu Ye argued that once Hanzhong fell, 「蜀人望風，破膽失守……蜀可傳檄而定」[1]. And the passes themselves were notoriously brutal — Cao Cao called them 「山峻難登」[51], and the Wei court remembered his saying 「南鄭直為天獄，中斜谷道為五百里石穴耳」[73] ("Nanzheng is simply a natural prison; the Xie Valley road is nothing but a 500-li stone hole"), which is exactly why Liu Ye/Sun Zi advised against marching on Hanzhong [73], and why Cao Zhen's multi-road invasion collapsed in the rains [27][36].

### 3. Why it mattered for **sending armies north**

Hanzhong was the only base from which Shu could push into the north, so every northern campaign started there:

- Zhuge Liang 「率諸軍北駐漢中」[24], and from Hanzhong he struck at Qishan, at Chencang, and up the Xie Valley road [23][9].
- The routes all ran out of Hanzhong toward the north: the Xie Valley (斜谷), Ziwu (子午), and Luo Valley (駱谷) roads toward Chang'an/Guanzhong, and the road west toward Qishan and Longyou [21][27][76].
- Wei Yan even proposed a daring separate thrust from Hanzhong to Chang'an by way of Ziwu [21], and repeatedly asked to take ten thousand men and meet Zhuge Liang at Tong Pass "as in the Han Xin precedent" [77] — all of which presupposes Hanzhong as the launch point.

So the same geography works both ways: it is the gate Shu must keep shut to survive, and the gate it must pass through to threaten the north.

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载: Hanzhong (then 漢中/南鄭) is in the general area of present-day Hanzhong, Shaanxi province. The Qinling is an east–west mountain range separating the Guanzhong plain (around Xi'an, i.e. ancient Chang'an) from the Han River basin; Hanzhong sits in that basin on the southern flank of the Qinling.

q: How old were the brothers Ma Liang and Ma Su, respectively, when they died?
reply:
**结论：**《三国志》明确记载了兄弟二人去世时的年龄——**马良死时三十六岁，马谡三十九岁**，也就是说**弟弟马谡反而比哥哥马良大三岁**（古人记的是虚岁，但这里只按原文的数字说）。

**依据（原文）：**

- 马良与马谡的年龄同见于《三国志·蜀书·董刘马陈董吕传》马良传的末尾一句：「良死時年三十六，謖年三十九。」[1]
- 同一段还交代了两人各自的死因和背景：
  - 马良：「先主稱尊號，以良為侍中。及東征吳，遣良入武陵招納五溪蠻夷……會先主敗績於夷陵，良亦遇害。」[1]——即先主（刘备）称帝后任马良为侍中，东征吴国时派他入武陵招纳五溪蛮夷，恰逢先主在夷陵大败，马良也遇害。
  - 马谡：「建興六年，亮出軍向祁山……與魏將張郃戰於街亭，為郃所破，士卒離散……謖下獄物故，亮為之流涕。」[1]——建兴六年（公元 228 年）[era: 蜀汉建兴六年 = 228]，诸葛亮出兵祁山，违背众议提拔马谡为先锋，马谡在街亭被魏将张郃击败，下狱而死，诸葛亮为他流泪。
- 兄弟关系与出身：「馬良字季常，襄陽宜城人也。兄弟五人，並有才名，鄉里為之諺曰：『馬氏五常，白眉最良。』」[2]；「良弟謖，字幼常」[1]——马良字季常，襄阳宜城人，兄弟五人都有才名；马谡是马良的弟弟，字幼常。
- 关于马谡之死的另一说：裴注引《襄阳记》载马谡临终给诸葛亮写信，「明公視謖猶子，謖視明公猶父」[12]；而《三国志·王平传》则记「丞相亮既誅馬謖及將軍張休、李盛」[15]，诸葛亮自己在疏中也说「戮謖以謝眾」[17]。可见正文与裴注对马谡是"下狱物故"还是被处死，说法略有不同。

**据此推断：** 既然原文说马良死时三十六、马谡死时三十九 [1]，而马谡又明确是马良的弟弟 [1]，那么马谡比马良年长约三岁；两人都在蜀汉前期去世，马良死于夷陵之败那一年，马谡死于建兴六年（228 年）街亭之败之后 [1]。

**以下不是《三国志》的记载：** 《三国志》只说「良死時年三十六，謖年三十九」[1]，并未给出两人出生的具体年份，也没有记载他们死于何月何日；上面推出的出生年份只是据此做的估算。

q: When Guan Yu flooded the seven armies, how many of Yu Jin's men did he capture? And how many men did Cao Ren have holding out in Fancheng at the time?
reply:
##结论

**于禁被俘的人数：《三国志》只有《吴主传》给了一个数字——三万（步骑三万）。** 其他各传只说"七军皆没"、于禁投降，没有写人数。

- 「會漢水暴起，羽以舟兵盡生虜禁等步騎三萬送江陵，惟城未拔。」[6]（《吴书·吴主传》）
- 「秋，大霖雨，漢水溢，平地水數丈，禁等七軍皆沒。……羽乘大船就攻禁等，禁遂降」[1]（《魏书·于禁传》）
- 「禁所督七軍皆沒。禁降羽」[3]（《蜀书·关羽传》）

**曹仁守樊城的兵力：几千人。**

- 「仁人馬數千人守城，城不沒者數板。」[2]（《魏书·曹仁传》）

## 依据与背景

此事系于建安二十四年（据年号换算为公元 219 年）：

- 《魏书·武帝纪》：「秋七月……遣于禁助曹仁擊關羽。八月，漢水溢，灌禁軍，軍沒，羽獲禁，遂圍仁。使徐晃救之。」[11]
- 曹仁被围的处境，《曹仁传》记：「羽乘船臨城，圍數重，外內斷絕，糧食欲盡，救兵不至」[2]；满宠劝曹仁不要弃城夜走，「會徐晃等救至，寵力戰有功，羽遂退」[5]（《魏书·满宠传》）。

**据此推断：** 于禁所督七军既被水淹没、随后投降并被送江陵，则"三万人"应是于禁等七军被俘的总数（《吴主传》说的是"尽生虏禁等步骑三万"）；而曹仁在樊城城内另有人马数千，两者不是同一支部队，不可相加。至于曹仁这几千人是否也含水淹后的残兵，《曹仁传》只作"仁人馬數千人守城"，未说明其构成，不作推断。

另需说明一点：庞德与于禁同时被围，庞德不屈而死。《于禁传》《关羽传》记「惟龐德不屈節而死」「羽又斬將軍龐德」[1][3]；《庞德传》则记庞德战至矢尽、船覆被擒，拒不跪降而骂关羽[10]——几种记载对庞德结局的用词（"不屈节而死""斩""被擒"）不完全一致，这里并列说明，不替读者裁定。

q: What was Sima Yi's father's name? How old was he when he died, and in which year? How many sons did he have, and where did Sima Yi rank among them?
reply:
## Answer

**Sima Yi's father:** Sima Fang (司馬防), courtesy name Jiangong (建公).

**His age and year of death:** He died at 71, in Jian'an 24 (219 CE).

**Number of sons and Sima Yi's rank:** He had eight sons; Sima Lang (司馬朗) was the eldest, and Sima Yi — referred to as "the Jin Emperor Xuan" (晉宣皇帝) — was second.

### Evidence

The key passage is Pei Songzhi's annotation to the biography of Sima Lang, quoting Sima Biao's *Xu Zhuan* (司馬彪《序傳》):

「父防，字建公，性質直公方，雖閑居宴處，威儀不忒……年七十一，建安二十四年終。有子八人，朗最長，次即晉宣皇帝也。」[1]

("His father Fang, courtesy name Jiangong, was by nature upright and impartial; even in leisure his dignity never lapsed... He was seventy-one years old and died in Jian'an 24. He had eight sons; Lang was the eldest, and the next was the Jin Emperor Xuan.")

The Jian'an 24 date converts to 219 CE [era tool].

The main text of the same biography confirms Sima Lang's place as the eldest son and his father's name:

「司馬朗字伯達，河内溫人也。」[23] — Sima Lang's courtesy name was Boda (伯達), the "Bo" (eldest) indicating his seniority. And later: 「朗父防爲治書御史」[7] ("Lang's father Fang served as Attendant Censor").

That Sima Yi was the second son is also supported by a Pei annotation citing the *Jin Shu* (裴注引《晉書》), which speaks of "the Grand Commander's fifth younger brother, named Tong" [12] — showing the brothers were ranked by age, with Sima Yi not the eldest.

### Summary of the facts
- **Father:** Sima Fang, courtesy name Jiangong [1]
- **Offices:** in his youth he served in the province and commandery, successively holding the posts of Prefect of Luoyang (洛陽令) and Metropolitan Governor of the Capital Region (京兆尹), later transferring to Cavalry Commandant (騎都尉) on account of age [1]
- **Death:** at 71, in Jian'an 24 = 219 CE [1]
- **Sons:** eight in all [1]
- **Sima Yi's rank:** second, after the eldest, Sima Lang [1]

q: Before the Battle of Red Cliffs, what did Chou Yü privately estimate to Sun Ch'üan as Ts'ao Ts'ao's actual troop strength? How many did Ts'ao Ts'ao claim in his letter? And how many picked troops did Chou Yü say would be enough to deal with them?
reply:
**Short answer**

Before Red Cliffs (Jian'an 13 = 208 AD), Zhou Yu told Sun Quan privately that Cao Cao's real strength was far below what Cao claimed:

- **Cao Cao's own claim in his letter to Sun Quan: 800,000 (水军八十万众).**
- **Zhou Yu's private estimate: the Central Plains troops Cao actually led were "no more than 150,000–160,000" (不過十五六萬), plus at most 70,000–80,000 of Liu Biao's surrendered troops (所得表眾，亦極七八萬耳).**
- **Troops Zhou Yu said would be enough: 50,000 picked soldiers (得精兵五萬，自足制之).**

**Evidence**

The letter is preserved in Pei Songzhi's annotation to the *Wu Zhu zhuan*, quoting the *Jiang Biao Zhuan* (《江表傳》):

「近者奉辭伐罪，旄麾南指，劉琮束手。今治水軍八十萬眾，方與將軍會獵於吳。」[12]

("Lately I have received the command to punish the guilty; my banners point south, and Liu Cong has surrendered with hands bound. I have now marshalled a host of 800,000 sailors, and am about to go hunting with you in Wu.") — Sun Quan showed the letter to his assembled officials, and none failed to turn pale with fear.

Zhou Yu's private audience with Sun Quan that night is likewise from the *Jiang Biao Zhuan*, quoted in Pei Songzhi's annotation to Zhou Yu's biography:

「諸人徒見操書，言水步八十萬，而各恐懾，不復料其虛實……今以實校之，彼所將中國人，不過十五六萬，且軍已久疲，所得表眾，亦極七八萬耳，尚懷狐疑。夫以疲病之卒，御狐疑之眾，眾數雖多，甚未足畏。得精兵五萬，自足制之，原將軍勿慮。」[1]

("The others merely saw Cao's letter, saying 800,000 land and naval troops, and each was frightened, no longer weighing whether it was true or false… Now, reckoning by the reality, the Central Plains men he leads are no more than 150,000 or 160,000, and his army has long been exhausted; the host he obtained from Liu Biao is at most 70,000 or 80,000, and they still harbor doubts. With exhausted, sick troops to drive a doubtful multitude, though the numbers be many, they are not to be feared. Give me 50,000 picked soldiers, and that is enough to master them; I beg you, General, not to worry.")

Sun Quan's reply in the same passage is also worth noting: 「五萬兵難卒合，已選三萬人，船糧戰具俱辦」[1] — "Fifty thousand troops are hard to assemble at short notice; I have already selected 30,000, and the ships, grain and war gear are all ready."

Note on sourcing: both the letter and Zhou Yu's reckoning come from the *Jiang Biao Zhuan* (《江表傳》) as quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary, not from Chen Shou's main text. Chen Shou's main text of the Zhou Yu biography says only that Cao Cao "obtained his navy, ships and foot-soldiers several hundred thousand" (「曹公得其水軍，船步兵數十萬」) [4], which is the figure that frightened Sun Quan's officers. In the same passage of the *Jiang Biao Zhuan*, Pei Songzhi adds his own note that the plan to resist Cao Cao in fact originated with Lu Su (「臣松之以為建計拒曹公，實始魯肅」) [1].

**Timing**: the main text dates Cao Cao's entry into Jingzhou and Liu Cong's surrender to the ninth month of Jian'an 13, i.e. 208 AD [4][era: 建安13 = 208].

**Inference**: reckoning from Zhou Yu's own figures, Cao's genuine strength was roughly 220,000–240,000 at most (150,000–160,000 of his own plus 70,000–80,000 of Liu Biao's men) — well under a third of the 800,000 his letter claimed; hence his conclusion that 50,000 picked troops would suffice. This is my arithmetic on Zhou Yu's stated numbers, not a figure given directly in the text.

q: In the year Cao Pi usurped the Han throne and declared himself emperor, how many times did the reign era change, and what were the era names? What year was that in the Western calendar?
reply:
## 结论

曹丕篡汉称帝那一年（公元 220 年），**年号改了两次**，涉及的年号是**延康**和**黄初**。

## 依据

那一年本为汉建安二十五年。正月曹操去世，曹丕继任丞相、魏王，随即把年号改为延康：

- 「太子丕代爲丞相魏王，改年爲延康」[1]（裴注 47-0017n0 未显示，此处为《吴主传》正文）
- 「改建安二十五年爲延康元年」[8]（《文帝纪》）

到冬天曹丕即帝位，又改延康为黄初：

- 「冬，魏嗣王稱尊號，改元爲黃初」[1]
- 「改延康爲黃初，大赦」[5]（《文帝纪》）
- 裴注引《献帝传》所载诏书亦云「其以延康元年爲黃初元年」[14]

所以这一年内年号先后为：建安二十五年 → 延康元年 → 黄初元年，共改元**两次**（建安改延康、延康改黄初）。

**公元年份**：经年号换算，建安二十五年、延康元年、黄初元年均为**公元 220 年**。

**据此推断**：题中"曹丕篡汉称帝之年"即延康元年、黄初元年，也就是公元 220 年；由于曹丕在正月继位魏王时已改元延康，同年十一月（《文帝纪》载「黃初元年十一月癸酉」）受禅称帝时再改元黄初，故这一年出现了两个新起用的年号、两次改元。

q: In the year Zhuge Liang died at Wuzhang Plains, which year of which reign era was it in Shu-Han, and which in Wei? What year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
## 结论

诸葛亮死于五丈原的这一年：

- **蜀汉**：后主**建兴十二年**（《诸葛亮传》记「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出……據武功五丈原」，同传下文「其年八月，亮疾病，卒于軍」）[1]；《后主传》也记「十二年春二月，亮由斜谷出……秋八月，亮卒渭濱」[6]。
- **曹魏**：魏明帝**青龙二年**（《明帝纪》在「二年春二月乙未」以下叙事，接着「是月，諸葛亮出斜谷，屯渭南」，然后「司馬宣王與亮相持……會亮卒，其軍退還」）[24][21][12]。
- **公元年**：蜀汉建兴十二年 = **公元 234 年**；曹魏青龙二年 = **公元 234 年**。两边是同一年。

## 依据

蜀汉方面，诸葛亮本传：

> 「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出，以流馬運，據武功五丈原，與司馬宣王對於渭南……其年八月，亮疾病，卒于軍，時年五十四。」[1]

《后主传》同年：

> 「十二年春二月，亮由斜谷出，始以流馬運。秋八月，亮卒渭濱。」[6]

曹魏方面，《明帝纪》青龙二年：

> 「是月，諸葛亮出斜谷，屯渭南，司馬宣王率諸軍拒之。」[21]
> 「司馬宣王與亮相持，連圍積日，亮數挑戰，宣王堅壘不應。會亮卒，其軍退還。」[12]

年号换算由工具给出：建兴十二年（蜀汉）＝234 年，青龙二年（曹魏）＝234 年。

**据此推断**：正因为两国各自用本朝年号纪年，同一年在蜀汉记为建兴十二年、在曹魏记为青龙二年，所以诸葛亮卒于五丈原这件事，在两国史书里是同一年的两种年号写法。

## 补充（不算《三国志》本文的记载）

关于死因，《魏书》说「亮糧盡勢窮，憂恚歐血，一夕燒營遁走，入谷，道發病卒」，《汉晋春秋》说「亮卒于郭氏塢」，《晋阳秋》则记星坠之兆；裴松之按语认为「歐血」之说是魏人自夸，并解释「入谷而卒」是因蜀人入谷发丧而生讹[2]。这些异说并列，裴松之并未替读者裁定。

q: In which year did Sun Quan formally take the imperial title? Which year of which reign era was in use before he did so, and what era name did he adopt afterward? What year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
## Answer

**Conclusion:** Sun Quan formally took the imperial title in the 4th month of the 1st year of Huanglong (黃龍元年夏四月) [1]. The reign era in use before that was **Huangwu (黃武)** — the record counts the same event as occurring in "the 8th year of Huangwu" (黃武八年夏) [11], so Huangwu had run to its 8th year. The era name he adopted afterward was **Huanglong (黃龍)**, and the 1st year of Huanglong = **AD 229** [era tool].

### Evidence from the《三国志》

- Main account of Sun Quan's accession: 「黃龍元年春，公卿百司皆勸權正尊號。夏四月，夏口、武昌並言黃龍、鳳凰見。丙申，南郊即皇帝位。是日大赦。改年……」 [1] — In the spring of Huanglong 1, the officials urged Quan to assume the honored title; in the 4th month (summer), on the bing-shen day, he ascended the imperial throne at the southern suburb, proclaimed a general amnesty, and changed the era [1].
- The old era and the change of era: 「黃武八年夏，黃龍見舉口，於是權稱尊號，因瑞改元。」 [11] — In the 8th year of Huangwu, in summer, a yellow dragon appeared at Jukou (舉口); thereupon Quan assumed the honored title and, on account of the omen, changed the era [11]. This shows the era in force beforehand was Huangwu, and it was changed to Huanglong.
- Sun Quan's own announcement of accession, cited in Pei Songzhi's commentary from the《吳錄》: 「皇帝臣權敢用玄牡昭告於皇皇后帝……謹擇元日，登壇燎祭，即皇帝位。」 [16] (Pei note quoting《吳錄》).

**Calendar conversion (only from the era tool):** Huanglong 1 = AD 229; Huangwu 8 = AD 229 (the same year, consistent with the era change) [era tool].

**Inference (so labeled):** Since the same accession is dated both as "Huanglong 1" [1] and as "the 8th year of Huangwu" [11], and both convert to AD 229, we may infer that the change of era took place as part of the accession itself — i.e., the former era Huangwu was terminated in its 8th year and replaced by Huanglong in the same year, AD 229.

One further record, cited in Pei Songzhi's commentary from the《吳書》, relates to the accession: 「初，權即尊號，令達算作天子之後，當復幾年？」 [2] (Pei note quoting《吳書》) — after taking the title, Sun Quan had Zhao Da divine how many more years he would reign; this is a note, not the main account.

No background paragraph is needed here: the era names Huangwu and Huanglong and the accession are all attested in the《三国志》text itself.

q: In the year Ma Su lost Chieh-t'ing, which year of which reign era was Shu-Han using? What year was it on the Wei side? And what year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
## 结论

马谡在街亭战败的那一年，蜀汉用的是**建兴六年**，曹魏方面是**魏明帝太和二年**，也就是公元**228 年**。

## 依据

**蜀汉一方：建兴六年**

《诸葛亮传》在这一年下记：「六年春，揚聲由斜谷道取眉，使趙雲、鄧芝為疑軍，據箕谷……亮使馬謖督諸軍在前，與郃戰于街亭。謖違亮節度，舉動失宜，大為張郃所破。」[1]

这里的「六年」是接在《后主传》的年号序列里：该传先记「建興四年春」「五年春」，接着是「六年春，亮出攻祁山，不克」[15]，可知这个「六年」即建兴六年。

《马良传》记马谡事也说：「建興六年，亮出軍向祁山……與魏將張郃戰於街亭，為郃所破」[8]；《王平传》同样作「建興六年，屬參軍馬謖先鋒……大敗於街亭」[7]。

**曹魏一方：太和二年**

《明帝纪》太和二年下记：「蜀大將諸葛亮寇邊，天水、南安、安定三郡吏民叛應亮。遣大將軍曹真都督關右，並進兵。右將軍張郃擊亮於街亭，大破之。亮敗走，三郡平。」[37]

《张郃传》记同一事：「諸葛亮出祁山。加郃位特進，遣督諸軍，拒亮將馬謖於街亭。謖依阻南山，不下據城。郃絶其汲道，擊，大破之。」[16]

**公元年**

建兴六年 = 公元 228 年（蜀汉）[era 工具]；太和二年 = 公元 228 年（曹魏）[era 工具]。两条纪年指向同一年。

**一点推断**

蜀汉用建兴、曹魏用太和，是两国各自纪年：蜀汉在建兴年号下记此事，曹魏在太和年号下记此事。据此推断，这是同一场战事在两国史书中的两种纪年写法，而非两件事。

以下不是《三国志》的记载：问题中说的「Chieh-t'ing」即街亭，当时的地名，在今甘肃庄浪、秦安一带。

q: What year in the Western calendar is the 'first year of Ganlu' in the Records of the Three Kingdoms?
reply:
**Answer:** In the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, "Ganlu" (甘露) is used as a reign title by **two different regimes**, so "the first year of Ganlu" has two possible values:

- **Cao Wei** (under the boy emperor Cao Mao, the Duke of Gaoguixiang): the 1st year of Ganlu = **256 AD**.
- **Sun Wu** (under Sun Hao): the 1st year of Ganlu = **265 AD**.

If the question means the Wei reign title (by far the more commonly cited "Ganlu"), the answer is **256 AD**.

**Evidence from the text:**

The Wei record opens the era: 「甘露元年春正月辛丑，青龍見軹縣井中」[3] — "In the first year of Ganlu, spring, first month, on the xinchou day, a blue-green dragon appeared in a well in Zhi County." The preceding passage shows the era being proclaimed: 「夏六月丙午，改元為甘露」[2] — "In summer, sixth month, on the bingwu day, the reign was changed to Ganlu."

The Wu record separately uses the same title: 「甘露元年三月，皓遣使隨紹、彧報書曰……」[1] — "In the third month of the first year of Ganlu, Sun Hao sent envoys..." Note that this Wu Ganlu runs so late that the same passage ends 「十二月，晉受禪」[1] ("in the twelfth month, Jin received the abdication"), which fits a year after Wei's own end.

That the two are distinct is confirmed by a Wu passage dating itself to the Wei era: 「是歲，於魏甘露三年也」[4] — "This year was the third year of Wei's Ganlu."

**Conversion to the Western calendar (from the era tool):**

- Ganlu, year 1: Western Han −53; **Cao Wei 256**; **Sun Wu 265**.

So the "first year of Ganlu" in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* is **256 AD** if the Wei era is meant, and **265 AD** if the Wu era is meant.

q: In which year did Zhuge Ke build the great dam at Dongxing and crush the Wei army? Is that 'first year of Jianxing' the same thing as the first year of Jianxing in Shu-Han in Zhuge Liang's day?
reply:
## Short answer

Yes to the first question, no to the second — the two "Jianxing 1"s are **not** the same year.

**The Dongxing campaign: winter of 252 AD.**

- In the **10th month of Jianxing 1** Zhuge Ke gathered his forces at Dongxing and rebuilt the dam: 「恪以建興元年十月會眾於東興，更作大堤，左右結山俠築兩城，各留千人，使全端、留略守之，引軍而還」[1] (Wu record).
- The Wei army then came and was crushed: 「恪興軍四萬，晨夜赴救……魏軍驚擾散走，爭渡浮橋，橋壞絕，自投於水，更相蹈藉。樂安太守桓嘉等同時並沒，死者數萬」[1]. The Sun Liang annals date the Wei siege and the battle to the **12th month**, with day-by-day dates: 「十二月朔丙申……魏使將軍諸葛誕、胡遵等步騎七萬圍東興……戊午，兵及東興，交戰，大破魏軍，殺將軍韓綜、桓嘉等」[2].
- Wu's Jianxing 1 = **252 AD** (era tool). The same event is dated in Wei terms as Jiapin 4: 「四年春正月癸卯……冬十一月，詔征南大將軍王昶、征東將軍胡遵、鎮南將軍毌丘儉等征吳。十二月，吳大將軍諸葛恪拒戰，大破衆軍於東關」[3], and Wei's Jiapin 4 = **252 AD** (era tool).

So: dam built in the 10th month, victory won in the 12th month, both in 252 AD.

**The two Jianxing eras are different.**

- Wu 建興 1 = **252 AD** (the year of the Dongxing victory).
- Shu-Han 建興 1 = **223 AD** (era tool) — that is Liu Shan's accession year, the era in which Zhuge Liang was regent. So they are different years, 29 years apart, and belong to two different states that happened to use the same era name.

In fact, in 252 AD Zhuge Liang had been dead for eighteen years (he died in Shu-Han Jianxing 12, i.e. 234 AD); Zhuge Ke, his nephew, was the Wu regent under Sun Liang.

## Evidence (original text)

- 「恪以建興元年十月會眾於東興，更作大堤」[1]
- 「魏以吳軍入其疆土，恥於受侮，命大將胡遵、諸葛誕等率眾七萬，欲攻圍兩塢，圖壞堤遏」[1]
- 「戊午，兵及東興，交戰，大破魏軍」[2]
- 「十二月，吳大將軍諸葛恪拒戰，大破衆軍於東關」[3]
- 裴注引《漢晉春秋》on the same event: 「是歲諸葛恪帥軍更於隄左右結山，挾築兩城，使全端、留略守之，引軍而還」[4]

## A note on the dating (inference)

The three records use three different calendars for one campaign: Wu's 建興元年 (10th month, dam; 12th month, battle) [1][2], and Wei's 嘉平四年 (11th month, the Wei court orders the campaign; 12th month, the defeat) [3]. Since Wu 建興 1 = 252 AD and Wei 嘉平 4 = 252 AD, these are consistent: the dam was built in the 10th month and the battle fought in the 12th month of 252.

q: Is the Zhang Wen under whom Sun Jian served on the western campaign against Liang Province the same person as the Wu statesman Zhang Wen who went as envoy to Shu?
reply:
**结论：不是同一个人。**《三国志》及裴注里至少有两位叫张温的人物，你问的这两位正好分别就是这两个人。

**一、随孙坚西征凉州的张温，是东汉的朝廷重臣**

《孙破虏讨逆传》(孙坚传) 记载：

> 「邊章、韓遂作亂涼州，中郎將董卓拒討無功。中平三年，遣司空張溫行車騎將軍，西討章等。溫表請堅與參軍事，屯長安。」[6]

即：中平三年 (公元 186 年，据 era 工具)，朝廷派**司空**张温代理车骑将军，西讨边章、韩遂；张温上表请孙坚参军事。孙坚劝他按军法斩董卓一事也发生在这时 [6]，孙坚本传的评语因此说「導溫戮卓」[3]。同一次出征中，张温还「又請謙爲參軍事」，即请陶谦做参军事 [24]。

这个张温是东汉的三公之臣。裴注引《傅子》把他列入灵帝时买官的三公：「太尉段熲、司徒崔烈、太尉樊陵、司空張溫之徒，皆入錢上千萬下五百萬以買三公」[28]；《董卓传》又记：「故太尉張溫時爲衞尉，素不善卓，卓心怨之，因天有變，欲以塞咎，使人言溫與袁術交關，遂笞殺之」[27]——他做过太尉，董卓时官居卫尉，后被董卓鞭杀。

**二、出使蜀汉的张温，是孙吴的大臣**

《吴书·张温传》：

> 「張溫字惠恕，吳郡吳人也。」[22]

他任选曹尚书、太子太傅，很受孙权信重 [22]。黄武三年 (公元 224 年，据 era 工具) 孙权「遣輔義中郎將張溫聘於蜀」[23]，本传作「時年三十二，以輔義中郎將使蜀」[15]，去回访邓芝使吴修好之后的事 [16]。后来他因暨艳案被孙权斥还本郡，废黜，六年后病死 [26]、[20]。

**三、据此推断**

依据上面的事实：西征凉州那位张温，中平三年 (186) 已是东汉的司空、后来官至太尉、卫尉，被董卓杀害；出使蜀汉的这位张温，吴郡吴县人，黄武三年 (224) 三十二岁出使蜀汉。据此推断：224 年才三十二岁的吴臣张温，在 186 年尚未出生，两人年代相差近四十年，官职系统 (东汉三公—卫尉 vs. 孙吴选曹尚书—太子太傅)、籍贯出身都不同，因此绝非一人。《三国志》人物表也把他们分列为两个同名者：一个是「汉司空，行车骑将军西讨边章，表请孙坚参军事」，另一个是「汉太尉，曾任卫尉，因不善董卓被笞杀」，与吴臣张温 (字惠恕) 各为一传或各见一处。

以下不是《三国志》的记载：问题把两人当成一人来问，这种混同《三国志》里没有记载，可能是后人不注意同名而致；吴郡吴县 (张温的籍贯) 在今江苏苏州一带。

q: What is the relationship between the silent hermit Sun Deng whom Ji Kang met in the mountains and Sun Deng, Sun Quan's crown prince?
reply:
## Conclusion

They are **two entirely different men who happen to share the name Sun Deng (孙登)**. There is no relationship between them in the *Sanguozhi*. They differ in courtesy name, region, and era:

- **The hermit** whom Ji Kang met: 孙登, courtesy name **Gonghe (公和)**, a man of no known origin, no family, living in a cave on the northern mountain of Jixian (汲县) in Wei territory.
- **Sun Quan's crown prince**: 孙登, courtesy name **Zigao (子高)**, Sun Quan's eldest son.

## Evidence

**1. The hermit (courtesy name Gonghe).** In Pei Songzhi's commentary to the *Sanguozhi* life of Wang Can (attached biography of Ji Kang), the *Wei shi chunqiu* records the mountain encounter:

「初，康採藥於汲郡共北山中，見隱者孫登。康欲與之言，登默然不對。踰時將去，康曰：『先生竟無言乎？』登乃曰：『子才多識寡，難乎免於今之世。』」[2]

*(At first, Ji Kang was gathering herbs in the northern mountain of Gongxian in Jijun, and met the recluse Sun Deng. Ji Kang wanted to speak with him, but Sun Deng silently did not answer...)*

The *Ji Kang ji mulu* gives his courtesy name and dwelling:

「康集目錄曰：登字公和，不知何許人，無家屬，於汲縣北山土窟中得之。夏則編草爲裳，冬則被髮自覆。好讀易鼓琴，見者皆親樂之。」[1]

*(Sun Deng, courtesy name Gonghe, of unknown origin, no family; found in an earthen cave in the northern mountain of Jixian...)*

And the *Jin yangqiu* explains the "silence" motif:

「又《晉陽秋》云：康見孫登，登對之長嘯，踰時不言。康辭還，曰：『先生竟無言乎？』登曰：『惜哉！』」[1]

*(...Sun Deng faced him and gave a long whistle, and for a long while said nothing...)*

**2. The crown prince (courtesy name Zigao).** The *Sanguozhi·Wu shu* opens the biography of Sun Deng:

「孫登字子高，權長子也。」[11]

*(Sun Deng, courtesy name Zigao, was Sun Quan's eldest son.)*

He was made a "king's crown prince" after Sun Quan was enfeoffed as King of Wu, and became crown prince when Sun Quan took the imperial title in the Huanglong era; he died after serving as heir for twenty-one years, aged thirty-three, and was posthumously titled "Xuan Taizi" (宣太子).[11][12]

## Inference

From the two sets of facts above — the hermit's courtesy name 公和 versus the prince's 子高, the hermit's cave in Jixian in Wei territory versus the prince's position at Sun Quan's court in the Wu capital, and the hermit's appearance in Ji Kang's story (Ji Kang lived in the Wei/Jin transition) versus the prince's tenure as heir in the Huanglong–Chiwu period — it follows that these are simply two homonymous persons, with no recorded connection of kinship, office, or acquaintance.

## Background

The *Sanguozhi* proper (Chen Shou's main text) does not itself narrate the hermit Sun Deng's encounter with Ji Kang; that story comes from Pei Songzhi's quoted sources (《魏氏春秋》, 《晉陽秋》, 《嵇康集目錄》). The "silent hermit" is thus preserved in the commentary rather than in the base text. The place 汲县 (Jixian) mentioned for the hermit is in present-day Weihui, Henan province.

q: How many different people named Li Feng appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and who were they?
reply:
**Conclusion: two different men named Li Feng (李豐) appear in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国志》).** One was a Wei official of the Zhengshi–Jiaping era, the other was a Shu Han official, the son of Li Yan (李嚴).

---

**1. Li Feng of Wei, courtesy name Anguo (安国)**

He was the son of Li Yi (李义), former Commandant of the Guards (衞尉). The Pei note quoting the *Weilüe* says: 「豐字安國，故衞尉李義子也」[2] (Pei note quoting 《魏略》: "Li Feng, courtesy name Anguo, was the son of the former Commandant of the Guards Li Yi").

Note a discrepancy in the sources about his courtesy name: a Pei note in the *Biography of Pei Qian* calls him 「義子豐，字宣國，見《夏侯玄傳》」[21] (Pei note: "Li Yi's son Li Feng, courtesy name Xuanguo, see the *Biography of Xiahou Xuan*") — i.e., the same man, but that note gives his courtesy name as Xuanguo rather than Anguo.

His career: under Huangchu he was summoned with the army because of his father's appointment, and as a commoner of seventeen or eighteen he was famed in Ye for his purity and his skill at judging men (裴注引《魏略》)[2]; he later served as 黄门郎, 骑都尉, 给事中, and after Emperor Ming's death as 永宁太仆, then in the Zhengshi era as 侍中尚书仆射, and after the fourth year of Jiaping as 中书令 [1][2].

He was executed for plotting with Xiahou Xuan (夏侯玄) and Zhang Ji (张缉) against Sima Shi. The main text says: 「中書令李豐雖宿爲大將軍司馬景王所親待，然私心在玄，遂結皇後父光祿大夫張緝，謀欲以玄輔政」[10] ("Although the Palace Secretary Li Feng had long been treated with favor by the Grand General Sima Jingwang, his private sympathies lay with Xuan, so he joined with the Empress's father, the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Zhang Ji, plotting to make Xuan regent"); and 「嘉平六年二月……大將軍微聞其謀，請豐相見，豐不知而往，即殺之」[10] ("In the second month of the sixth year of Jiaping … the Grand General got wind of the plot, invited Li Feng to a meeting; Feng went without knowing, and he was killed on the spot"). The outcome: 「於是豐、玄、緝、敦、賢等皆夷三族」[14] ("Thereupon Li Feng, Xuan, Ji, Dun, Xian and the others were all exterminated to the third degree"). The Pei note quoting the *Wei shi chunqiu* adds that Sima Shi had him killed by a warrior striking his waist with the ring of a blade: 「使勇士以刀環築豐腰，殺之」[2].

**2. Li Feng of Shu Han, son of Li Yan (李嚴 / 李平)**

Zhuge Liang memorialized to appoint him to office: 「亮表嚴子豐為江州都督督軍，典嚴後事」[18] ("Zhuge Liang memorialized to appoint Yan's son Feng as Commander-Dupervisor of Jiangzhou and Army Supervising Officer, to take charge of Yan's rear affairs"). After his father's fall he ended his career as Administrator of Zhuti: 「豐官至硃提太守」[12] ("Feng's office reached Administrator of Zhuti"). Zhuge Liang also addressed an instruction (教) to him [20].

---

So the two are clearly distinct: different states (Wei vs. Shu), different fathers (Li Yi 李义 vs. Li Yan 李嚴), and different fates (executed for treason vs. serving in Shu to the rank of Administrator of Zhuti). No third man named Li Feng is found in the searched material.

q: Is the general Zhang Xiu whom Zhuge Liang dealt with together with Ma Su when he executed Ma Su the same person as the Zhang Xiu in the entourage of Wu's crown prince Sun Deng?
reply:
**No — they are two different men who happen to share the same name.** In the *Sanguozhi* the name 張休 (Zhāng Xiū) belongs to at least two distinct persons, and the two you mention are not the same.

**1. The general executed by Zhuge Liang (Shu Han)**

This 張休 was a Shu general. The record is in Wang Ping's biography:

「丞相亮既誅馬謖及將軍張休、李盛，奪將軍黃襲等兵。」[2] ("After Chancellor Liang had executed Ma Su and the generals Zhang Xiu and Li Sheng, he took away the troops of the general Huang Xi and others.")

So he is listed only as a Shu 將軍 (general), killed together with Ma Su and Li Sheng after the Jieting defeat. Zhuge Liang's own biography says 「戮謖以謝眾」[3] (he executed Ma Su to answer to the army). Nothing further about this man — no courtesy name, no family — is recorded.

**2. The associate of Wu's crown prince Sun Deng**

This 張休 is a quite different, well-documented man: 張休字叔嗣, younger son of Zhang Zhao of Wu. His own biography says:

「休字叔嗣，弱冠與諸葛恪、顧譚等俱爲太子登僚友，以《漢書》授登。從中庶子轉爲右弼都尉。」[12] ("Zhang Xiu, courtesy name Shusi, in his early twenties was a companion of Crown Prince Sun Deng together with Zhuge Ke, Gu Tan and others, and taught Sun Deng the *Hanshu*. He went from Palace Cadet to Right Assisting Commandant.")

Sun Deng's biography adds 「於是諸葛恪、張休、顧譚、陳表等以選入」[15] and that when Sun Quan took the throne, 「以恪爲左輔，休右弼……是爲四友」[15] (Zhuge Ke as Left Assistant, Zhang Xiu as Right Assistant — the "Four Friends"). This Zhang Xiu later was slandered, exiled to Jiaozhou, and forced to take his own life by order of Sun Hong, 「時年四十一」[12] (aged 41).

**Inference (from the facts above):** The two entries come from different books (Shu and Wu), describe different roles (an unnamed Shu general versus Zhang Zhao's son and Sun Deng's tutor), and give entirely different fates (executed at Jieting versus exiled and forced to die in Wu). The one died in Shu in the Jieting affair; the other lived on in Wu into the succession strife under Sun Quan. Therefore they cannot be the same person — they are simply two men sharing the name 張休.

Note on the name: the man you call "Zhang Xiu" in the Jieting affair is 張休, not the famous 張繡 (Zhang Xiu of Wan, the general who surrendered to Cao Cao), who is a separate third person entirely.

---

q: Is the Zhang Nan who led Liu Bei's vanguard at the Battle of Yiling the same man as the Zhang Nan who surrendered to Cao Cao?
reply:
**Conclusion (based on the records):** In the *Sanguozhi* these are two separate entries, and the text never links them or says they are the same man. Their recorded origins and spheres of activity also differ. So the evidence indicates they were **not the same person** — though this last point is my inference, since the text contains no explicit statement either way.

**1. The Zhang Nan at Yiling (vanguard of Liu Bei)**

He is identified in the *Jihanzuochen zan* as Zhang Nan, courtesy name Wenjin (文進), a man of Jingzhou:
- 「文進名南，亦自荊州隨先主入蜀，領兵從先主徵吳，與習俱死。」[45] — "Wenjin's name was Nan; he too followed the Former Lord from Jingzhou into Shu, led troops with the Former Lord in the campaign against Wu, and died together with Xi (Feng Xi)."

His role as vanguard appears in Lu Xun's biography:
- 「使將軍馮習為大督，張南為前部」[58] — "He made the general Feng Xi grand commander, and Zhang Nan commander of the vanguard."

His death is recorded under Zhangwu 2 (222):
- 「陸議大破先主軍於猇亭，將軍馮習、張南等皆沒。」[32] — "Lu Yi [Lu Xun] routed the Former Lord's army at Xiaoting; the generals Feng Xi, Zhang Nan and others all perished."
- 「斬張南、馮習及胡王沙靡柯等首」[58] — "They cut off the heads of Zhang Nan, Feng Xi, and the Hu king Shamike."

**2. The Zhang Nan who surrendered to Cao Cao**

This man appears under Jian'an 10 (205) as a general of Yuan Xi:
- 「袁熙大將焦觸、張南等叛攻熙、尚，熙、尚奔三郡烏丸。觸等舉其縣降，封爲列侯。」[1] — "Yuan Xi's senior generals Jiao Chu, Zhang Nan and others rebelled and attacked Xi and Shang; Xi and Shang fled to the Wuhuan of the three commanderies. Jiao Chu and the rest surrendered their counties and were enfeoffed as marquises."
- The same event in Yuan Shao's biography: 「熙、尚爲其將焦觸、張南所攻，奔遼西烏丸」[6] — "Xi and Shang were attacked by their generals Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, and fled to the Wuhuan of Liaoxi."

**Inference:** The Yiling Zhang Nan is a Jingzhou man (courtesy name Wenjin) who followed Liu Bei from Jingzhou into Shu and died at Xiaoting in 222. The Zhang Nan who surrendered is recorded as a general under Yuan Xi in the north, rebelling and going over to Cao Cao in 205, after which the text gives him no further career. Because the two records assign different origins and different theaters, and because no passage identifies them with each other, the most reasonable reading is that they are **two different men**. Note, however, that this is an inference from the absence of any linking record, not a claim the *Sanguozhi* makes outright.

q: How many versions do the historical sources give of Cao Cao's killing of Lü Boshe's family? Which book gives which version?
reply:
## Conclusion

In the *Sanguozhi*, **three** different versions of the killing of Lü Boshe's household are recorded — and all three come not from Chen Shou's main text but from Pei Songzhi's annotation to the *Wudi Ji* (武帝紀). The main text itself says only that Cao Cao changed his name and slipped away eastward, without any mention of Lü Boshe:

> 「太祖乃變易姓名，間行東歸。」[17]

The three versions appear together in one annotation block [1]:

**1. 《魏書》 (Wei Shu) — self-defense / Lü's family were the aggressors**

> 「《魏書》曰：太祖以卓終必覆敗，遂不就拜，逃歸鄉里。從數騎過故人成臯呂伯奢；伯奢不在，其子與賔客共劫太祖，取馬及物，太祖手刃擊殺數人。」[1]

Here Cao Cao, with a few riders, passed the home of his old acquaintance Lü Boshe of Chenggao; Boshe was out, and his son and retainers robbed Cao Cao of horse and goods, so Cao Cao killed several of them with his own hand.

**2. 《世語》 (Shiyu) — a pre-emptive night killing of eight men**

> 「《世語》曰：太祖過伯奢。伯奢出行，五子皆在，備賔主禮。太祖自以背卓命，疑其圖己，手劔夜殺八人而去。」[1]

Here Boshe's five sons were at home and received Cao Cao with proper host-and-guest courtesy; Cao Cao, because he had disobeyed Dong Zhuo's order, suspected they were plotting against him, and killed eight men at night before leaving.

**3. 孫盛《雜記》 (Sun Sheng, *Zaji*) — the "I would rather betray others" version**

> 「孫盛雜記曰：太祖聞其食器聲，以爲圖己，遂夜殺之。旣而悽愴曰：『寧我負人，毋人負我！』遂行。」[1]

Here Cao Cao heard the clatter of food vessels, took it as a plot against him, killed them at night, and then said with grief, "Rather I betray others than have others betray me," and went on his way.

## Summary

| Source (as cited by Pei Songzhi) | Version of events |
|---|---|
| 《魏書》 | Lü Boshe's son and guests attacked and robbed Cao Cao first; Cao Cao killed several in self-defense |
| 《世語》 | The five sons received him politely; Cao Cao, fearing betrayal, killed eight at night |
| 孫盛《雜記》 | Cao Cao misheard the sound of food vessels as a plot, killed them at night, and uttered the famous "寧我負人，毋人負我" line |

So: **three versions**, attributed respectively to the *Wei Shu*, the *Shiyu*, and Sun Sheng's *Zaji* — all preserved in Pei Songzhi's commentary. Pei Songzhi does not adjudicate among them; he simply records them side by side. Note that the main text of the *Wudi Ji* contains no account of the Lü Boshe episode at all.

q: Did Liu Bei make three visits to the thatched cottage to recruit Zhuge Liang, or did Zhuge Liang go to see Liu Bei first? Do the historical sources agree?
reply:
**Short answer:** The sources disagree, and Pei Songzhi (裴松之) noticed the contradiction and sided with the "three visits" story.

**1. Chen Shou's main text (正文): Liu Bei went to Zhuge Liang three times**

In the Zhuge Liang biography, when Liu Bei was stationed at Xinye, Xu Shu recommended Zhuge Liang and told Liu Bei he must go in person rather than summon him:

「此人可就見，不可屈致也。將軍宜枉駕顧之」[1]

The text then states: 「由是先主遂詣亮，凡三往，乃見」[1] — "Thereupon the Former Lord went to Zhuge Liang; in all he went three times before he was received."

The closing appraisal of the same biography repeats it: 「時左將軍劉備以亮有殊量，乃三顧亮於草廬之中」[3] — Liu Bei "thrice visited Liang in his thatched cottage."

**2. Pei Songzhi's commentary (裴注): a rival version — Zhuge Liang went to Liu Bei first**

Pei Songzhi quotes 《魏略》: 「劉備屯於樊城……亮乃北行見備，備與亮非舊，又以其年少，以諸生意待之」[5] — Liu Bei was camped at Fancheng; Zhuge Liang went north to see Liu Bei, who did not know him and, because he was young, treated him as an ordinary scholar. It tells the story of Zhuge Liang staying behind after the guests left while Liu Bei was plaiting a yak-tail ornament, then advising him how to register the floating population of Jing province to strengthen his army. Pei notes that 「九州春秋所言亦如之」[5] — the 《Jiuzhou Chunqiu》 says the same thing.

**3. Pei Songzhi's own verdict**

Pei Songzhi rejects the 《魏略》 version, citing Zhuge Liang's own memorial (the 出師表): 「先帝不以臣卑鄙，猥自枉屈，三顧臣於草廬之中，諮臣以當世之事」, and concludes: 「則非亮先詣備，明矣。雖聞見異辭，各生彼此，然乖背至是，亦良為可怪」[2] — "then it is clear that Zhuge Liang did not go to Liu Bei first. Although accounts differ and each produces its own version, that they should contradict each other to this degree is truly strange."

So, on the record: Chen Shou's main text and Zhuge Liang's own memorial support the three visits; the 《魏略》 and 《九州春秋》 (preserved in Pei's commentary) support Zhuge Liang going to Liu Bei first. Pei Songzhi, having weighed them, preferred the three-visits version. The two traditions cannot both be right, and the sources do not agree.

**Inference (推断):** Since Pei Songzhi's argument rests on Zhuge Liang's own memorial, and Chen Shou's main text says "three visits," the weight of the 《三国志》 material is on Liu Bei's side; but because Pei explicitly records the opposing account and calls the discrepancy "strange," we cannot treat the matter as settled by the text alone — the honest answer is that the sources conflict and Pei chose one side.

---

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The famous dramatized telling of the three visits — with Zhang Fei and Guan Yu accompanying Liu Bei, the "Longzhong Plan" dialogue staged at the cottage, and the visits numbered in detail — belongs to 《三国演义》 and later popular tradition rather than to the plain record of 《三国志》.

q: In exactly which year, and how, did Sun Chien die? Do the various sources agree?
reply:
## Sun Jian's death: the year and manner

**Bottom line:** Chen Shou's main biography of Sun Jian dates the death to **Chuping 3 (192 CE)**, and says he was **shot by soldiers of Huang Zu while riding alone on Xian Mountain (岘山)** after besieging Xiangyang. But the sources **do not agree**: the *Han Ji* of Zhang Fan and the *Wu Li* put it in **Chuping 2 (191 CE)** — and Pei Songzhi himself says that dating is the correct one and the main biography is in error; the *Yingxiong Ji* puts it in **Chuping 4, first month, 7th day (193 CE)** and gives a different killer and a different weapon (a stone to the head, thrown by Lü Gong's troops).

### The main text (Chen Shou)

The *Sun Polu–Taoni* biography (Wu Shu 46) states:

- 「初平三年，術使堅征荊州，擊劉表。表遣黃祖逆於樊鄧之間。堅擊破之，追渡漢水，遂圍襄陽，單馬行峴山，爲祖軍士所射殺。」[1]

  *(Chuping 3, Yuan Shu sent Jian to campaign in Jing province and attack Liu Biao. Biao sent Huang Zu to meet him between Fan and Deng. Jian defeated him, pursued across the Han River, besieged Xiangyang, rode alone on Xian Mountain, and was shot dead by Zu's soldiers.)*

So the main biography: **Chuping 3 = 192 CE**, killed by **Huang Zu's soldiers, shot** (射殺).

Liu Biao's biography in the Wei Shu agrees on the manner but not the year: 「袁術之在南陽也，與孫堅合從，欲襲奪表州，使堅攻表。堅爲流矢所中死，軍敗」[11] — *Sun Jian died from being hit by a stray arrow*.

### The variant accounts (Pei Songzhi's notes)

Pei Songzhi cites a cluster of differing versions:

- **《典略》**: Liu Biao shut the gates, sent Huang Zu out secretly by night; Huang Zu fled into Xian Mountain, and Sun Jian chased him at night; 「祖部兵從竹木間暗射堅，殺之」— *Zu's soldiers shot Jian secretly from among the bamboo and trees, killing him* [2].
- **《吳錄》**: 「堅時年三十七」— *Sun Jian was then 37* [2].
- **《英雄記》**: 「堅以初平四年正月七日死」— *Sun Jian died on the 7th day of the first month of Chuping 4* [2]. It also gives a completely different story: 「劉表將呂公將兵緣山向堅，堅輕騎尋山討公。公兵下石。中堅頭，應時腦出物故」— *Liu Biao's general Lü Gong came along the mountain toward Sun Jian; Sun Jian rode light to hunt him down; Lü Gong's soldiers threw stones down, hit Jian's head, and his brains burst out at once* [2]. Pei Songzhi's own comment closes the note: 「其不同如此也」— *such are the discrepancies* [2].
- **《張璠漢紀》and《吳歷》**: both say Sun Jian died in **Chuping 2**. Pei Songzhi rules on it: 「張璠漢紀及呉歷並以堅初平二年死，此爲是而本傳誤也」— *Zhang Fan's Han Ji and the Wu Li both have Jian dying in Chuping 2; this is correct and the main biography is wrong* [5].
- Pei Songzhi also notes an internal inconsistency in the ages: since the biography says Sun Jian died in Chuping 3 and Sun Ce died in Jian'an 5 at age 26, Sun Ce should have been 18 when his father died — yet Sun Ce's own memorial says he was 17: 「則爲不符」[28].

**Years:** Chuping 2 = 191 CE; Chuping 3 = 192 CE; Chuping 4 = 193 CE (converted with the era tool).

### Supporting details

- Sun Jian's nephew **Sun Ben** took over the remaining troops and escorted the coffin: 「堅薨，賁攝帥餘眾，扶送靈柩」[10]; the main text similarly says 「兄子賁，帥將士衆就術」[1]. Sun Ce buried him at Qu'e: 「堅薨，還葬曲阿」[4].

### My inference

Putting the evidence together: all versions agree Sun Jian died in the fighting against Liu Biao's forces in Jing province (Yuan Shu having sent him), and that the immediate agent was **Huang Zu's men** (the *Dianlüe* and the main biography) — with the *Yingxiong Ji* alone substituting **Lü Gong**. The manner also splits into **shot** (main text, *Dianlüe*, Liu Biao's biography) versus **struck by a falling stone** (*Yingxiong Ji*). The year is the sharpest disagreement: **191 (Chuping 2)** per the *Han Ji* and *Wu Li*, **192 (Chuping 3)** per Chen Shou, **193 (Chuping 4)** per the *Yingxiong Ji*. Since Pei Songzhi explicitly endorses Chuping 2 over the main biography, and since the *Yingxiong Ji*'s Chuping 4 clashes with both, one cannot simply adopt the main biography's year as settled — the records genuinely conflict, and each version should be weighed on its own. The *Wu Lu*'s age of 37 is consistent with the figure in Sun Ce's memorial (17) only if one accepts the earlier dating, which is part of why Pei Songzhi sided with Chuping 2.

---

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:**

q: Is the story of Liu Bei's horse Dilu leaping across Tan Creek to save his life recorded in the Records of the Three Kingdoms? Is it credible?
reply:
## Conclusion

**Partly.** The story of Dilu leaping over Tan Creek appears in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* — but **not in Chen Shou's main text (正文)**. It is found only in **Pei Songzhi's annotation (裴注)**, quoting an earlier work, the *Shiyu* (《世語》). And immediately after that annotation, the Jin-dynasty historian **Sun Sheng (孙盛)** pronounces it false. So: the story is *in* the book, but as an annotated hearsay account that the annotator's own source rejects.

## What the record says

Chen Shou's main text, on Liu Bei's years in Jing province under Liu Biao, says only:

「荊州豪傑歸先主者日益多，表疑其心，陰禦之。」[20]

*("More and more Jing province heroes attached themselves to the Former Lord; Liu Biao suspected his intentions and secretly guarded against him.")* — no banquet, no assassination plot, no horse.

The Tan Creek story is in Pei Songzhi's note to that same passage, cited from the *Shiyu*:

「備屯樊城，劉表禮焉，憚其為人，不甚信用。曾請備宴會，蒯越、蔡瑁欲因會取備，備覺之，偽如廁，潛遁出。所乘馬名的盧，騎的盧走，墮襄陽城西檀溪水中，溺不得出。備急曰：『的盧：今日厄矣，可努力！』的盧乃一踴三丈，遂得過，乘桴渡河，中流而追者至，以表意謝之，曰：『何去之速乎！』」[1]

*("Liu Bei was stationed at Fancheng; Liu Biao treated him with courtesy but feared his character and did not much trust or employ him. He once invited Liu Bei to a banquet; Kuai Yue and Cai Mao wanted to seize Liu Bei at the gathering. Liu Bei noticed, pretended to go to the privy, and slipped away. His horse was named Dilu; riding Dilu he fled, fell into Tan Creek west of Xiangyang city, and sank so that he could not get out. Liu Bei said urgently: 'Dilu! Today is dire — you must exert yourself!' Dilu then leaped three zhang in one bound, and so got across; he crossed the river on a raft, and in midstream his pursuers arrived, apologized on Liu Biao's behalf, and said: 'Why did you leave so quickly!'"*)

## Is it credible?

The annotation itself carries its own rebuttal, from Sun Sheng:

「孫盛曰：此不然之言。備時羈旅，客主勢殊，若有此變，豈敢晏然終表之世而無釁故乎？此皆世俗妄說，非事實也。」[1]

*("Sun Sheng says: this is not a true account. Liu Bei was at the time a sojourner, and the host–guest positions were very unequal; had such a disturbance occurred, how would he have dared to pass the whole of Liu Biao's lifetime in peace without any breach or quarrel? These are all vulgar tales, not facts.")*

Sun Sheng's argument is an argument from circumstance: Liu Bei remained safely in Liu Biao's territory until Liu Biao's death, which he thinks is incompatible with a failed assassination attempt and a dramatic escape. So the only explicit ancient verdict on the story in this material is **negative**.

Pei Songzhi's own stance: note that elsewhere in the same biography, when he rejects a dubious anecdote, he writes his own 「臣松之以為……」[23][17]. Here he does not add his own verdict — he simply quotes Sun Sheng after the *Shiyu* passage. So the material presents the story together with a rejection, without Pei himself ruling on it.

**My assessment (inference, not a recorded fact):** the text as given supports treating the story as *doubtful*. The reasoning is: (1) the story comes only from the *Shiyu* via annotation, not from Chen Shou's main narrative [20][1]; (2) the main text records Liu Biao's attitude as suspicion plus covert precaution, not an attempt on Liu Bei's life [20]; (3) the one ancient commentator quoted on the point calls it a "vulgar tale" [1]. That does not prove the event never happened — Sun Sheng's reasoning is circumstantial, and absence of an event from the main text is not proof of its absence — but it does mean the leap over Tan Creek cannot be treated as established history.

---

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** The elaborate version of this episode — with the horse refusing to jump, Liu Bei whipping it, and the famous "Dilu, Dilu, today is your day" scene dramatized — belongs to *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* and later storytelling. In the *Records* the episode exists only as the annotated *Shiyu* passage above, already labeled by Sun Sheng as a vulgar tale rather than fact. The Tan Creek (檀溪) is in the area of modern Xiangyang, Hubei.

q: How did Cao Pi's Empress Zhen die? Do the historical sources disagree about it?
reply:
## Short answer

Cao Pi (Emperor Wen of Wei) had Empress Zhen put to death by an imperial envoy in the sixth month of the second year of Huangchu (221 CE) — that is Chen Shou's main text. But the sources do disagree: the *Weishu* (quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary) claims she merely fell ill and died, and Pei Songzhi himself rejects that account and says she was killed. The sources also differ over how she was buried, and over how Guo the Empress (文德郭皇后) later died.

## What Chen Shou's main text says

The main text of the *Record of Consorts* (后妃傳) says:

「踐阼之後，山陽公奉二女以嬪於魏，郭后、李、陰貴人並愛幸，后愈失意，有怨言。帝大怒，二年六月，遣使賜死，葬於鄴。」[13]

"After he ascended the throne, the Duke of Shanyang presented two daughters to be concubines in Wei; Empress Guo, and the Consorts Li and Yin were all favored, and the Empress [Zhen] grew ever more disappointed and had resentful words. The Emperor was greatly enraged, and in the sixth month of the second year sent an envoy to order her to die, and she was buried at Ye."

The "second year" is Huangchu 2 = 221 CE [era tool]. The same text notes earlier: 「延康元年正月，文帝即王位，六月，南征，后留鄴」[13] — so she was left behind at Ye while Cao Pi was away.

Chen Shou also states plainly in the *Record of Empress Wen-de Guo*: 「甄后之死，由后之寵也。」[15] — "The death of Empress Zhen was due to this Empress's [Guo's] favor." And in the *Annals of Emperor Ming* (明帝紀), regarding Cao Rui: 「以其母誅，故未建為嗣。」[27] — "Because his mother had been executed, he was not established as heir." So Chen Shou's own text treats her death as an execution (誅).

## Where the sources disagree

**(1) How she died — execution or illness?**

Pei Songzhi quotes the *Weishu* (魏書):

「有司奏建長秋宮，帝璽書迎后……璽書三至而后三讓……時盛暑，帝欲須秋涼乃更迎后。會后疾遂篤，夏六月丁卯，崩於鄴。帝哀痛咨嗟，策贈皇后璽綬。」[14]

This version has Cao Pi repeatedly sending sealed letters to summon her to be made empress, Zhen declining three times, and then — because of the heat, waiting until autumn — she instead fell gravely ill and "died at Ye" on the *dingmao* day of the sixth month, with Cao Pi mourning and posthumously granting her the empress's seal and ribbons.

Pei Songzhi explicitly rejects this:

「臣松之以為……文帝之不立甄氏，及加殺害，事有明審。魏史若以為大惡邪，則宜隱而不言，若謂為小惡邪，則不應假為之辭，而崇飾虛文乃至於是，異乎所聞於舊史。」[14]

Pei Songzhi's own judgment (臣松之以為, i.e. Pei Songzhi's note, not a quotation) is that "Emperor Wen's not establishing Lady Zhen [as empress], and his adding to it the killing, are clear and certain" — and that the Wei court history dressed it up with empty rhetoric, unlike what he had heard from older histories.

**(2) How she was buried**

The *Han-Jin Chunqiu* (漢晉春秋, quoted by Pei Songzhi) adds the detail about the encoffining:

「初，甄后之誅，由郭后之寵，及殯，令被髮覆面，以糠塞口，遂立郭后，使養明帝。」[18]

"At first, Empress Zhen's execution was due to Empress Guo's favor; at her encoffining, she was ordered to be buried with her hair loose over her face and her mouth stuffed with chaff; then Empress Guo was established and made to raise Emperor Ming."

The *Weilüe* (魏略, also quoted by Pei Songzhi) agrees on the mistreatment and adds: 「甄后臨沒，以帝屬李夫人」[18] — that at the end she entrusted Cao Rui to Consort Li.

**(3) A related disagreement — how Empress Guo died**

Pei Songzhi quotes two conflicting accounts side by side:

- The *Weilüe*: 「明帝既嗣立，追痛甄后之薨，故太后以憂暴崩。」[18] — Emperor Ming, grieving for Empress Zhen, caused the Empress Dowager to die suddenly of grief.
- The *Han-Jin Chunqiu*: 「帝知之，心常懷忿，數泣問甄后死狀。郭后曰：『先帝自殺，何以責問我？……』明帝怒，遂逼殺之，敕殯者使如甄后故事。」[18] — Emperor Ming repeatedly asked weeping about his mother's death; Empress Guo retorted that the former emperor had killed her himself; enraged, Ming forced her to die and had her buried exactly as Zhen had been.

## Inference

Putting these together (this is my inference, marked as such): Chen Shou's main text, the *Han-Jin Chunqiu*, the *Weilüe*'s remark on the burial, and Pei Songzhi's own note all point to Zhen having been executed by Cao Pi's order in the sixth month of Huangchu 2 (221 CE), with the *Weishu*'s "died of illness" version being the one that conflicts with them. The sources do not, however, agree on whether the humiliating burial was ordered at the time or whether the *Weilüe*'s "died of grief" or the *Han-Jin Chunqiu*'s "forced to die" is right about Empress Guo. Note also that Pei Songzhi's comment is his own judgment, not a fact recorded by Chen Shou, and the *Weishu* passage is his quotation of a Wei court history, not of Chen Shou.
