q: Did Cao Cao really have fewer than ten thousand men at the Battle of Guandu?
reply:
## Short answer

Yes — *Chen Shou's* main text of the *Sanguozhi* does say Cao Cao had fewer than ten thousand men at Guandu, but **Pei Songzhi explicitly rejects this figure**, and Chen Shou's own record of Cao Cao's troop numbers elsewhere makes the "under ten thousand" claim hard to square. So the honest answer is: the *Sanguozhi* says it, but the *Sanguozhi*'s own commentator says it is not true.

## What the text actually says

Chen Shou's main text in the *Wudi ji*, in the eighth month of the Guandu campaign:

> 「八月，紹連營稍前，依沙塠爲屯，東西數十里。公亦分營與相當，合戰不利。時公兵不滿萬，傷者十二三。」[4]

("In the eighth month, Shao's linked camps advanced gradually... At that time the Duke's troops were less than ten thousand, with twenty to thirty percent wounded.")

Note that this is dated to the eighth month — the figure is given for that moment of the stand-off, not for the whole campaign.

By contrast, Yuan Shao's numbers:

> 「是時袁紹旣并公孫瓚，兼四州之地，衆十餘萬，將進軍攻許」[6]

and the *Benji* is quoted by Pei as saying 「紹衆十餘萬，屯營東西數十里」[2].

One more figure from Chen Shou's main text: at the Yanjin engagement the cavalry was tiny — 「時騎不滿六百」[10] — though that is cavalry only, at a different action.

## Pei Songzhi's rebuttal (裴注)

Pei Songzhi argues at length that "fewer than ten thousand" cannot be right:

> 「臣松之以爲魏武初起兵，已有衆五千，自後百戰百勝，敗者十二三而已矣。但一破黃巾，受降卒三十餘萬，餘所吞并，不可悉紀；雖征戰損傷，未應如此之少也。」[2]

He gives three reasons: (1) Cao could divide his camps to face Yuan's camps stretched over dozens of *li*; (2) Cao was able to send Xu Huang to raid Yuan's grain carts and to lead the strike on Chunyu Qiong himself, moving in and out without being blocked; (3) the various books say Cao buried 80,000 (or 70,000) of Yuan's men — 8,000 men could not have bound 80,000. His conclusion:

> 「將記述者欲以少見奇，非其實錄也。」[2]

He also catches an inconsistency: the *Zhong Yao zhuan* says Zhong Yao, as Director of Retainers, sent 「馬二千餘匹」 to the army, yet the *Benji* and the *Shiyu* both say Cao had only about 600 cavalry — so where did Zhong Yao's horses go?[2]

In the *Xun Yu* chapter Pei makes the same point from a different angle:

> 「臣松之以爲于時徐州未平，兖州又叛，而云十萬之衆，雖是抑抗之言，要非寡弱之稱。益知官渡之役，不得云兵不滿萬也。」[1]

That is: in Xun Yu's earlier argument about the Xu province campaign, Cao's own force is spoken of as 「十萬之衆」[19]; even allowing for rhetorical exaggeration, this is not the language of a weak, tiny army — so Guandu cannot have been under ten thousand.

## Inference (clearly marked as such)

Putting the cited facts together: Chen Shou states "under ten thousand" for the eighth month of the stand-off; Pei Songzhi states that Cao Cao began with 5,000, absorbed 300,000+ Yellow Turban surrendered troops, and that the sources report 70,000–80,000 of Yuan Shao's men killed or buried, plus a separate record of 2,000+ horses supplied by Zhong Yao against a stated 600 cavalry. From these, one may reasonably infer that the "fewer than ten thousand" figure, **as a total army strength for the whole Guandu campaign, is probably too low** — Pei's argument is that it is a literary topos of "the few defeating the many" rather than a straight record. But note carefully: this is an inference from Pei's reasoning, not something Chen Shou himself concedes. Chen Shou's main text does assert the figure, and the *Sanguozhi* preserves both positions side by side; the sources are in conflict, and the conflict is not resolved in the text. It is also worth noting that even Chen Shou ties the figure to a specific month and adds 「傷者十二三」, so it may describe a particular low point rather than the campaign's opening strength.

## Bottom line

- If you mean "does the *Sanguozhi* say Cao Cao had under ten thousand at Guandu?" — yes, in the eighth month of the campaign [4].
- If you mean "is that accepted as reliable?" — no; Pei Songzhi, the standard commentator, flatly says 「不得云兵不滿萬也」[1] and 「非其實錄也」[2], and the *Sanguozhi* itself elsewhere reports Cao's forces in terms of 「十萬之衆」[19] and Yuan's buried troops in the tens of thousands [2].

q: Is the Liu Tai of the Records of the Three Kingdoms a single person? Is the Liu Tai who was Inspector of Yen Province during the campaign against Tung Cho the same man as the Liu Tai whom Ts'ao Ts'ao later sent to attack Liu Pei?
reply:
## Conclusion

No. The two are not the same man. The *Records of the Three Kingdoms* mentions a Liu Tai (劉岱) in both contexts, but the Yan Province Inspector who rose against Dong Zhuo was already dead long before Cao Cao sent a Liu Tai against Liu Bei; the records also give the two men different places of origin. They are two men who share the name (and, confusingly, the courtesy name).

## 1. Liu Tai, Inspector of Yan Province (兗州刺史劉岱)

He is identified as the elder brother of Liu Yao (劉繇), of Donglai Moungping:

- 「繇兄岱，字公山，歷位侍中、兗州刺史。」[2] — Liu Yao's elder brother Liu Tai, courtesy name Gongshan, successively held the offices of Palace Attendant and Inspector of Yan Province. Pei Songzhi's note confirms: 「岱，劉繇之兄，事見《吳志》。」[22] Pei's note on Liu Yao's biography adds that the two brothers were both men of talent [20].

He was one of the men Dong Zhuo installed in the provinces: 「用其所舉韓馥、劉岱、孔伷、張咨、張邈等出宰州郡」[1]. He joined the coalition of 初平元年: 「初平元年春正月，後將軍袁術、冀州牧韓馥、豫州刺史孔伷、兗州刺史劉岱……同時俱起兵，衆各數萬，推紹爲盟主」[36]. He killed Qiao Mao: 「劉岱與橋瑁相惡，岱殺瑁，以王肱領東郡太守。」[9].

And he died fighting the Qingzhou Yellow Turbans:

- 「劉岱欲擊之，鮑信諫曰……岱不從，遂與戰，果爲所殺。」[5] — Liu Tai wanted to attack them; Bao Xin remonstrated, Liu Tai did not listen, gave battle, and was killed. Immediately after, Cao Cao was brought in to take over Yan Province: 「岱旣死，陳宮謂太祖曰：『州今無主，而王命斷絕……』」[43], and 「劉岱為黃巾所殺。太祖臨兗州」[45-context, see 5/43].

## 2. Liu Tai, the general sent against Liu Bei

This Liu Tai appears together with Wang Zhong, in the affair of Liu Bei's revolt after killing the Inspector of Xu Province, Che Zhou:

- 「備之未東也，陰與董承等謀反，至下邳，遂殺徐州刺史車冑，舉兵屯沛。遣劉岱、王忠擊之，不克。」[15] — the same is recorded in Liu Bei's biography 「曹公遣劉岱、王忠擊之，不克」[12] and in the Yuan Shao material [16].

Pei Songzhi's note on this passage quotes 《魏武故事》:

- 「岱字公山，沛國人。以司空長史從征伐有功，封列侯。」[11] — Liu Tai, courtesy name Gongshan, a man of Pei kingdom, who followed the campaigns as Chief Clerk (長史) of the Minister of Works and was enfeoffed as a marquis. The same note quotes 《獻帝春秋》: 「備謂岱等曰：『使汝百人來，其無如我何；曹公自來，未可知耳！』」[11]

## Inference (from the facts above)

- Fact: the Yan Province Inspector Liu Tai was killed by the Yellow Turbans, and Cao Cao succeeded him in Yan Province [5][43].
- Fact: the Liu Tai sent against Liu Bei is recorded immediately before 「五年春正月」, when Cao Cao personally campaigned east against Liu Bei [15][17] — the era tool converts 建安五年 to AD 200.
- Therefore the man killed in the early 190s cannot be the man campaigning around 199–200. They must be two different men of the same name.
- This is supported independently by origin: the Inspector was of Donglai Moungping, brother of Liu Yao [2][22]; 《魏武故事》 calls the general a man of Pei kingdom, who had served as 司空長史 [11].

One point I cannot resolve from the sources: both are given the courtesy name 公山 — 「岱，字公山」[2] and 「岱字公山，沛國人」[11]. The two notices disagree on his place of origin, and Pei Songzhi adds no comment there. So the conclusion that these are two men rests on the death date and the differing origin, not on the courtesy name, which the records happen to give identically.

I searched under several headings (劉岱 with 兗州刺史, 討董卓, 黃巾, 沛國, 司空長史, 劉備) and found no third bearer of the name.

q: Where did Chu-ko Liang die, and how old was he? What instructions did he leave about his burial?
reply:
**Answer (based on the《三国志》record):**

**Where and at what age he died.** Zhuge Liang (諸葛亮, styled Kongming) died in the army camp, at the Wuzhang Plain (五丈原) by the Wei River (渭水), during the 8th month of the 12th year of Jianxing (建興), at age 54.

- 「其年八月，亮疾病，卒于軍，時年五十四。」[16] (In the 8th month of that year Zhuge Liang fell ill and died in the army, aged 54.)
- He had led his whole army out through the Xie Valley (斜谷) that spring and encamped at Wuzhang Plain, facing Sima Xuanwang (司馬宣王, i.e. Sima Yi) south of the Wei: 「十二年春，亮悉大眾由斜谷出，以流馬運，據武功五丈原，與司馬宣王對於渭南。」[16]
- The Later Ruler's annals likewise place the death "by the Wei River": 「秋八月，亮卒渭濱。」[7]
- The 12th year of Jianxing corresponds to 234 CE [era].

**Burial instructions.** His testamentary command was to be buried at Dingjun Mountain (定軍山) in Hanzhong, using the hill itself as the mound, with the grave just large enough to hold the coffin, encoffined in ordinary clothes, with no grave goods: 「亮遺命葬漢中定軍山，因山為墳，塚足容棺，斂以時服，不須器物。」[11] The court then issued a decree conferring on him the seal and cord of Chancellor and Marquis of Wuxiang, and the posthumous title Zhongwu Hou (忠武侯): 「贈君丞相武鄉侯印綬，謚君為忠武侯。」[11]

**A discrepancy worth noting (inference / source difference).** The main text says he died at Wuzhang Plain by the Wei River [16]. Pei Songzhi's commentary records variant accounts: Pei notes that 《魏書》 says he burned his camp and fled into the valley, falling ill and dying on the road, and that 《漢晉春秋》 says 「亮卒于郭氏塢」[2]. Pei Songzhi himself argues the "vomiting blood" story is a boastful Wei fabrication, and explains the "died in the valley" version as arising from the fact that the Shu army only held mourning after entering the valley. 《漢晉春秋》 also records that the army withdrew and only held mourning after entering the valley [18]. So on the location of death the sources differ; I present them side by side rather than deciding.

**Age note.** The age 54 comes from Zhuge Liang's own biography [16]; his own biography and the Later Ruler's annals agree on the 8th month of Jianxing 12 [7][16].

Below is not from the《三国志》:
- Wuzhang Plain (五丈原) is in present-day Mei County, Shaanxi; Dingjun Mountain (定軍山) is in present-day Mian County, Shaanxi.
- The elaborate "borrowed arrows" and other such tales about Zhuge Liang are from《三國演義》and other non-official sources; the《三国志》record is as cited above.

q: What did Liu Bei say to Zhuge Liang when he entrusted his heir to him on his deathbed? How did Zhuge Liang reply? And what instructions did Liu Bei leave for the Later Sovereign?
reply:
## What Liu Bei said to Zhuge Liang

According to Zhuge Liang's biography, in the spring of Zhangwu 3 (223 CE), Liu Bei, gravely ill at Yong'an, summoned Zhuge Liang from Chengdu and entrusted the aftermath to him:

> 「君才十倍曹丕，必能安國，終定大事。若嗣子可輔，輔之；如其不才，君可自取。」[10]
> *"Your ability is ten times that of Cao Pi; you will surely be able to stabilize the state and ultimately settle the great enterprise. If my heir is worth supporting, support him; if he lacks ability, you may take [the throne] yourself."*

Liu Bei's own biography records the same event more briefly: 「先主病篤，託孤於丞相亮，尚書令李嚴為副」[22] — "The Former Lord, gravely ill, entrusted the orphan [his heir] to Chancellor Liang, with Prefect of the Masters of Writing Li Yan as deputy." Li Yan's biography likewise says 「三年，先主疾病，嚴與諸葛亮並受遺詔輔少主」[21] ("in the third year, the Former Lord fell ill, and Li Yan together with Zhuge Liang both received the testamentary edict to assist the young ruler").

## Zhuge Liang's reply

> 「臣敢竭股肱之力，效忠貞之節，繼之以死！」[10]
> *"How would your servant dare not to exhaust the strength of a limb-and-pillar minister, to render loyal and steadfast fidelity, and to continue in it unto death!"*

The text says 「亮涕泣曰」[10] — Zhuge Liang replied weeping.

## Instructions for the heir (Liu Shan, the Later Sovereign)

In Zhuge Liang's biography, the instruction is given in one line:

> 「汝與丞相從事，事之如父。」[10]
> *"You are to serve the Chancellor in affairs, and treat him as a father."*

The fuller testamentary edict is preserved in Pei Songzhi's commentary, quoted from the *Zhuge Liang Collection* (裴注引《諸葛亮集》). It reads in part:

> 「朕初疾但下痢耳，後轉雜他病，殆不自濟。人五十不稱夭，年已六十有餘，何所复恨，不復自傷，但以卿兄弟為念。……勉之，勉之！勿以惡小而為之，勿以善小而不為。惟賢惟德，能服於人。汝父德薄，勿效之。可讀漢書、禮記，間暇歷觀諸子及六韜、商君書，益人意智。聞丞相為寫申、韓、管子、六韜一通已畢，未送，道亡，可自更求聞達。」[14]
> *"My illness began as mere diarrhea, then turned into a mix of other ailments, and I can hardly save myself. A man who lives to fifty is not called cut short; I am already past sixty, so what regret is there... Strive, strive! Do not do an evil because it is small; do not fail to do a good because it is small. Only worthiness and virtue can win men's submission. Your father was thin in virtue — do not imitate him. You may read the Han Shu and the Book of Rites, and at leisure review the various philosophers and the Six Secret Teachings and the Book of Lord Shang, for they benefit a man's mind and wisdom. I hear the Chancellor has finished copying out one set of Shen [Buhai], Han [Feizi], Guanzi and the Six Secret Teachings for you; it was not yet delivered and was lost on the way — you may seek it out yourself."*

The same passage ends with his dying words to the Prince of Lu (Liu Yong): 「臨終時，呼魯王與語：『吾亡之後，汝兄弟父事丞相，令卿與丞相共事而已。』」[14] — "At the point of death he called the Prince of Lu and spoke to him: 'After I die, you brothers are to serve the Chancellor as a father, and simply let you and the Chancellor work together.'"

## Dating and aftermath

The event is dated by the text to the spring of Zhangwu 3, and Liu Bei died that summer: 「夏四月癸巳，先主殂於永安宮，時年六十三」[22] ("In the fourth month, on the day guisi, the Former Lord passed away in the Yong'an Palace, aged sixty-three"). Per the era conversion, Zhangwu 3 = 223 CE. He was buried in the autumn: 「五月，梓宮自永安還成都，諡曰昭烈皇帝。秋，八月，葬惠陵」[13].

## A note on the two texts

The famous line "if he lacks ability, you may take it yourself" comes from Zhuge Liang's biography [10]; the long testamentary edict with "do not do an evil because it is small" comes from the *Zhuge Liang Collection* as quoted in Pei's commentary [14]. Pei Songzhi also records Sun Sheng's criticism of Liu Bei's words as improper for a deathbed charge (裴注引孫盛, [6]) — a dissenting opinion, not the main narrative.

---

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** The scene of Liu Bei "entrusting the orphan at Baidicheng," often dramatized in later storytelling, corresponds in the histories to the events above as recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; the *Sanguozhi* does not record any additional dialogue beyond what is quoted.

q: How old was Cao Cao when he died? What did his testamentary edict say about his funeral and burial?
reply:
## Cao Cao's age at death

Cao Cao was **66 years old (by Chinese reckoning) when he died** — this is stated explicitly in the *Record of Emperor Wu* (武帝紀):

> 「庚子，王崩于洛陽，年六十六。」[11]
> ("On the gengzi day, the King died at Luoyang, aged sixty-six.")

He died at Luoyang in the first month of the 25th year of Jian'an [11], which the era tool converts to **220 CE** [era]. The same passage records that in the second month, on the *dingmao* day, he was buried at Gaoling (高陵) [11].

## What the testamentary edict said

The edict (遺令) is quoted verbatim in the same passage [11]:

> 「天下尚未安定，未得遵古也。葬畢，皆除服。其將兵屯戍者，皆不得離屯部。有司各率乃職。斂以時服，無藏金玉珍寶。」[11]

In English, it says:

- **"The realm is not yet settled, so the ancient [mourning] rules cannot be followed."** — i.e., a shortened, simplified mourning.
- **"When the burial is finished, all are to remove their mourning garments."** — mourning to end immediately after interment.
- **"Those who command troops on garrison duty must not leave their posts."** — no officers may abandon their stations to attend the funeral.
- **"The officials are each to attend to their duties."**
- **"Encoffin me in the clothing of the season; do not bury gold, jade, or precious treasures."** — a plain coffin, seasonal clothing, no valuables.

The posthumous title given was **King Wu (武王)** [11].

## Corroborating Pei note

Pei Songzhi's commentary supplies an additional detail on Cao Cao's own funeral arrangements:

> 《魏書》曰：……故預自制終亡衣服，四篋而已。[22]
> (Pei note citing the *Wei Shu*: "...therefore he had beforehand himself prepared the clothing for his death — only four boxes' worth.")

The same *Wei Shu* note describes his habitual austerity — plain clothes in the palace, patched curtains and screens, undecorated bedding [21] — which fits the tone of the edict. Note that this passage [21][22] is Pei Songzhi's citation of the *Wei Shu* (裴注引《魏書》), not Chen Shou's main text.

**Inference (my own reasoning):** The edict's five clauses cohere with the austerity attributed to him in the *Wei Shu* [21][22] and with the *Fu Zi*'s note that even his daughters' weddings used plain black curtains [23]. Taken together, the edict reads as a deliberately modest, state-first disposition: abbreviated mourning, no disruption of the army, no grave goods. But note that the *Sanguozhi* records these as his instructions and the fact of burial at Gaoling; it does not itself report what was actually placed in the tomb.

**Sources:** Chen Shou, *Sanguozhi*, *Weishu*, *Wudi ji* [11]; Pei Songzhi's commentary citing the *Wei Shu* [21][22], the *Fu Zi* [23], and Zhang Hua's *Bowu zhi* [24].

q: Is the story of Ts'ao Ch'ung weighing the elephant in the Records of the Three Kingdoms? How did he weigh it? And how old was Ts'ao Ch'ung when he died?
reply:
**Yes — the elephant story is in the Records of the Three Kingdoms.** It appears in the Wei section, in the "Biographies of the Empresses and Princes" (武文世王公傳), in the biography of Cao Chong, Prince Ai of Deng (鄧哀王沖), i.e. Chen Shou's main text, not merely a commentary.

**How he weighed it.** Sun Quan had sent a giant elephant, and Cao Cao (魏太祖, "the Grand Progenitor") wanted to know its weight, but none of his subordinates could think of a way. Cao Chong said:

「置象大船之上，而刻其水痕所至，稱物以載之，則校可知矣。」[1]

That is: put the elephant on a large boat, mark where the waterline comes to, then load weighed objects onto the boat until it sinks to the same mark — and by comparison the weight can be known. Cao Cao was delighted and had it carried out at once: 「太祖大悅，卽施行焉」[1].

The same passage also records his cleverness in saving the keeper of the granary whose carelessness had let rats gnaw Cao Cao's saddle: Cao Chong pierced his own single garment to look rat-bitten, then persuaded Cao Cao that rat-gnawing was mere superstition, so that when the matter of the saddle was reported Cao Cao simply laughed and asked nothing [1]. Chen Shou adds that dozens of people condemned to punishment were saved by Cao Chong's quiet advocacy, and that Cao Cao repeatedly praised him before his officials, 「有欲傳後意」 — intending to make him his heir [1].

**Age at death.** He died at thirteen (年十三). The text says: 「年十三，建安十三年疾病，太祖親爲請命。及亡，哀甚。」[1] — in the thirteenth year of Jian'an he fell ill, Cao Cao personally prayed for his life, and when he died Cao Cao mourned deeply. Jian'an 13 = **208 CE** [era tool]. So he was **13 years old** at death, in 208.

Two further points from the text:
- Cao Cao said to the grieving Cao Pi (Emperor Wen): 「此我之不幸，而汝曹之幸也。」[1] — "This is my misfortune, but your good fortune."
- Pei Songzhi's commentary quotes the *Weilüe*: Cao Pi used to say, 「家兄孝廉，自其分也。若使倉舒在，我亦無天下。」[3] — "That my elder brother was a filial and incorrupt candidate was his due; had Cangshu (Cao Chong) lived, I would not have possessed the empire." Pei also quotes Sun Sheng, who criticizes Cao Cao for having spoken of making Cao Chong heir, arguing that by the *Spring and Autumn* principle the heir is the eldest son, not the worthy one — and that Cao Chong should not have been made heir even had he lived [5].

Note on the commentary: the *Weishu* passage quoted by Pei Songzhi praises Cao Chong's appearance and kindheartedness; Pei Songzhi's own remark (裴松之按) is a stylistic criticism of how that passage was arranged, not a denial of the story [4].

Sources cited above are all from the biography of Cao Chong [1], its continuation on his posthumous enfeoffment [2], and the Pei commentary blocks [3][4][5].

q: Does the name Huang Yueying, as Zhuge Liang's wife, actually appear in the historical sources? Who was her father, and how do the sources describe her?
reply:
**Short answer: No — the name "Huang Yueying" (黄月英) does not appear anywhere in the *Sanguozhi* or Pei Songzhi's annotations. In fact, Zhuge Liang's wife is never given a name at all in these sources. What the sources do record is that her father was Huang Chengyan (黄承彦), a famous scholar of Miannan, and that she is described as ugly but talented.**

**The father**

The only passage on this is a Pei Songzhi annotation to the *Zhuge Liang* biography (Shu 5), quoting the *Xiangyang Ji* (《襄阳记》):

「黃承彥者，高爽開列，為沔南名士」[4] — "Huang Chengyan was lofty, frank and magnanimous, a famous scholar of Miannan."

**How the daughter is described**

The same annotation:

「聞君擇婦；身有醜女，黃頭黑色，而才堪相配。」[4] — "I hear you are choosing a wife; I have an ugly daughter — yellow hair, black skin — but her talent is a fit match for you."

「孔明許，即載送之。」[4] — "Kongming agreed; he at once loaded her up and sent her over."

「時人以為笑樂，鄉里為之諺曰：『莫作孔明擇婦，正得阿承醜女。』」[4] — "People of the time found it a joke, and the villagers made a proverb: 'Don't follow Kongming in choosing a wife — you'll end up with Ah Cheng's ugly daughter.'"

So per the *Sanguozhi* corpus, we get: her father's name (Huang Chengyan), his standing (a Miannan scholar), her physical description ("yellow hair, black skin"), her talent ("才堪相配"), that Zhuge Liang married her, and the villagers' mocking proverb. She is **never named**, no birth/death years, no account of her later life, and no record of her mother.

**On the "Yueying" name and the Cai family link**

These are not in the *Sanguozhi*. To be clear about what I could and could not confirm:

- I searched for the name "黄月英" and it returns nothing relevant in the corpus — the name simply does not occur.
- The commonly told story that her mother was a sister of Cai Mao (蔡瑁) or connected to Liu Biao's Cai wife is **not** something I found stated in the sources I searched; the *Sanguozhi* does not record her mother. (I am not asserting it is false — only that it is not in this corpus.)

以下不是《三国志》的记载: The name "Huang Yueying" (黄月英) is not found in the *Sanguozhi*; the wife of Zhuge Liang is left unnamed there, and the name, along with much of her later legendary biography, comes from later fiction and folk tradition (such as the *Sanguo Yanyi* and associated tales) rather than from Chen Shou's text or Pei Songzhi's annotations.

q: How did Zhang Song persuade Liu Zhang to invite Liu Bei into Yi Province? What reasons did he give?
reply:
## How Zhang Song persuaded Liu Zhang to invite Liu Bei

**Short answer:** Zhang Song gave Liu Zhang two related arguments. First, that Cao Cao was unstoppable and, if he used Zhang Lu's base to attack Shu, no one could defend it. Second, that Liu Bei (Liu Yuzhou) was both Liu Zhang's kinsman and Cao Cao's bitter enemy, skilled at war, so he should be sent against Zhang Lu — if Zhang Lu fell, Yi Province would be strong and Cao Cao could do nothing. In a later round of persuasion he added a third argument about internal danger: the province's own generals were arrogant and disloyal, so without Liu Bei, Yi Province would face enemies outside and rebellion inside.

### The reasons he gave

**Stage 1 — after Zhang Song's mission to Cao Cao.** Zhang Song had gone to see Cao Cao and was slighted; he came back resentful, slandered Cao Cao, and urged Liu Zhang to break with him. He then said:

- 「劉豫州，使君之肺腑，可與交通。」[2] — "Liu Yuzhou is your close kin; you can have dealings with him." Liu Zhang agreed and sent Fa Zheng to open relations with the Prior Lord.

**Stage 2 — the decisive argument, when Cao Cao threatened Hanzhong.** In the 16th year of Jian'an, Liu Zhang heard that Cao Cao was going to send Zhong Yao and others toward Hanzhong to attack Zhang Lu, and was frightened. Zhang Song then said:

- 「曹公兵強無敵於天下，若因張魯之資以取蜀土，誰能御之者乎？」[1] — Cao Cao's army is strong, unmatched in the world; if he uses Zhang Lu's resources to seize the soil of Shu, who can resist him?
- When Liu Zhang replied that he worried about this but had no plan, Zhang Song continued: 「劉豫州，使君之宗室而曹公之深讎也，善用兵，若使之討魯，魯必破。魯破，則益州強，曹公雖來，無能為也。」[1] — Liu Yuzhou is your imperial kinsman and Cao Cao's deep enemy, good at using troops; if you send him to attack Zhang Lu, Zhang Lu will surely be defeated. Once Zhang Lu is defeated, Yi Province will be strong, and even if Cao Cao comes he will be powerless.

**Stage 2 (parallel account) — the internal danger.** The Liu Zhang biography records the second persuasion with a different emphasis:

- 「今州中諸將龐羲、李異等皆恃功驕豪，欲有外意，不得豫州，則敵攻其外，民攻其內，必敗之道也。」[2] — The generals Pang Xi, Li Yi and others rely on their merit, are arrogant and overbearing, and have outside intentions; without Yuzhou, enemies will attack from outside and the people from within — that is the road to certain defeat.

The Fa Zheng biography confirms the sequence and the underlying motive: Zhang Song and Fa Zheng were friends who judged Liu Zhang incapable of great things and "常竊嘆息" (constantly sighed in private), and it was "後因璋聞曹公欲遣將征張魯之有懼心也，松遂說璋宜迎先主，使之討魯" [4] — later, exploiting Liu Zhang's fear at hearing Cao Cao wanted to send a general to attack Zhang Lu, Zhang Song persuaded him it was proper to welcome the Prior Lord and have him attack Zhang Lu.

### Result

Liu Zhang was convinced: 「璋然之，遣法正將四千人迎先主，前後賂遺以巨億計」[1]. Opposition was overruled — Huang Quan laid out the pros and cons, and Wang Lei "自倒縣於州門以諫," but "璋一無所納" [2]. In a Pei note, Liu Ba also warned: 「備，雄人也，入必為害，不可內也」and later 「若使備討張魯，是放虎於山林也」— but "璋不聽" (Pei note citing《零陵先賢傳》)[7]. Liu Zhang went to meet Liu Bei at Fu; the year is given as 建安十六年 [2], i.e. 211 CE.

### A relevant detail on why Zhang Song acted as he did

The Pei notes fill in Zhang Song's resentment: Cao Cao slighted him when he came as envoy. 「曹公時已定荊州，走先主，不復存錄松，松以此怨」[2]; Pei note citing《漢書春秋》: 「張松見曹公，曹公方自矜伐，不存錄松。松歸，乃勸璋自絕」[13]; and Pei note citing《益部耆舊雜記》describes Zhang Song as short in stature, unrestrained in conduct, but "識達精果，有才幹," and that Cao Cao's Registrar Yang Xiu admired him greatly and recommended summoning him, but Cao Cao refused [17].

### Inference

Drawing these facts together: Zhang Song's three arguments map onto three distinct fears of Liu Zhang — an external threat (Cao Cao through Zhang Lu), a military solution requiring a capable general who was also politically safe (a kinsman and Cao Cao's enemy, i.e. Liu Bei), and an internal threat (unreliable provincial generals). Since Zhang Song and Fa Zheng had already privately decided Liu Zhang was "不足與有為" [4] and aimed to install Liu Bei, the persuasion was designed to use Liu Zhang's fear to bring in the man who would later take his province — which is exactly what followed, with Zhang Song subsequently executed for the plot [3].

q: Who was Himiko (Beimihu), and what dealings did she have with Cao-Wei?
reply:
## Who Himiko was, and her dealings with Cao-Wei

**Who she was (per the *Wei zhi*, "Account of the Wa people"):**

Himiko (卑彌呼) was the shaman-queen of the Wa (倭) people, ruling from the state the text calls Yamatai (邪馬壹國, "the queen's capital"). The *Sanguozhi* says the Wa had originally been ruled by men, but after some seventy or eighty years the country fell into chaos and years of mutual warfare, so the people jointly raised a woman as king:

> 「其國本亦以男子爲王，住七八十年，倭國亂，相攻伐歷年，乃共立一女子爲王，名曰卑彌呼，事鬼道，能惑衆。」[2]

*(Their country had originally been ruled by men; after seventy or eighty years Wa fell into disorder and fought for years, so together they set up a woman as king, named Himiko, who practiced the way of spirits and could bewitch the people.)*

She was already advanced in years, unmarried, and had a younger brother who helped govern. She rarely appeared in public, was served by a thousand maids, and had only one man to bring her food and relay messages [2]. Her capital was Yamatai, reached from the commandery by about 12,000 *li*; south of her realm was the male-ruled Kuna state (狗奴國), which did not submit to her [5]. (Note: in the text the name of her capital is written 邪馬壹國; the spelling "Yamatai/邪馬台" is not the form used in the *Sanguozhi*.)

**Her dealings with Cao-Wei — the embassies:**

1. **Jingchu 2 (238), the first embassy.** The Wa queen sent the grandee Nanshengmi (難升米) and others to the commandery, asking to go to the emperor to present tribute; the administrator Liu Xia (劉夏) had them escorted to the capital. In the 12th month the throne issued a rescript:

> 「制詔親魏倭王卑彌呼……今以汝爲親魏倭王，假金印紫綬，裝封付帶方太守，假授汝。」[3]

*(Rescript to Himiko, "Wa King Friendly to Wei": … now We make you Wa King Friendly to Wei, granting a gold seal and purple cord, sealed and given to the Daifang administrator to confer on you.)*

The rescript also made Nanshengmi a Shuaishan zhonglangjiang (率善中郎將) and the secondary envoy Dushi Niuli (都市牛利) a Shuaishan xiaowei (率善校尉), and sent back large gifts: brocades, woolens, silks, 8 *jin* of gold, two five-foot swords, a hundred bronze mirrors, pearls and lead-vermilion, etc. [3]

2. **Zhengshi 1 (240).** The Daifang administrator Gong Zun (弓遵) sent the Jianzhong xiaowei Ti Jun (梯儁) with an imperial rescript and seal-cords to Wa, invested the Wa king, and brought gifts of gold, silk, woolens, swords, mirrors and colored goods; the Wa king in turn sent up a memorial thanking the throne [1].

3. **Zhengshi 4 (243).** The Wa king again sent envoys — the grandees Yishengqi (伊聲耆), Yexieju (掖邪拘) and eight others — presenting slaves, Wa brocade, silks, cotton clothes, cloth, cinnabar-wood and short bows and arrows; Yexiegou and the others were all given the seal and cord of Shuaishan zhonglangjiang [1]. The same embassy is recorded in the annals of the Qi Prince (Cao Fang):

> 「冬十二月，倭國女王俾彌呼遣使奉獻。」[6]

4. **Zhengshi 6 (245).** An imperial rescript granted the Wa man Nanshengmi a yellow banner (黄幢), to be conferred through the commandery [1].

5. **Zhengshi 8 (247).** The new administrator Wang Qi (王頎) arrived. Himiko, long on bad terms with the male king of Kuna, Bimigonghu (卑彌弓呼), sent envoys to the commandery to describe their mutual attacks; the court sent the Saicao yuan official Zhang Zheng (張政) and others with a rescript and yellow banner to invest Nanshengmi and issue a proclamation to admonish them. Then:

> 「卑彌呼以死，大作冢，徑百餘步，徇葬者奴婢百餘人。」[1]

*(Himiko died; a great tomb was made for her, over a hundred paces across, with more than a hundred male and female slaves buried with her.)*

A male king was set up in her place, but the country refused to submit and killed each other until over a thousand had died; finally Himiko's kinswoman Iyo (壹與), aged thirteen, was made king and the country settled. Zhang Zheng admonished Iyo by proclamation, and Iyo sent the Wa grandee Yexiegou and twenty men to escort Zhang Zheng back and to go to the capital, presenting thirty male and female slaves, five thousand strings of white pearls, two large blue-green "ju" pearls, and twenty bolts of patterned brocade [1].

**Summary:** In the *Sanguozhi*, Himiko appears as the shaman-queen of Wa/Yamatai who ended a period of civil war; under Wei she received the title "Wa King Friendly to Wei" (親魏倭王) with a gold seal and purple cord in Jingchu 2 (238), exchanged embassies with Wei (via the Daifang commandery) in 238, 240, 243, 245 and 247, and died around Zhengshi 8 (247), being succeeded briefly by a male king and then by her kinswoman Iyo.

**A note on the title:** The *Sanguozhi* consistently writes the queen's name as 卑彌呼 ("Himiko") and calls her 倭女王 ("Wa queen"); the form "Beimihu" is just a reading of the same characters. The account is the "Account of the Wa people" in the *Wei zhi*, Book 30, and the material from the *Weilüe* cited in Pei Songzhi's commentary in the same section concerns the Xirong and Daqin, not Wa, so it is not a source for Himiko.

q: What was the background of Liu Pei's Empress Wu? Who was her elder brother, and what became of her in the end?
reply:
## Conclusion

Liu Bei's empress — called **Empress Mu (穆皇后)** in the *Sanguozhi* — was a native of Chenliu (陳留). Her **elder brother was Wu Yi (吳壹), styled Ziyuan (子遠)**, who became one of Shu's senior generals. She herself died in **Yanxi 8 (AD 245)** and was buried together with Liu Bei at Hui Ling (惠陵).

## Background

Her family came to Shu because of her brother's father: 「先主穆皇后，陳留人也。兄吳壹，少孤，壹父素與劉焉有舊，是以舉家隨焉入蜀」[1] — she was from Chenliu; her elder brother Wu Yi lost his father young, and because Wu Yi's father had long been an old friend of Liu Yan, the whole family followed Liu Yan into Shu.

Her first marriage was to Liu Yan's son: 「焉有異志，而聞善相者相后當大貴。焉時將子瑁自隨，遂為瑁納后。瑁死，后寡居」[1] — Liu Yan had disloyal ambitions, and having heard a physiognomist say she would one day be greatly honored, married her to his son Liu Mao (劉瑁), whom he had with him; after Liu Mao died she lived as a widow.

Her marriage to Liu Bei: 「先主既定益州，而孫夫人還吳，群下勸先主聘后，先主疑與瑁同族，法正進曰：『論其親疏，何與晉文之於子圉乎？』於是納后為夫人」[1] — after Liu Bei had settled Yi province and Lady Sun had returned to Wu, his subordinates urged him to take her; Liu Bei hesitated, thinking she was of the same clan as Liu Mao, and Fa Zheng persuaded him by comparing the case to Duke Wen of Jin and Zi Yu.

Titles: in **Jian'an 24 (AD 219)** she was made Queen of Hanzhong: 「建安二十四年，立為漢中王后」[1]. In the fifth month of summer of **Zhangwu 1 (AD 221)** she was made Empress by a formal proclamation: 「今以后為皇后，遣使持節丞相亮授璽綬，承宗廟，母天下」[1]. In the fifth month of **Jianxing 1 (AD 223)**, when the Later Ruler took the throne, 「尊后為皇太后，稱長樂宮」[1] — she was honored as Empress Dowager, her palace called Changle.

Her end: 「延熙八年，后薨，合葬惠陵」[1] — she died in Yanxi 8 (AD 245) and was buried together at Hui Ling.

## Her elder brother Wu Yi

Wu Yi already appears among the men Liu Bei employed after taking Shu: 「吳壹、費觀等又璋之婚親也……皆處之顯任，盡其器能」[20]. The *Jihàn Fuchen Zan* gives his career in full:

- Under Liu Zhang he was a General of the Household who resisted Liu Bei: 「劉璋時，為中郎將，將兵拒先主於涪，詣降」[14].
- After Liu Bei settled Yi province: 「以壹為護軍討逆將軍，納壹妹為夫人」[14] — made Protector of the Army and General Who Repels Rebels, and married Wu Yi's younger sister (i.e., the future empress).
- **Zhangwu 1 (AD 221)**: 「為關中都督」[14].
- **Jianxing 8 (AD 230)**: with Wei Yan he entered Nan'an and defeated the Wei general Fei Yao; he was moved to Marquis of a Pavilion, then promoted to Marquis of Gaoyang Township and General of the Left [14].
- **Jianxing 12 (AD 234)**, after Zhuge Liang's death: 「以壹督漢中，車騎將軍，假節，領雍州刺史，進封濟陽侯」[14] — he supervised Hanzhong as General of Chariots and Cavalry with credentials, concurrently Inspector of Yongzhou, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiyang.
- **Jianxing 15 (AD 237)**: 「十五年卒。失其行事，故不為傳」[14] — he died; because his administrative record was lost, no separate biography was made for him.

The empress's own biography matches this: 「壹官至車騎將軍，封縣侯」[1]. A clan-brother, Wu Ban (吳班), styled Yuanxiong, son of Wu Kuang who had been an officer under the Grand General He Jin, was also a Shu general who rose to General of Chariots and Cavalry and Marquis of Mianzhu [17].

## Note on the surname

The empress is entered in the *Sanguozhi* as 「先主穆皇后」, while her elder brother is 「吳壹」 — the text records the brother's surname as Wu but styles her "Empress Mu," so I give both as the source has them. The empress's own brother is thus Wu Yi (吳壹, 子遠); his grandson Wu Qiao (吳喬), according to Sun Sheng's *Shu Shipu* cited in Pei's commentary, 「沒李雄中三十年，不為雄屈也」 — was stranded among Li Xiong's people for thirty years without submitting to him [13].

## 以下不是《三国志》的记载:

The empress is commonly known as "Empress Wu" (吳氏); the *Sanguozhi* text itself titles her 「先主穆皇后」 while naming her brother 「吳壹」, and does not state her personal name.

q: How was Cao Jie related to Cao Cao? Which members of his household do the historical sources record?
reply:
**Short answer: the sources contain two different people named Cao Jie (曹節), and they stand in opposite relations to Cao Cao.**

1. **Cao Jie 曹節, father of Cao Teng — Cao Cao's paternal great‑grandfather.**
2. **Cao Jie 曹節, one of Cao Cao's daughters — she became the Han Emperor Xian's consort and was posthumously titled Empress Xianmu (獻穆皇后).**

---

**1. The elder Cao Jie (great‑grandfather)**

Pei Songzhi's note to the *Wudi ji*, quoting Sima Biao's *Xu Han shu*, gives his style and character: 「騰父節，字元偉，素以仁厚稱。」[1] — "Teng's father Jie, courtesy name Yuanwei, was known for his kindness and generosity." The same note records his household, i.e. his sons:

「長子伯興，次子仲興，次子叔興。騰字季興，少除黃門從官。」[1]

So the *Xu Han shu* lists four sons — Bo Xing, Zhong Xing, Shu Xing, and Teng (courtesy name Ji Xing). The genealogy runs Cao Jie → Cao Teng → Cao Song → Cao Cao: the *Wudi ji* main text says 「桓帝世，曹騰爲中常侍大長秋，封費亭侯。養子嵩嗣，官至太尉……嵩生太祖。」[3] — under Emperor Huan, Cao Teng was Regular Attendant and Grand Prolonger of Autumn, enfeoffed as Marquis of Fei Village; his **adopted son** Cao Song inherited, rose to Grand Commandant, and Cao Song begot Taizu (Cao Cao). Note that Cao Song is explicitly called an 養子 (adopted son), and the text adds 「莫能審其生出本末」[3] — no one could ascertain his true origins.

*Inference:* since Cao Jie was Cao Teng's father, Cao Teng the adoptive father of Cao Song, and Cao Song the father of Cao Cao, Cao Jie was Cao Cao's paternal great‑grandfather. (The link through Cao Song is by adoption, not blood.)

**2. Cao Jie the daughter (Empress Xianmu)**

The *Wudi ji* records that in the 7th month of a certain year, 「天子娉公三女爲貴人，少者待年於國。」[36] — the Emperor (Xian) took three of the Duke's daughters as 貴人 (Honoured Ladies), the youngest remaining in Wei until of age. Pei's note quoting the *Xiandi qiju zhu* adds the betrothal mission: 「使使持節行太常大司農安陽亭侯王邑，齎璧、帛、玄纁、絹五萬匹之鄴納娉」[41] — Wang Yi was sent with jade, silk and 50,000 bolts of cloth to Ye to deliver the betrothal gifts. The *Xun Yu* passage in Pei's note also has Cao Cao say 「今朝廷有伏后，吾女何得以配上」[14] — "the court now has Empress Fu, how can my daughter be given in marriage to the Emperor?" (The Fu empress was later deposed and died: 「后廢黜死，兄弟皆伏法」[13], and per the *Cao Man zhuan* she was dragged out of hiding and killed [12].)

Cao Jie's own end is recorded in the annals of the Prince of Chenliu: 「己未，故漢獻帝夫人節薨，帝臨于華林園，使使持節追謚夫人為獻穆皇后。及葬，車服制度皆如漢氏故事。」[21] — on the jiwei day, Lady Jie, former consort of Han Emperor Xian, died; the Wei emperor came to Hualin Park, sent a bearer of credentials to posthumously title her Empress Xianmu, and her funeral was conducted according to Han precedent.

*Household record for this Cao Jie:* the *Sanguozhi* records that she was one of **three daughters** of Cao Cao sent to Emperor Xian [36], that she was Emperor Xian's 夫人 [21], and that her father was Cao Cao (called 公 / 太祖 throughout). The *Sanguozhi* does **not** give the personal names of the other two daughters in the passages retrieved; only Cao Jie's own name (節) appears.

---

**Points to be careful about**

- There is no statement in the retrieved material that Cao Jie the daughter and Cao Jie the great‑grandfather were the same person — they are two distinct individuals sharing a name, generations apart.
- The *Sanguozhi* does not record the names of Cao Cao's other two daughters given to Emperor Xian, nor any children of Cao Jie.

**以下不是《三国志》的记载:** The names often given for Cao Cao's three daughters (Cao Xian 曹憲 and Cao Hua 曹華 alongside Cao Jie) come from other, non‑*Sanguozhi* sources; the *Sanguozhi* text retrieved here names only Cao Jie. Also, "Cao Jie" is a name shared by more than one figure in Han‑Wei history, so the identification depends on which Cao Jie the question means.
